ELA.overview: Each day combines reading, discussion, writing and a short word-study or grammar focus; read most texts aloud together, then have the child reread independently. Always ask the child to point to the words in the text that support an answer, and keep every draft in a writing folder so growth is visible in the week 36 portfolio. Preview novels (especially Island of the Blue Dolphins, which includes deaths, and some Just So Stories with dated racial language) before reading them with your child.

weeks.prep: Download Just So Stories (Kipling) from Project Gutenberg and preview 'How the Whale Got His Throat' and 'How the Camel Got His Hump' (read aloud — Kipling's playful language and 'O Best Beloved' asides are meant to be heard). Choose a 200-250 word grade 4 passage for the fluency read, a timer, a reader's notebook and a library book. Note: some Just So stories use dated or racially insensitive language (notably 'How the Leopard Got His Spots'); preview and plan to discuss or skip those lines.
misconceptions: Confusing the problem with the solution in a story map. The problem is what goes wrong or what a character wants; the solution is how it is fixed.
Answering 'from the text' questions from memory or opinion. Teach the habit: point to the sentence, then answer.

days.guide: Have the child complete an interest survey and choose a library book they can read with few errors. For the fluency read, the child reads a grade 4 passage aloud for 1 minute while you mark errors; record words correct per minute (WCPM) as the baseline (spring benchmark for grade 4 is roughly 120-140 WCPM).

questions.q: How do you compute words correct per minute?
questions.a: Count all words read in 1 minute and subtract the errors.

days.guide: Read 'How the Whale Got His Throat' aloud, pausing to let the child predict. Together fill in the story map: characters, setting, problem, events, solution.

questions.q: What is the Whale's problem at the start, and who causes it?
questions.a: The Whale has eaten almost all the fish in the sea; the small 'Stute Fish tricks him into swallowing a man (the Mariner).

questions.q: How does the Mariner solve his problem?
questions.a: He jumps and dances inside the Whale until it gets hiccups and lets him out, and he leaves a grating (from his raft, tied with his suspenders) in the Whale's throat so it can only eat small fish.

days.guide: Reread 'How the Camel Got His Hump.' Model one answer: state the answer, then quote or point to a detail. The child answers 4 questions the same way.

questions.q: What does the Camel say whenever the other animals ask him to work? What does it show?
questions.a: He only says 'Humph!' — it shows he is lazy and rude.

questions.q: How does the Camel get his hump?
questions.a: The Djinn of All Deserts magics his 'humph' into a hump on his back so he can work three days without eating, as punishment for his idleness.

days.guide: Model drawing a heart map with important people, places and memories. The child draws one, chooses a memory, and quick-writes for 10 minutes without stopping.

questions.q: What makes a good memory for a personal narrative?
questions.a: A small, specific moment the writer remembers clearly and has feelings about (e.g., the first time I jumped off the diving board), not a whole vacation.

days.guide: Discuss both stories using stems like 'I agree because...' and 'In the text it says...'. Then give a short check: name the character, setting, problem and solution of one story.

questions.q: Name the setting of 'How the Camel Got His Hump.'
questions.a: The middle of a Howling Desert at the beginning of the world.

weeks.assessment_key: Story map: proficient = names the Whale, the 'Stute Fish and the Mariner; setting the sea; problem (Whale ate all the fishes / Mariner swallowed); solution (Mariner makes Whale let him out and blocks his throat with a grating). Cited answers: 3 points each — correct answer + supporting detail (e.g., 'Humph!'; the Djinn gives him a hump to work three days without food). Fluency baseline: record WCPM and accuracy (aim for 95%+ accuracy); no grade, used for comparison in week 35.

weeks.prep: Just So Stories ('The Elephant's Child'), writer's notebook. Write 20 prefix words (unhappy, unlock, unfair, unkind, untie, retell, rewrite, reread, rebuild, return, replay, disagree, disappear, dislike, dishonest, disobey, disconnect, unwrap, reheat, discover) and 12 sentences (half fragments/run-ons) for Day 4.
misconceptions: Thinking a run-on is just a long sentence. A run-on joins two complete thoughts without correct punctuation; fix with a period, or a comma plus and/but/so.
Assuming every word starting with re- or dis- has the prefix (read, dish). Test it: remove the prefix and see if a real base word remains.

days.guide: Read 'The Elephant's Child' aloud. The child charts traits (curious, persistent, brave) with evidence from his words and actions.

questions.q: What is the Elephant's Child's main trait? Give evidence.
questions.a: He is extremely curious ('full of 'satiable curtiosity') — he keeps asking questions, like what the Crocodile has for dinner, even when he is spanked for asking.

questions.q: How does the Elephant's Child get his trunk?
questions.a: The Crocodile grabs his nose at the Limpopo River and pulls; the Elephant's Child pulls back (helped by the Bi-Coloured-Python-Rock-Snake) and his nose is stretched into a trunk.

days.guide: Teach un- = not/opposite, re- = again/back, dis- = not/opposite. The child sorts the 20 words, defines each using the prefix, and writes 5 sentences.

questions.q: What does 'disobey' mean?
questions.a: To not obey.

questions.q: What does 'rebuild' mean?
questions.a: To build again.

days.guide: Model a story mountain: beginning (setting, characters), rising events, high point (most exciting/emotional moment), ending. The child plans one small moment from the heart map.

questions.q: Where on the story mountain does the most exciting moment go?
questions.a: At the top — the high point (climax).

days.guide: Model fixing a fragment (add a subject or verb) and a run-on (split or join with comma + conjunction). The child fixes 12 items and checks their own first sentences.

questions.q: Fix: 'Ran to the park after lunch.'
questions.a: Add a subject: 'We ran to the park after lunch.'

questions.q: Fix: 'I was tired I went to bed.'
questions.a: 'I was tired, so I went to bed.' or 'I was tired. I went to bed.'

days.guide: The child drafts an opening scene with a hook (action, dialogue, sound or question) and reads it aloud. Give the prefix/sentence quiz.

questions.q: Name two ways to hook a reader.
questions.a: Start with action, dialogue, a sound effect, or a question.

weeks.assessment_key: Character chart: proficient lists at least 3 traits each with a quote or action (curious — asks everyone questions; persistent — keeps asking despite spankings; brave — goes alone to the Limpopo). Quiz key (sample): un- 'not': unkind = not kind; re- 'again': retell = tell again; dis- 'not/opposite': disagree = not agree; dislike = not like; reread = read again. Sentence types: 'Under the table.' = fragment; 'The dog barked it ran away.' = run-on (fix: The dog barked, and it ran away.); 'My sister laughed.' = complete. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: Just So Stories ('How the Leopard Got His Spots' — preview first: it contains a racial term and dated depictions; you may read a selected passage or discuss why such language is hurtful), highlighters, the narrative draft, the independent reading book and a timer.
misconceptions: Placing end punctuation outside quotation marks ("Let's go". ). The comma, period, question mark or exclamation point goes inside the closing quotation marks.
Starting dialogue for each new speaker on the same line. Start a new paragraph when the speaker changes.

days.guide: Reread a selected section of 'How the Leopard Got His Spots' and highlight dialogue in one color and description in another. Discuss how Kipling shows feelings through what characters say.

questions.q: Why did the Giraffe and Zebra become hard to see?
questions.a: They moved into the forest, where the shade and sunlight made them blotchy and stripy, so they blended into the shadows.

questions.q: How does the Leopard get his spots?
questions.a: The Ethiopian presses his fingertips all over the Leopard's coat, leaving spots so he can hide in the forest.

days.guide: Model time-order transitions (first, next, after that, suddenly, later, finally). The child drafts the middle events and underlines at least two transitions.

questions.q: Give three time-order transition words.
questions.a: First, next, later (also: then, after that, suddenly, finally).

days.guide: Model the rules: quotation marks around spoken words, comma before the closing mark when the tag follows, capital letter to start the quote. The child punctuates 10 sentences and adds 3 lines of dialogue to the draft.

questions.q: Punctuate: we're late said Mom
questions.a: "We're late," said Mom.

questions.q: Punctuate: Sam asked where is my hat
questions.a: Sam asked, "Where is my hat?"

days.guide: Show 'I was scared' vs 'My hands shook and my heart thumped.' The child rewrites 4 telling sentences and revises one paragraph with sensory details.

questions.q: Rewrite 'It was cold' as a showing sentence.
questions.a: Example: 'Wind bit my cheeks, and I could see my breath puffing like smoke.'

days.guide: The child drafts the ending (how the moment resolved and how they felt or what they learned). Then do a timed 1-minute read from the independent book and record WCPM.

questions.q: What should a narrative ending do?
questions.a: Wrap up the moment and show the writer's feelings or what they learned, rather than just 'The end.'

weeks.assessment_key: Complete draft rubric (4-point): 4 = clear beginning-middle-end focused on one moment, at least two time-order transitions, 3+ lines of correctly punctuated dialogue, sensory details, an ending that reflects; 3 = all parts present with minor punctuation errors; 2 = sequence unclear or dialogue missing; 1 = incomplete draft.

weeks.prep: Just So Stories ('The Cat That Walked by Himself' and 'How the Rhinoceros Got His Skin' for the reading check), editing checklist, computer and printer. Prepare a 5-question reading check on the Rhinoceros story (key below).
misconceptions: Stating a topic instead of a theme ('independence'). A theme is a full sentence lesson: 'Being independent can mean being lonely, but it lets you live by your own rules.'
Including small details or opinions in a summary. A summary tells only the most important events in order, in the reader's own words.

days.guide: Read 'The Cat That Walked by Himself.' Help the child find a theme and two supporting details, then write a 5-sentence summary.

questions.q: What bargain does the Cat make with the Woman?
questions.a: If she ever says one word in his praise he may come into the Cave; with a second, sit by the fire; with a third, drink the warm white milk. He earns all three by amusing the Baby and catching a mouse.

questions.q: State a theme with evidence.
questions.a: Example: Independence has a cost — the Cat keeps his freedom ('all places are alike to me'), but Man and Dog never make a bargain with him, so they chase him and throw things at him.

days.guide: The child rereads the narrative with the checklist (strong lead, clear sequence, dialogue, satisfying ending) and makes at least 3 revisions in colored pencil.

questions.q: What makes a strong lead?
questions.a: It grabs the reader immediately — action, dialogue, a sound or a question — instead of 'One day I...'

days.guide: Conference: the child reads aloud while you both look for capitals, commas, quotation marks and spelling; the child makes the corrections.

questions.q: Correct: "can we go to the beach" asked lily.
questions.a: "Can we go to the beach?" asked Lily.

days.guide: The child types the final narrative (at least one page) with a title, then proofreads once aloud.

questions.q: Why read your final copy aloud?
questions.a: You hear missing words and awkward sentences that eyes skip over.

days.guide: The child reads the narrative to family. Then give the reading check on 'How the Rhinoceros Got His Skin.'

questions.q: In 'How the Rhinoceros Got His Skin,' why does the Parsee put cake crumbs in the Rhinoceros's skin?
questions.a: To get revenge because the Rhinoceros ate his cake; the crumbs make the skin itch so badly the Rhino rubs it into folds.

weeks.assessment_key: Narrative rubric (4 levels): 4 = engaging lead, events in clear order with transitions, dialogue and sensory detail, reflective ending, few errors; 3 = all elements present, some errors; 2 = missing two elements or many errors; 1 = incomplete. Reading check key ('How the Rhinoceros Got His Skin'): 1) Setting: an uninhabited island on the Red Sea. 2) The Rhinoceros upsets the Parsee's stove and eats his cake. 3) Revenge: when the Rhino takes off his skin to bathe, the Parsee fills it with cake crumbs (and burnt currants). 4) Result: the Rhino rubs until the skin folds and the buttons come off, giving him folds and a bad temper. 5) It is a 'how' (origin) story explaining a feature of an animal. Proficient: 4/5.

weeks.prep: Aesop's Fables (Gutenberg). Choose 6 fables: The Ant and the Grasshopper, The Fox and the Grapes, The Tortoise and the Hare, The Boy Who Cried Wolf, The Lion and the Mouse, The Milkmaid and Her Pail. Write 12 adage cards with meanings.
misconceptions: Restating what happened instead of the moral. The moral is a lesson for people, e.g., 'Slow and steady wins the race.'
Not noticing that suffixes change part of speech: hope (noun/verb) → hopeful (adjective) → hopefulness (noun).

days.guide: Read the six fables aloud with the child. After each, the child states the moral in their own words.

questions.q: What is the moral of 'The Fox and the Grapes'?
questions.a: People sometimes pretend they don't want what they can't have ('sour grapes').

questions.q: What is the moral of 'The Lion and the Mouse'?
questions.a: Even small or weak friends can help; kindness is rewarded.

days.guide: Explain that adages and proverbs are short sayings with a lesson. The child matches 12 adages to meanings and fables.

questions.q: What does 'Don't count your chickens before they hatch' mean, and which fable fits?
questions.a: Don't plan on something before it happens — 'The Milkmaid and Her Pail.'

questions.q: Which fable matches 'Slow and steady wins the race'?
questions.a: 'The Tortoise and the Hare.'

days.guide: Teach -ful (full of), -less (without), -ness (state of). The child builds 15 words and labels the part of speech.

questions.q: What does 'fearless' mean and what part of speech is it?
questions.a: Without fear; adjective.

questions.q: Change 'kind' into a noun using a suffix.
questions.a: Kindness.

days.guide: Discuss: Did the grasshopper deserve help? The child must cite what the grasshopper and ants said or did.

questions.q: What did the grasshopper do all summer, according to the fable?
questions.a: He sang (played) instead of storing food, while the ants worked to gather food for winter.

days.guide: The child writes a 1-paragraph original fable with animal characters and a stated moral; give the suffix quiz.

questions.q: What are the parts of a fable?
questions.a: A short story, usually with animal characters who act like people, and a moral (lesson) at the end.

weeks.assessment_key: Original fable rubric: 4 = animal characters with human traits, a clear problem and outcome, and a moral that follows from the events; 3 = moral present but weakly connected; 2 = story without clear moral; 1 = incomplete. Suffix quiz key (sample): hopeful = full of hope (adj.); careless = without care (adj.); darkness = state of being dark (noun); thankful = full of thanks (adj.); helpless = without help (adj.); sadness = state of being sad (noun). Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: A Wonder-Book for Girls and Boys (Hawthorne, Gutenberg) — 'The Golden Touch' and 'The Paradise of Children' — or D'Aulaires' Book of Greek Myths. Paper for a 5-box comic, index cards for allusions and roots.
misconceptions: Using an allusion literally ('My dad has a Midas touch' means he turns things to gold). Allusions borrow the meaning: everything he tries succeeds or makes money.
Mixing up roots: tele = far, photo = light, graph = write, micro = small, scope = see/look at.

days.guide: Read 'The Golden Touch' (King Midas). The child summarizes in a 5-box comic: wish, joy, problem, loss, solution.

questions.q: Why does Midas come to regret his wish?
questions.a: His food turns to gold so he can't eat, and when he hugs his daughter Marygold she turns into a gold statue.

questions.q: How is the golden touch undone?
questions.a: The stranger tells him to bathe in a river and sprinkle its water on anything he wants changed back; Marygold is restored.

days.guide: Read 'The Paradise of Children.' Discuss what Pandora's curiosity releases and what remains.

questions.q: What comes out of the box, and what is left?
questions.a: Troubles (cares, sorrows, sickness) fly out into the world; Hope remains to comfort people.

questions.q: State a theme.
questions.a: Example: Curiosity can cause trouble, but hope helps people endure hardship.

days.guide: Explain each allusion with its source story. The child explains 8 and uses 4 in sentences.

questions.q: What does 'Achilles' heel' mean?
questions.a: A weak spot — Achilles could only be wounded in his heel.

questions.q: What is a 'Herculean' task?
questions.a: A task needing enormous strength or effort, like the labors of Hercules.

days.guide: Teach the five Greek roots and build words together. The child builds 12 words and defines them.

questions.q: What does 'telescope' literally mean?
questions.a: 'Far' + 'see': a tool to see far away.

questions.q: Use the roots to define 'micrograph.'
questions.a: A picture (writing/recording) of something very small, made through a microscope.

days.guide: Give the quiz, then do a 1-minute fluency read of a myth passage and record WCPM.

questions.q: What does 'opening Pandora's box' mean?
questions.a: Starting something that causes many unexpected problems.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Allusions — 1) Midas touch: everything one does succeeds/makes money 2) Pandora's box: a source of many troubles 3) Achilles' heel: a weakness 4) Herculean: needing great strength/effort. Roots — 5) tele = far 6) photo = light 7) graph = write/draw 8) micro = small 9) scope = see 10) photograph = picture made with light; telephone = sound from far; microscope = tool to see small things. Proficient: 8/10.

weeks.prep: A library collection of California Native Coyote stories (e.g., a version of how Coyote stole/brought fire), an Anansi tale (e.g., 'Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom' or 'How Anansi Got the Stories'), Venn diagram. Read both stories beforehand so you can answer from your version.
misconceptions: Treating all trickster tales as the same story. Compare details: the tricks, who is fooled, and the lesson differ.
Changing events when rewriting in first person. Point of view changes what the narrator knows and feels, not what happens.

days.guide: Read the Coyote story aloud. Identify the trickster pattern: a clever (often greedy or foolish) character uses tricks, which may help others or backfire.

questions.q: What makes Coyote a trickster?
questions.a: He uses cleverness and deception rather than strength to get what he wants; in fire stories he steals fire from those who keep it and brings it to people (answers should cite your version).

days.guide: Read the Anansi tale. The child records the sequence of events and the theme.

questions.q: Who is Anansi and where do his stories come from?
questions.a: A spider trickster from West African (Akan/Ashanti) folklore.

questions.q: State the theme of the tale you read with a detail.
questions.a: Answers depend on the version; e.g., in 'Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom,' no one person can hold all the wisdom — his small son shows him how to climb the tree, and the wisdom spills out to everyone.

days.guide: Complete a Venn diagram: both tricksters' traits, tricks, outcomes, lessons. Ask what is similar across cultures and why.

questions.q: Name one way the two tricksters are alike.
questions.a: Both are animals who act like people and use clever tricks; both stories often explain how something came to be or teach a lesson.

days.guide: The child rewrites a short scene in first person as Coyote ('I crept toward the fire...'). Discuss what we now learn (his thoughts) and lose (others' views).

questions.q: What changes when the story is told by Coyote in first person?
questions.a: We hear Coyote's thoughts and feelings using 'I,' but we only know what he knows; the narrator can't see inside other characters.

days.guide: The child writes a compare/contrast paragraph with a topic sentence, two similarities, two differences and details from each tale.

questions.q: What words signal comparison and contrast?
questions.a: Comparison: both, similarly, also. Contrast: however, but, unlike, on the other hand.

weeks.assessment_key: Compare/contrast paragraph rubric: 4 = clear topic sentence naming both tales, at least two similarities and two differences in theme or pattern of events, a specific detail from each story, transition words, concluding sentence; 3 = mostly complete but details general; 2 = only similarities or only differences; 1 = summary of one story only.

weeks.prep: Writer's notebook, computer. Show photos of Golden Gate fog and Half Dome. Prepare 12 sentence-combining items with relative pronouns. Unit 2 test for Day 5 (key below).
misconceptions: Using 'which' for people ('the girl which...'). Use who for people, which for things, that for either, whose for ownership.
Writing a myth without explaining the phenomenon. The ending must clearly show how the natural feature came to be.

days.guide: Review features of myths (gods/heroes, explains nature). The child picks a California phenomenon and plans hero, problem, events and explanation.

questions.q: What is an origin myth?
questions.a: A traditional-style story that explains how something in nature or a custom came to be.

days.guide: Model combining: 'I met a girl. She surfs.' → 'I met a girl who surfs.' The child combines 12 pairs.

questions.q: Combine: 'This is the trail. We hiked it yesterday.'
questions.a: 'This is the trail that (which) we hiked yesterday.'

questions.q: Combine: 'That is the boy. His dog ran away.'
questions.a: 'That is the boy whose dog ran away.'

days.guide: The child drafts the myth with a hero, problem and explanation of the phenomenon.

questions.q: What must the ending of your myth include?
questions.a: How the hero's actions caused the natural feature (e.g., why fog creeps over the Golden Gate each afternoon).

days.guide: The child revises to add at least two relative clauses and edits with the checklist.

questions.q: Underline the relative clause: 'The giant, who loved the sea, breathed fog over the bay.'
questions.a: 'who loved the sea'

days.guide: The child tells the myth aloud as a storyteller (eye contact, expression). Give the Unit 2 test.

questions.q: What is the moral of 'The Ant and the Grasshopper'?
questions.a: Prepare today for the needs of tomorrow; hard work pays off.

weeks.assessment_key: Myth rubric: 4 = hero, clear problem, events that build, explanation of the phenomenon, two relative clauses used correctly, storytelling with expression; 3 = all parts, minor errors; 2 = explanation unclear; 1 = incomplete. Unit 2 test key: 1) Theme of 'The Golden Touch': greed can cost what matters most (love/family) 2) Pandora's box = source of troubles 3) Herculean = requiring great strength 4) Midas touch = success at making money 5) Moral of 'The Tortoise and the Hare': slow and steady wins the race 6) Compare Coyote and Anansi: both are tricksters who use cleverness (accept supported differences) 7) Achilles' heel = weakness 8) Relative pronoun for people: who. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: ReadWorks grade 4 passages on sea otters and California condors (free account), a new animal passage for Day 5, highlighters, a list of 10 science words from the passages.
misconceptions: Choosing an interesting detail as the main idea. The main idea is what the whole passage is mostly about; details support it.
Adding opinions to summaries ('Condors are cool'). Summaries are objective.

days.guide: Read the sea otter passage. Model asking 'What is this mostly about?' and highlighting 3 key details that support it.

questions.q: Give a key fact about sea otters you can verify.
questions.a: Examples: sea otters have the thickest fur of any animal (no blubber), use rocks as tools to open shellfish, and eat sea urchins, which helps protect kelp forests.

days.guide: Read the condor passage. The child writes a 4-sentence summary: topic, 2 key points, conclusion; no opinions.

questions.q: What is one key fact about the California condor?
questions.a: It is the largest North American land bird (wingspan about 9.5 feet); it nearly went extinct — by 1987 all remaining wild condors were captured for breeding — and captive-bred birds have been released back into the wild.

questions.q: Which sentence does not belong in a summary: 'Condors eat carrion.' or 'I think condors are ugly.'
questions.a: 'I think condors are ugly' — it is an opinion.

days.guide: Model using context, then the glossary, to define a science word. The child defines 10.

questions.q: Define 'endangered.'
questions.a: At risk of becoming extinct (dying out).

questions.q: Define 'carrion.'
questions.a: The flesh of dead animals.

days.guide: Teach port = carry, rupt = break, struct = build, dict = say. The child builds and defines 12 words.

questions.q: What does 'interrupt' mean using the root?
questions.a: To break in (between) while someone is talking.

questions.q: Name a word with 'dict' and define it.
questions.a: Predict = say before; dictionary = book of words (sayings).

days.guide: The child reads a new passage independently and writes the main idea, 3 details and a summary.

questions.q: How can you check if your main idea is right?
questions.a: Each key detail should support it, and it should cover the whole passage, not one part.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = main idea stated in one sentence covering the whole passage, 3 accurate supporting details, objective 3-5 sentence summary in own words; 3 = main idea correct, one detail weak or summary slightly copied; 2 = main idea is a detail or summary includes opinion; 1 = off-topic.

weeks.prep: Short nonfiction articles on the Golden Gate Bridge, the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, drought solutions, and a comparison of two animals; graphic organizers (timeline, cause-effect, problem-solution, Venn). Key facts: Golden Gate Bridge construction began 1933, opened May 1937; the 1906 earthquake struck April 18, 1906 and the fires that followed destroyed much of the city.
misconceptions: Thinking text structure is the topic. Structure is HOW information is organized (sequence, cause/effect, compare/contrast, problem/solution, description).
Confusing cause and effect. The cause happens first and makes the effect happen; test with 'because'.

days.guide: Read the Golden Gate Bridge article and build a timeline. Point out signal words (first, in 1933, then, finally).

questions.q: When did construction start and when did the Golden Gate Bridge open?
questions.a: Construction began in 1933; it opened in 1937.

days.guide: Read about the 1906 earthquake and chart causes and effects.

questions.q: What caused most of the destruction in 1906?
questions.a: The fires that broke out after the earthquake (broken gas lines, damaged water mains made them hard to fight) burned for days and destroyed much of the city.

questions.q: Name an effect of the earthquake on people.
questions.a: Hundreds of thousands were left homeless and lived in camps/tents; much of the city had to be rebuilt.

days.guide: Read about drought and record the problem and solutions; then read the animal comparison and fill in a Venn diagram.

questions.q: Name two solutions to drought in California.
questions.a: Examples: water conservation (shorter showers, drought-tolerant plants), recycling wastewater, storing water in reservoirs/groundwater.

days.guide: The child reads 6 short paragraphs, circles signal words, and names each structure.

questions.q: Which structure uses 'as a result' and 'therefore'?
questions.a: Cause and effect.

questions.q: Which structure uses 'however' and 'both'?
questions.a: Compare and contrast.

days.guide: Give the quiz: name the structure of 4 passages and draw the matching organizer.

questions.q: Which organizer matches problem/solution?
questions.a: A box for the problem with arrows to boxes for solutions.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Passage 1 (sequence of the bridge's construction) = chronology/sequence, timeline. Passage 2 (why the earthquake caused fires) = cause/effect, cause→effect chart. Passage 3 (drought and conservation) = problem/solution, problem box with solution boxes. Passage 4 (otters vs. seals) = compare/contrast, Venn diagram. 2 points each (name + organizer); proficient 6/8.

weeks.prep: Two nonfiction books or sites on a California animal (e.g., gray whale, banana slug, desert tortoise, California quail), note cards, a short online video about the animal.
misconceptions: Copying sentences onto note cards. Teach: read, cover the source, write key words in your own words.
Using progressive tenses incorrectly ('She is swam'). Progressive = a form of be + -ing verb: was swimming, is swimming, will be swimming.

days.guide: Look at a diagram, map and chart in the nonfiction book. The child explains what each adds that the text alone does not.

questions.q: What does a range map show?
questions.a: Where the animal lives (its geographic range).

days.guide: The child chooses an animal and writes 5-6 research questions (habitat, diet, adaptations, life cycle, threats).

questions.q: Is 'Are sea lions cute?' a good research question? Why?
questions.a: No — it is an opinion. A good one can be answered with facts, e.g., 'What do sea lions eat?'

days.guide: Model paraphrasing one fact. The child takes notes from two sources, writing the source on each card.

questions.q: What information should you record about each source?
questions.a: Title, author (if any), and publisher or website.

days.guide: Teach the three progressive tenses. The child writes 12 sentences about the animal.

questions.q: Write 'The whale swims' in past, present and future progressive.
questions.a: The whale was swimming. The whale is swimming. The whale will be swimming.

days.guide: Watch a 2-minute video; the child paraphrases it aloud, then sorts all notes into categories.

questions.q: What are good categories for animal notes?
questions.a: Habitat, diet, adaptations, life cycle, threats/protection.

weeks.assessment_key: Notes check (4-point): 4 = at least 12 notes in own words from 2 sources, each labeled with its source, sorted into 3+ categories; 3 = 8-11 notes or some copied phrases; 2 = notes mostly copied or one source; 1 = few notes. Source list must give title and author/site for each.

weeks.prep: Notes from week 11, computer, paper for a diagram. Prepare a Unit 3 informational reading test using a new passage (rubric/key below).
misconceptions: Writing sections that wander from their heading. Each section's sentences should all be about that heading.
Ending without a conclusion. A conclusion sums up the main points and leaves a final thought.

days.guide: The child arranges notes into an outline: introduction, 3 headed sections, conclusion.

questions.q: What goes in the introduction of a report?
questions.a: A hook and a sentence telling what the report is about.

days.guide: The child drafts the introduction and two sections using linking words (also, for example, because).

questions.q: Use 'for example' in a sentence about your animal.
questions.a: Example: 'Sea otters use tools. For example, they crack shellfish on rocks resting on their bellies.'

days.guide: The child drafts the last section and conclusion and draws a labeled diagram with a caption.

questions.q: What does a caption do?
questions.a: Explains what the picture or diagram shows.

days.guide: Revise for precise vocabulary (domain words like 'habitat,' 'predator'), edit, and type the report.

questions.q: Replace the vague word: 'Condors eat stuff.'
questions.a: 'Condors eat carrion (dead animals).'

days.guide: The child presents the report to family, then takes the Unit 3 test.

questions.q: What should a good presenter do?
questions.a: Speak clearly at a good pace, make eye contact, and explain facts in order.

weeks.assessment_key: Report rubric: 4 = clear introduction, 3 headed sections with accurate facts in own words, linking words, domain vocabulary, labeled diagram with caption, conclusion, few errors; 3 = all parts with some weak sections; 2 = missing a section or many errors; 1 = incomplete. Unit 3 test: main idea (1 sentence covering whole passage), 3 key details, objective summary, text structure correctly named, 2 vocabulary words defined from context, meaning of a text feature explained. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: Island of the Blue Dolphins (Scott O'Dell); preview chapters 1-6, which include a battle in which many island men, including Karana's father, are killed. Print a map of the Channel Islands (San Nicolas is the farthest out, about 60 miles off the coast).
misconceptions: Making inferences without evidence. An inference = clue from the text + what I know.
Breaking words into syllables randomly. Split between double consonants, before consonant-le, and keep vowel teams together.

days.guide: Read chapters 1-2 together. Locate San Nicolas Island on the map and discuss how the island setting (sea, little wood, otters) shapes life.

questions.q: Who narrates the novel and what island does she live on?
questions.a: Karana, a girl from the village of Ghalas-at, on the Island of the Blue Dolphins (San Nicolas Island) off California.

questions.q: Why have the Aleuts come to the island?
questions.a: With Captain Orlov, to hunt sea otters for their pelts.

days.guide: Read chapters 3-4. The child writes 3 inferences about Captain Orlov, each with a clue from the text.

questions.q: What can you infer about Captain Orlov? Give evidence.
questions.a: He is not trustworthy — he offers a deal for the otters, but Karana's father (Chief Chowig) is suspicious, and Orlov later tries to sail away without paying the agreed share.

days.guide: Read chapters 5-6 and discuss the battle and its effects with your child.

questions.q: Why does the fight with the Aleuts happen?
questions.a: Orlov tries to leave without paying the agreed price; Chowig confronts him and a battle breaks out.

questions.q: What are the effects of the battle on Karana's people?
questions.a: Many men, including her father Chowig, are killed; the village has few men left, and women must take on new work.

days.guide: Teach syllable rules. The child divides 15 multisyllabic words from the novel.

questions.q: Divide 'dolphin' and 'abalone' into syllables.
questions.a: dol-phin; ab-a-lo-ne.

days.guide: The child answers 6 text-dependent questions on chapters 1-6 in complete sentences with evidence.

questions.q: Why does Karana's father being careless with his secret name matter?
questions.a: Her people believed using one's secret name with a stranger weakened its power; Chowig told Orlov his real name, which seemed to foreshadow trouble.

weeks.assessment_key: Key (6 questions): 1) Narrator: Karana. 2) Setting: the Island of the Blue Dolphins (San Nicolas), off the California coast. 3) Aleuts came with Captain Orlov to hunt sea otters. 4) Inference about Orlov: dishonest/greedy — tries to leave without paying fairly. 5) Battle effect: many men, including Chief Chowig, die. 6) Change in village life: women take on men's work; a new chief (Kimki) eventually leaves to find a new homeland. Each answer must include a detail from the text. Proficient: 5/6.

weeks.prep: Novel (chapters 7-14). Preview: Karana's brother Ramo is killed by wild dogs in this section — prepare to discuss grief.
misconceptions: Confusing first-person narration with the author's voice. Karana is the narrator; Scott O'Dell is the author.
Labeling every comparison as a simile. A simile uses 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor says one thing is another.

days.guide: Read chapters 7-9. The child charts Karana's actions and feelings after Ramo's death.

questions.q: Why does Karana jump from the ship?
questions.a: She sees that her little brother Ramo has been left behind on the island and won't leave him.

questions.q: What happens to Ramo, and how does Karana respond?
questions.a: He is killed by the wild dogs; she is grief-stricken, vows to kill the dogs, and burns the village.

days.guide: Discuss how first person limits us to Karana's thoughts. The child rewrites a paragraph in third person.

questions.q: Change 'I walked to the cliff and looked at the sea' to third person.
questions.a: 'Karana walked to the cliff and looked at the sea.'

days.guide: Read chapters 10-12. The child lists survival decisions Karana makes.

questions.q: Why is making weapons a hard decision for Karana?
questions.a: Her tribe's law forbids women to make weapons; she fears the consequences but decides she must to survive.

questions.q: Name two survival decisions she makes.
questions.a: Examples: making a bow, arrows and a spear; trying to leave by canoe (and turning back when it leaks); building a house and a fence of whale ribs on the headland; storing food.

days.guide: The child finds 5 similes or metaphors in chapters 13-14 and explains each.

questions.q: What is the difference between a simile and a metaphor?
questions.a: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor compares by saying one thing is another.

days.guide: The child writes a paragraph on how Karana has changed, using two quotations.

questions.q: How has Karana changed so far?
questions.a: She has gone from depending on her people to being self-reliant and brave — breaking the weapons law, building her own shelter and providing for herself.

weeks.assessment_key: Character change paragraph rubric: 4 = clear claim about change from start to now, two accurately quoted and cited passages with explanation, conclusion; 3 = claim with one strong quote; 2 = retelling with little analysis; 1 = off-topic. Expected content: Karana moves from relying on her family and village to independence, courage and skill.

weeks.prep: Novel (chapters 15-22). List 10 context-clue words from chapters 18-19.
misconceptions: Mixing up theme and topic ('friendship'). Write a full sentence: 'Friendship can grow even between enemies.'
Guessing word meaning without rereading the sentence before and after.

days.guide: Read chapters 15-17. Discuss how Karana's choice to spare and care for the wounded leader dog shows her values.

questions.q: Why doesn't Karana kill the wounded leader dog?
questions.a: She feels pity once she sees him hurt and helpless; she cares for him, names him Rontu ('Fox Eyes'), and he becomes her loyal companion.

questions.q: What does this show about her?
questions.a: She is compassionate and lonely; she values companionship over revenge.

days.guide: Model using context clues. The child defines 10 words and checks with a dictionary.

questions.q: What is a strategy for context clues?
questions.a: Reread the sentences around the word, look for a definition, example, synonym or contrast, then test your meaning in the sentence.

days.guide: Read chapters 18-20 and discuss Karana's friendship with Tutok.

questions.q: Who is Tutok, and why is the friendship surprising?
questions.a: An Aleut girl who comes with the hunters; Karana's people fought the Aleuts, yet the two become friends.

questions.q: How does Karana show trust in Tutok?
questions.a: She tells Tutok her secret name, Won-a-pa-lei, and they exchange gifts (Tutok gives her a necklace of black stones).

days.guide: Read chapters 21-22. The child drafts a theme statement with two supporting details.

questions.q: Write a theme statement for the novel so far.
questions.a: Example: 'Forgiveness and kindness can replace anger and loneliness' — Karana spares Rontu and befriends Tutok.

days.guide: The child answers comprehension questions and shares the theme statement aloud.

questions.q: What does Karana learn from Tutok's leaving?
questions.a: She feels how much she has missed friendship; loneliness returns after Tutok sails away.

weeks.assessment_key: Theme statement rubric: 4 = a complete sentence that applies beyond the book, supported by two accurate details (e.g., Rontu, Tutok) and explained; 3 = theme with one detail; 2 = topic word only; 1 = summary. Questions key: Rontu = the wild dog leader Karana spares; Tutok = Aleut girl who becomes her friend; secret name Won-a-pa-lei; Karana's values: compassion, friendship. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: Novel (chapters 23-29). Prepare a novel comprehension test (key below). Preview: Rontu dies in this section.
misconceptions: Thinking a summary should include every event. Select only the most important events: beginning, key turning points, ending.
Reading fast instead of expressively. Fluency = accuracy, phrasing and expression that matches meaning.

days.guide: Read chapters 23-25. Track how Karana's attitude toward animals changes.

questions.q: How does Karana's attitude toward animals change?
questions.a: She decides not to kill animals anymore (except for food from the sea she needs) — she tames birds and an otter and sees animals as friends.

days.guide: Finish the novel and discuss whether the ending is happy, sad or both.

questions.q: How does Karana leave the island?
questions.a: After many years alone, a ship comes and its crew take her to the mainland; she leaves with her dog Rontu-Aru.

questions.q: Is the ending happy, sad or both? Why?
questions.a: Both — she is rescued and will be among people, but she learns the ship that took her people had sunk and she leaves her island home.

days.guide: The child writes a one-paragraph summary of the whole novel.

questions.q: What must the summary include?
questions.a: Who Karana is, why she was left alone, how she survives and changes, and how she finally leaves.

days.guide: The child rehearses a favorite passage 3 times and records a 2-minute expressive reading.

questions.q: What makes a reading expressive?
questions.a: Changing voice for feelings and dialogue, pausing at punctuation, and reading at a natural pace.

days.guide: Give the novel comprehension test.

questions.q: Who are Rontu and Rontu-Aru?
questions.a: Rontu is the dog Karana tamed; Rontu-Aru ('son of Rontu') is the young dog she captures after Rontu dies.

weeks.assessment_key: Novel test key: 1) Narrator: Karana 2) Setting: Island of the Blue Dolphins (San Nicolas), off California, 1800s 3) Why she is alone: jumped from the ship to stay with Ramo, who was then killed by wild dogs 4) Law she breaks: women making weapons 5) Rontu: wild dog leader she spares and tames 6) Tutok: Aleut girl who becomes her friend 7) Change: from anger and revenge to compassion — she stops killing animals 8) Ending: rescued after many years, goes to the mainland with Rontu-Aru; learns her people's ship sank 9) Theme (accept supported): courage and self-reliance; forgiveness; harmony with nature. Proficient: 7/9 with evidence.

weeks.prep: Novel; a nonfiction article on the Lone Woman of San Nicolas Island (National Park Service Channel Islands site or a library article). Key facts: she was left behind when the island's people were moved to the mainland in 1835; she lived alone about 18 years; she was found by George Nidever's party in 1853; she was taken to Santa Barbara, given the name Juana Maria at baptism, and died about seven weeks later; no one could understand her language.
misconceptions: Assuming everything in historical fiction really happened. Separate documented facts from invented details (Karana's name, Ramo, Rontu's story).
Quoting without explaining. Every quotation needs a sentence telling how it proves the point.

days.guide: Read the nonfiction account; the child takes notes on key facts (dates, rescue, what happened afterward).

questions.q: When and how was the Lone Woman found?
questions.a: In 1853, by a party led by George Nidever, after she had lived alone on San Nicolas Island for about 18 years.

questions.q: What happened after she came to the mainland?
questions.a: She was taken to Santa Barbara, baptized Juana Maria, and died about seven weeks later; no one understood her language.

days.guide: The child makes a fact/fiction chart citing the novel and the article for each row.

questions.q: Name one fact and one invention in the novel.
questions.a: Fact: a woman lived alone on San Nicolas for about 18 years and was rescued. Invention: her name Karana, her brother Ramo, the dog Rontu and the friendship with Tutok are O'Dell's creations.

days.guide: Plan the essay: claim answering 'How does Karana survive, and what does it show about her?' plus 3 reasons with evidence.

questions.q: Write a possible claim.
questions.a: Example: 'Karana survives by building shelter, making weapons and befriending animals, which shows she is resourceful, brave and compassionate.'

days.guide: The child drafts and revises the essay with at least 3 quotations, each introduced and explained.

questions.q: How should you introduce a quote?
questions.a: With a lead-in like 'Karana explains,' then the quote in quotation marks, then a sentence explaining how it supports the claim.

days.guide: The child shares the essay as a book talk; score with the rubric.

questions.q: What makes a book talk engaging?
questions.a: A strong opening, a few key points about the book, a short quote, and clear speaking.

weeks.assessment_key: Literary essay rubric: 4 = clear claim answering both parts of the prompt; 3 body reasons each with an accurately cited quotation and explanation; conclusion; organized with transitions; few errors. 3 = claim and evidence present, explanations brief. 2 = mostly summary, 1-2 quotes. 1 = no clear claim. Fact/fiction chart: proficient lists at least 3 accurate facts and 3 invented elements.

weeks.prep: A Child's Garden of Verses (Stevenson): 'My Shadow' and 'The Land of Counterpane'; Carl Sandburg's 'Fog'; Robert Frost's 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening' (check copyright — it is in the public domain in the U.S. since 2019). Pick one short poem for memorization.
misconceptions: Thinking every poem must rhyme. 'Fog' is free verse; rhyme is one tool among many.
Confusing mood (the feeling the reader gets) with tone or with the poem's topic.

days.guide: Read both Stevenson poems aloud. The child marks rhyme scheme with letters and taps the beats.

questions.q: What is the rhyme scheme of 'My Shadow'?
questions.a: Rhyming couplets: AABB.

questions.q: What is the 'land of counterpane'?
questions.a: The child's bedspread (counterpane) while sick in bed, where he plays with toy soldiers, ships and cities among the hills of the blankets.

days.guide: Read 'Fog' twice. Explain extended metaphor: the fog is compared to a cat throughout.

questions.q: What is fog compared to and what details show it?
questions.a: A cat — it comes 'on little cat feet,' sits 'on silent haunches' looking over the harbor and city, and then moves on.

questions.q: Is 'Fog' rhyming or free verse?
questions.a: Free verse — it doesn't rhyme or keep a steady beat.

days.guide: Read Frost's poem and discuss the mood (quiet, peaceful, a little lonely) and the repeated last line.

questions.q: What line repeats at the end and what might it mean?
questions.a: 'And miles to go before I sleep' — the speaker has duties and a long way to go (it may also suggest a long life ahead).

questions.q: What does the horse think about stopping?
questions.a: The little horse 'must think it queer' to stop with no farmhouse near; he shakes his harness bells.

days.guide: The child writes a metaphor poem and a rhyming quatrain (ABAB or AABB) about a California place.

questions.q: What is a quatrain?
questions.a: A four-line stanza.

days.guide: The child recites a memorized poem with expression. Give the poetry terms quiz.

questions.q: What is a stanza?
questions.a: A group of lines in a poem, like a paragraph in prose.

weeks.assessment_key: Poetry terms quiz key: stanza = group of lines; rhyme scheme = pattern of end rhymes shown with letters; rhythm/meter = pattern of beats; free verse = poetry without regular rhyme or meter; simile = comparison with like/as; metaphor = direct comparison; imagery = words that appeal to the senses; repetition = repeating words/lines for effect; mood = feeling the poem creates. Recitation rubric: 4 = accurate, fluent, expressive, eye contact; 3 = 1-2 slips; 2 = several prompts needed; 1 = read from paper.

weeks.prep: 'Paul Revere's Ride' (Longfellow, public domain), an audio recording of the poem (many free on YouTube/LibriVox), a short factual account (e.g., from the Paul Revere House website). Key facts: on April 18-19, 1775, Revere and William Dawes rode to warn that British troops were coming; Revere was captured before reaching Concord; Samuel Prescott carried the warning to Concord; the lantern signal was sent from the Old North Church to patriots in Charlestown.
misconceptions: Treating a narrative poem as history. Longfellow wrote in 1860 to inspire readers and changed facts for drama.
Reading poetry in a sing-song rhythm. Pause at punctuation, not at line ends.

days.guide: Read the poem aloud. The child summarizes events stanza by stanza.

questions.q: What is the meaning of 'One if by land, and two if by sea'?
questions.a: The number of lanterns hung in the Old North Church tower to signal how the British were moving: one lantern for land, two for crossing by water.

questions.q: What towns does Revere ride through in the poem?
questions.a: Medford, Lexington and Concord.

days.guide: Listen to a recording and note how the reader's pace and volume change (faster during the ride, slower at suspense).

questions.q: Why would a reader speed up during the ride stanzas?
questions.a: To match the galloping horse and build excitement.

days.guide: Read the factual account. The child lists what Longfellow changed.

questions.q: Name two things the poem changes from history.
questions.a: Revere did not ride alone — William Dawes (and later Samuel Prescott) also rode; Revere was captured and did not reach Concord; the lanterns were a signal to others, not to Revere.

days.guide: The child rehearses 3 stanzas with expression and records them.

questions.q: What is one fluency goal for your recording?
questions.a: Pause at punctuation, vary volume for excitement, and read at a pace listeners can follow.

days.guide: The child performs with a sound effect or slides and self-evaluates fluency.

questions.q: How will you rate your accuracy, pace and expression?
questions.a: Child rates each on a 1-4 scale and names one improvement.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric: 4 = accurate reading of 3 stanzas, pace varies with action, expressive voice, clear volume, thoughtful self-evaluation; 3 = mostly fluent, some flat sections; 2 = several errors or monotone; 1 = incomplete. Fact vs. poem list: proficient names at least 2 accurate differences (other riders, capture, lantern signal purpose).

weeks.prep: Reader's theater script (an Aesop fable or 'The Emperor's New Clothes' — many free online), the prose version of the same story, simple props. Unit 5 test for Day 5 (key below).
misconceptions: Reading stage directions aloud as lines. Stage directions (often in parentheses/italics) tell actors what to do.
Thinking drama has a narrator like prose. Plays tell the story mostly through dialogue and action.

days.guide: Read the script and label the cast list, scenes and stage directions.

questions.q: What is a cast of characters?
questions.a: The list of characters in a play, usually at the beginning.

questions.q: What are stage directions?
questions.a: Instructions for actors about movement, expression or setting, not spoken aloud.

days.guide: Compare the script with the prose version and list structural differences.

questions.q: Name two differences between prose and drama.
questions.a: Prose uses paragraphs and narration; drama uses a cast list, dialogue after character names, stage directions and scenes/acts.

days.guide: The child converts a scene from Island of the Blue Dolphins into a script.

questions.q: How do you show what Karana feels in a script?
questions.a: Through her dialogue and stage directions, e.g., (Karana kneels, looking out to sea sadly).

days.guide: Rehearse the script with family using expression and blocking.

questions.q: What is blocking?
questions.a: Planning where and how actors move on stage.

days.guide: Perform the play, then give the Unit 5 test.

questions.q: In 'The Emperor's New Clothes,' who finally says the Emperor has no clothes?
questions.a: A small child in the crowd.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test key: 1) Stanza = group of lines 2) Rhyme scheme of 'My Shadow' = AABB 3) 'Fog' compares fog to a cat (extended metaphor) 4) Repeated line in Frost's poem: 'And miles to go before I sleep' 5) Free verse = no regular rhyme/meter 6) Cast of characters = list of roles 7) Stage directions = instructions to actors 8) Two prose vs. drama differences (dialogue format, scenes vs. paragraphs, stage directions) 9) 'One if by land, two if by sea' refers to lantern signals 10) One fact Longfellow changed. Performance rubric: 4 = lines known, expressive, follows blocking; 3 = minor slips; 2 = reads flatly; 1 = incomplete. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: Opinion articles for kids (CommonLit, newspaper kids' sections) including one on school uniforms; a short persuasive video; 15 fact/opinion statements about California.
misconceptions: Thinking an opinion with a number in it is a fact. Ask: can it be proven true or false?
Treating any reason as strong evidence. Strong evidence is specific, accurate and relevant (facts, statistics, expert quotes), not 'everyone knows.'

days.guide: The child sorts 15 statements and underlines clue words (best, should, beautiful, I think).

questions.q: 'Yosemite is the best park.' Fact or opinion?
questions.a: Opinion — 'best' is a judgment.

questions.q: 'Mount Whitney is the tallest mountain in the contiguous U.S.' Fact or opinion?
questions.a: Fact — it can be proven (14,505 ft).

days.guide: Read the uniform article and outline its claim, reasons and evidence.

questions.q: What is the difference between a reason and evidence?
questions.a: A reason explains why the author holds the opinion; evidence (facts, examples, data) supports the reason.

days.guide: The child rates each piece of evidence strong or weak and explains.

questions.q: Is 'All kids hate uniforms' strong evidence?
questions.a: Weak — it is an exaggeration with no data; a survey result would be stronger.

days.guide: Watch a persuasive video; the child records the speaker's reasons.

questions.q: What should you listen for in a persuasive speech?
questions.a: The claim, each reason, and the evidence for each reason.

days.guide: The child reads a new opinion article and fills in the organizer independently.

questions.q: What are the parts of the organizer?
questions.a: Author's claim, three reasons, and the evidence for each.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric for analysis: 4 = correctly states the claim, identifies all 3 reasons and matches evidence to each, judges strength with explanation; 3 = claim and reasons correct, evidence partly matched; 2 = confuses reasons and evidence; 1 = summary only. Answers must match the article used.

weeks.prep: Two short articles on single-use plastic bags (note: California banned most single-use plastic carryout bags at grocery stores starting in 2016 through Proposition 67, and a stronger 2024 law, SB 1053, bans plastic film bags at checkout starting 2026). Writer's notebook.
misconceptions: Using modals incorrectly ('We must to recycle'). Modals are followed by the base verb with no 'to': must recycle.
Choosing reasons that overlap. Each reason should be different (environment, wildlife, cost).

days.guide: The child chooses a question and writes a clear opinion statement.

questions.q: Write an opinion statement on plastic bags.
questions.a: Example: 'California should ban all single-use plastic bags because they harm wildlife and pollute our beaches.'

days.guide: The child gathers facts from two articles and records each with its source.

questions.q: Why should you record the source of each fact?
questions.a: So you can give credit and check the information later.

days.guide: Teach can (ability), may (permission/possibility), must (necessity), should (advice). The child writes 12 sentences.

questions.q: Choose the modal: 'You ___ bring a reusable bag; it's a good idea.'
questions.a: should.

questions.q: Choose the modal: 'Drivers ___ stop at a red light.'
questions.a: must.

days.guide: The child plans introduction, 3 reasons with evidence, conclusion.

questions.q: What goes in each body paragraph?
questions.a: One reason, at least two pieces of evidence, and an explanation.

days.guide: Debate with your child taking the opposite side; this strengthens counterargument thinking.

questions.q: What is a counterargument against banning bags?
questions.a: Example: paper bags also use resources and cost more; some people reuse plastic bags.

weeks.assessment_key: Outline check (4-point): 4 = clear opinion, 3 distinct reasons each with 2 pieces of sourced evidence, planned hook and conclusion; 3 = 3 reasons, some evidence missing; 2 = reasons overlap or little evidence; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Outline, computer, opinion rubric (4 levels: opinion, reasons, evidence, organization/linking words, conclusion, conventions).
misconceptions: Restating the hook in the conclusion word for word. Restate the opinion in new words and add a call to action.
Using the same linking word repeatedly. Vary: for instance, in addition, because, therefore, also.

days.guide: The child drafts an introduction with a hook (question, surprising fact) and an opinion statement.

questions.q: Write a hook for the plastic bag essay.
questions.a: Example: 'Did you know a plastic bag can take hundreds of years to break down?'

days.guide: The child drafts three body paragraphs: reason, two pieces of evidence, linking phrase.

questions.q: Name three linking phrases for opinions.
questions.a: For instance, in addition, because (also: therefore, as a result).

days.guide: The child drafts a conclusion that restates the opinion and calls readers to action.

questions.q: What is a call to action?
questions.a: Telling readers what to do, e.g., 'Bring a reusable bag every time you shop.'

days.guide: Revise for precise words and varied sentence beginnings and lengths.

questions.q: Make this sentence more precise: 'Bags are bad for animals.'
questions.a: Example: 'Sea turtles mistake floating plastic bags for jellyfish and can choke.'

days.guide: Conference with the rubric; the child sets 2-3 edit goals.

questions.q: Which rubric row is your strongest? Weakest?
questions.a: Child names rows with evidence from the draft.

weeks.assessment_key: Complete revised draft (4-point): 4 = hook and clear opinion, 3 body paragraphs each with a reason and 2 relevant pieces of evidence, varied linking words, conclusion with call to action, evidence of revision; 3 = all parts, one weak paragraph; 2 = missing a paragraph or evidence; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Computer, note cards, a sample text message and a short speech on the same topic. Unit 6 test for Day 5 (key below).
misconceptions: Joining two complete sentences with only a comma (comma splice). Use a comma + and/but/or/so.
Using informal language in formal writing ('gonna,' 'kinda,' 'super cool').

days.guide: The child edits for commas in compound sentences, spelling and capitalization.

questions.q: Add a comma: 'Plastic bags blow into the ocean and animals eat them.'
questions.a: 'Plastic bags blow into the ocean, and animals eat them.'

days.guide: The child types the final essay in one sitting, formats title and paragraphs, and proofreads aloud.

questions.q: What should the title of an opinion essay do?
questions.a: Hint at the opinion and catch interest, e.g., 'Bag the Plastic!'

days.guide: Compare a text message and a speech. The child rewrites informal sentences formally.

questions.q: Rewrite formally: 'Plastic bags r super bad lol.'
questions.a: 'Plastic bags are very harmful to the environment.'

days.guide: The child condenses the essay to a 2-minute speech on note cards (key words only) and rehearses.

questions.q: Why use key words instead of full sentences on note cards?
questions.a: So you look up and talk to the audience instead of reading.

days.guide: The child delivers the speech, then takes the Unit 6 test.

questions.q: What makes evidence strong?
questions.a: It is accurate, specific, relevant and from a reliable source.

weeks.assessment_key: Essay rubric: as week 23 plus conventions (4 = nearly error-free). Speech rubric: 4 = clear opinion and reasons in about 2 minutes, eye contact, good volume and pace, formal language; 3 = minor issues; 2 = reads from cards; 1 = incomplete. Unit 6 test key: 1) fact vs. opinion sort (fact = provable) 2) identify claim of a passage 3) list 3 reasons 4) match evidence to reasons 5) strong vs. weak evidence with explanation 6) modal choice: must = necessity, should = advice, may = permission, can = ability 7) linking words: for instance, in addition, because 8) formal rewrite of an informal sentence. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (L. Frank Baum, 1900, Gutenberg). Preview chapters 1-6: 1 The Cyclone, 2 The Council with the Munchkins, 3 How Dorothy Saved the Scarecrow, 4 The Road Through the Forest, 5 The Rescue of the Tin Woodman, 6 The Cowardly Lion. Note: in the book Dorothy's shoes are SILVER, not ruby.
misconceptions: Mixing up the book with the 1939 film. Answer only from the book this week; the film comes in week 28.
Predictions without reasons. A good prediction says 'I think... because in the text...'

days.guide: Read chapters 1-2. The child makes a two-column chart contrasting Kansas and Oz with details.

questions.q: How does Baum describe Kansas?
questions.a: Gray everywhere — the prairie, the house, even Aunt Em and Uncle Henry have turned gray; it is flat and dry.

questions.q: How is the Munchkin country different?
questions.a: Beautiful and colorful: green grass, stately trees with fruit, bright flowers, birds and a sparkling brook.

days.guide: Read chapters 3-4. The child lists the Scarecrow's traits with evidence.

questions.q: What does the Scarecrow want, and why?
questions.a: Brains, because he thinks he is foolish since his head is stuffed with straw.

questions.q: Give evidence that the Scarecrow is already clever or kind.
questions.a: Example: he is cheerful and helpful, and later in the story he thinks of plans that save the group (accept accurate details from chapters 3-4).

days.guide: Read chapters 5-6. The child describes the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion.

questions.q: Why does the Tin Woodman want a heart?
questions.a: He was once a man (a Munchkin woodman) who loved a Munchkin girl; the Wicked Witch of the East enchanted his axe and he was replaced piece by piece with tin, losing his heart and the ability to love.

questions.q: How does the Cowardly Lion show he is not really a coward?
questions.a: He roars to frighten enemies, and later in the journey he protects the group despite being afraid.

days.guide: The child writes predictions: what will the Wizard grant each character, with a reason from the text.

questions.q: What do Dorothy and her friends hope to get from the Wizard?
questions.a: Dorothy: a way home to Kansas; Scarecrow: brains; Tin Woodman: a heart; Lion: courage.

days.guide: The child answers comprehension questions on chapters 1-6.

questions.q: How does Dorothy's house kill the Wicked Witch of the East?
questions.a: The cyclone carries the house to Oz and it lands on the Witch.

weeks.assessment_key: Key: 1) Kansas is gray, flat and dry. 2) The cyclone carries Dorothy and Toto to Oz. 3) The house lands on and kills the Wicked Witch of the East; Dorothy takes her silver shoes. 4) The Good Witch of the North kisses Dorothy's forehead for protection and sends her to the Emerald City. 5) Scarecrow wants brains; Tin Woodman a heart; Lion courage. 6) Tin Woodman was rusted and Dorothy oiled him. Proficient: 5/6 with evidence.

weeks.prep: Novel chapters 7-12 (7 The Journey to the Great Oz, 8 The Deadly Poppy Field, 9 The Queen of the Field Mice, 10 The Guardian of the Gate, 11 The Wonderful City of Oz, 12 The Search for the Wicked Witch). Write 12 idiom cards (e.g., 'cold feet,' 'piece of cake,' 'break the ice,' 'hold your horses,' 'under the weather,' 'let the cat out of the bag').
misconceptions: Taking idioms literally. An idiom's meaning is different from its words; use context.
Missing the turning point. A turning point changes the direction of the story — here, the Witch's death.

days.guide: Read chapters 7-9. The child charts obstacles and how the friends solve them.

questions.q: How do the friends escape the Kalidahs?
questions.a: The Tin Woodman chops the tree bridge over the ditch as the Kalidahs cross, and they fall.

questions.q: How is the Lion rescued from the poppy field?
questions.a: The Queen of the Field Mice (whom the Tin Woodman saved from a wildcat) has thousands of mice pull the Lion out on a truck the Tin Woodman builds.

days.guide: Teach the 12 idioms. The child writes a short dialogue for the characters using four.

questions.q: What does 'got cold feet' mean?
questions.a: Became too nervous to do something.

questions.q: What does 'piece of cake' mean?
questions.a: Something very easy.

days.guide: Read chapters 10-11. Discuss what the Wizard demands.

questions.q: Why does everyone in the Emerald City wear green spectacles?
questions.a: The Guardian of the Gates says it is to protect their eyes from the city's brightness (we later learn it makes everything look green).

questions.q: What does Oz demand before he grants their wishes?
questions.a: That they kill the Wicked Witch of the West.

days.guide: Read chapter 12 and describe the turning point.

questions.q: How is the Wicked Witch of the West destroyed?
questions.a: Dorothy, angry that the Witch stole one of her silver shoes, throws a bucket of water on her and she melts away.

questions.q: Why is this a turning point?
questions.a: The friends are freed, the Winkies are free, and the group can return to claim their rewards.

days.guide: Give the quiz: explain 6 idioms and answer text-dependent questions.

questions.q: What does 'break the ice' mean?
questions.a: To do or say something to ease tension when meeting people.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Idioms — cold feet = nervous; piece of cake = easy; break the ice = ease first awkwardness; hold your horses = wait/be patient; under the weather = sick; let the cat out of the bag = reveal a secret. Text questions — 1) Kalidahs escaped by chopping the tree bridge 2) Field mice rescue the Lion from the poppies 3) Green spectacles in the Emerald City 4) Oz demands the Witch of the West be killed 5) Water melts the Witch 6) Dorothy throws it because the Witch stole her silver shoe. Proficient: 10/12.

weeks.prep: Novel chapters 13-18 (13 The Rescue, 14 The Winged Monkeys, 15 The Discovery of Oz the Terrible, 16 The Magic Art of the Great Humbug, 17 How the Balloon Was Launched, 18 Away to the South).
misconceptions: Quoting without explaining. Each quote needs a sentence connecting it to the theme.
Thinking the Wizard's gifts were magic. The Wizard is a 'humbug'; the gifts work because the friends believe in them.

days.guide: Read chapters 13-14. The child notes each friend's contribution to the rescue.

questions.q: How do the Winkies help the Tin Woodman and Scarecrow?
questions.a: They find and mend the battered Tin Woodman (tinsmiths) and restuff the Scarecrow with straw.

questions.q: What does the Golden Cap do?
questions.a: Its wearer can command the Winged Monkeys three times.

days.guide: Read chapters 15-16. Discuss who the Wizard really is.

questions.q: Who is the Wizard of Oz really?
questions.a: An ordinary man from Omaha, a former balloonist/ventriloquist, whose balloon drifted to Oz; he is a 'humbug' who tricks people.

questions.q: How does Toto expose him?
questions.a: Toto knocks over the screen in the corner, revealing the little old man.

days.guide: Read chapters 17-18. Analyze whether the friends already had what they wanted.

questions.q: What does the Wizard give each friend?
questions.a: Scarecrow: brains of bran mixed with pins and needles; Tin Woodman: a silk heart stuffed with sawdust; Lion: a drink he calls courage.

questions.q: Did they already have these qualities? Give evidence.
questions.a: Yes — the Scarecrow made clever plans, the Tin Woodman wept over hurting a beetle and cared for everyone, and the Lion faced danger to protect his friends.

days.guide: The child writes a theme paragraph with two quotations.

questions.q: State a theme.
questions.a: 'What you seek may already be inside you' — the friends showed brains, heart and courage before receiving the Wizard's gifts.

days.guide: Discuss the theme; the child revises the paragraph based on the conversation.

questions.q: Why does the Wizard leave without Dorothy?
questions.a: The balloon's rope breaks/it floats away while Dorothy is chasing Toto, so she is left behind.

weeks.assessment_key: Theme paragraph rubric: 4 = clear theme sentence, two accurately quoted examples from chapters 13-18 (or earlier) with explanation, concluding sentence; 3 = theme with one strong example; 2 = summary with little analysis; 1 = off-topic.

weeks.prep: Novel chapters 19-24 (19 Attacked by the Fighting Trees, 20 The Dainty China Country, 21 The Lion Becomes the King of Beasts, 22 The Country of the Quadlings, 23 Glinda the Good Witch Grants Dorothy's Wish, 24 Home Again). The 1939 MGM film (rated G; the Witch scenes can frighten sensitive children). Prepare a novel test (key below).
misconceptions: Assuming the film is 'the real story.' The book came first (1900); films adapt and change.
Opinion paragraphs without reasons. Each opinion needs reasons with examples from both versions.

days.guide: Read chapters 19-24. The child writes a 5-sentence summary of how Dorothy gets home.

questions.q: How does Dorothy get home?
questions.a: Glinda, the Good Witch of the South, tells her the silver shoes can carry her anywhere: she knocks her heels together three times and commands them to take her home.

questions.q: What happens to the Scarecrow, Tin Woodman and Lion?
questions.a: The Scarecrow rules the Emerald City, the Tin Woodman rules the Winkies, and the Lion rules the beasts of the forest (after killing a giant spider).

days.guide: Watch selected scenes of the 1939 film. The child notes differences.

questions.q: Name two differences between the book and the film.
questions.a: Silver shoes vs. ruby slippers; in the film Oz is a dream and Kansas is in black-and-white/sepia; the film leaves out the China Country and Quadlings; in the film Glinda is the Good Witch of the North.

days.guide: Complete the book-vs-film chart: characters, events, setting colors, ending.

questions.q: How do the endings differ?
questions.a: In the book Dorothy really travels home (the silver shoes fall off in the desert); in the film she wakes up in bed as if it were a dream.

days.guide: The child writes an opinion paragraph: which version tells the story better?

questions.q: What makes a strong answer?
questions.a: A clear opinion with 2-3 reasons supported by specific examples from both book and film.

days.guide: Give the novel comprehension test.

questions.q: What color are Dorothy's shoes in the book?
questions.a: Silver.

weeks.assessment_key: Novel test key: 1) Dorothy is carried to Oz by a cyclone 2) Her house kills the Wicked Witch of the East 3) Each friend's wish (brains, heart, courage; Dorothy home) 4) Oz demands they kill the Witch of the West 5) Dorothy melts her with a bucket of water 6) The Wizard is a humbug from Omaha 7) Gifts: bran brains, silk heart, courage drink 8) Glinda reveals the silver shoes' power 9) Theme supported with evidence. Comparison paragraph rubric: 4 = clear opinion, 2+ accurate book/film differences used as reasons, conclusion; 3 = one reason; 2 = opinion with vague reasons; 1 = no opinion. Proficient: 7/9.

weeks.prep: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland chapter 1 'Down the Rabbit-Hole' (Lewis Carroll, Gutenberg); the narrative checklist from week 4.
misconceptions: Losing Dorothy's character when writing a new adventure. Keep her traits (brave, kind, wants to go home) and her companions consistent.
Long dialogue with no paragraphs. New speaker, new paragraph.

days.guide: Read Alice chapter 1. Compare its journey pattern with Oz.

questions.q: How does each girl enter the strange world?
questions.a: Alice follows the White Rabbit and falls down a rabbit-hole; Dorothy is carried by a cyclone.

questions.q: What happens when Alice drinks from the 'DRINK ME' bottle?
questions.a: She shrinks to ten inches tall.

days.guide: The child plans a new episode for Dorothy in a California setting with problem, events and resolution.

questions.q: Name a California setting with built-in adventure.
questions.a: Examples: a redwood forest, Death Valley, a Pacific tide pool, Yosemite's waterfalls.

days.guide: The child drafts the episode with dialogue and sensory details.

questions.q: What should Dorothy's dialogue show?
questions.a: Her personality — kind, brave, practical — and move the plot forward.

days.guide: Revise with the checklist and edit for quotation marks.

questions.q: Punctuate: lets follow the yellow trail said Dorothy
questions.a: "Let's follow the yellow trail," said Dorothy.

days.guide: The child reads the episode aloud; score with the narrative rubric.

questions.q: What makes a satisfying ending?
questions.a: The problem is resolved in a way that fits the characters, and the reader feels closure.

weeks.assessment_key: Narrative rubric (4-point): 4 = engaging hook, Dorothy and companions in character, clear problem and resolution in a California setting, correctly punctuated dialogue, sensory details, satisfying ending; 3 = all elements, minor errors; 2 = weak plot or few details; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Library access and computer. Sample credible sources: nps.gov pages for Yosemite, Death Valley, Redwood National and State Parks; Tahoe info from state agencies or university sites. Index cards.
misconceptions: Thinking anything online is true. Check author, date and purpose; prefer .gov, .edu and museums.
Writing questions with yes/no answers. Research questions start with how, why, what.

days.guide: The child picks a natural wonder and writes 5-6 research questions.

questions.q: Turn 'Is Death Valley hot?' into a research question.
questions.a: 'Why is Death Valley so hot, and how hot has it gotten?' (Record 134°F in 1913.)

days.guide: The child evaluates 4 websites for author, date and purpose and rates each.

questions.q: Why is a personal blog less reliable than nps.gov?
questions.a: The blog may not have an expert author or fact-checking; the National Park Service is an official agency with experts.

days.guide: The child finds 3 sources, including one with maps or charts.

questions.q: Why include a source with maps?
questions.a: It shows location and data that text alone can't, and can be cited or adapted for the report.

days.guide: Paraphrased notes on note cards with source info.

questions.q: Paraphrase: 'Coast redwoods are the tallest trees on Earth, reaching over 360 feet.'
questions.a: Example: 'The tallest trees in the world are coast redwoods; some grow taller than 360 feet.'

days.guide: Check sources and notes with your child; fill gaps.

questions.q: What do you do if a question has no notes?
questions.a: Find another source or revise the question.

weeks.assessment_key: Check (4-point): 4 = 5+ open-ended research questions, 3 credible sources recorded (title, author/organization, site), 15+ paraphrased notes linked to questions; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = copied notes or weak sources; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A John Muir excerpt from 'My First Summer in the Sierra' or 'The Yosemite' (Gutenberg) and an encyclopedia article on Yosemite. Muir (1838-1914) spent the summer of 1869 in the Sierra and helped inspire the creation of Yosemite National Park (1890).
misconceptions: Confusing firsthand (written by someone who was there) with 'first person.' A secondhand account can quote people.
Copying both texts instead of combining. Integrate: 'Muir describes..., and the encyclopedia adds...'

days.guide: Read the Muir excerpt. The child notes what he saw and felt.

questions.q: How can you tell Muir's account is firsthand?
questions.a: He writes as 'I' about what he personally saw and felt in the mountains, with vivid emotional descriptions.

days.guide: Read the encyclopedia article. Note its focus (facts, dates, geography).

questions.q: What is the focus of the encyclopedia article?
questions.a: Facts — location, size, geology (glaciers carved the valley), history and features like Half Dome and El Capitan.

days.guide: Complete a chart comparing focus and information.

questions.q: How are the two accounts different?
questions.a: Muir's is personal, emotional and descriptive; the encyclopedia is objective and gives facts and dates.

days.guide: The child writes a paragraph integrating information from both.

questions.q: Write an integrating sentence.
questions.a: Example: 'Muir describes Yosemite's waterfalls with wonder, and the encyclopedia explains that glaciers carved the valley that the waterfalls plunge into.'

days.guide: Give the firsthand vs. secondhand quiz.

questions.q: A diary written by a gold miner in 1849 is ___.
questions.a: Firsthand.

questions.q: A textbook chapter on the Gold Rush is ___.
questions.a: Secondhand.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: firsthand — diary, letter, autobiography, interview with an eyewitness, photograph taken at the event; secondhand — encyclopedia, textbook, biography, news article written later by a non-witness. Chart rubric: 4 = notes the focus and type of information in each account and 2+ differences with examples; 3 = one difference; 2 = summary only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Notes and computer. Comma rules: commas separate items in a series (red, white, and blue); a comma follows an introductory phrase (In 1890, Yosemite became...).
misconceptions: Plagiarizing by stringing notes into sentences that copy the source. Write from notes, not from the source.
Inconsistent source list format. Choose one format: Title. Author/Organization. Website or publisher, year.

days.guide: The child outlines intro, 3-4 sections and conclusion.

questions.q: How many main ideas per section?
questions.a: One — each section has a heading and focuses on one subtopic.

days.guide: Draft an introduction with a surprising fact; draft the first section.

questions.q: Give a surprising-fact hook for Death Valley.
questions.a: 'Death Valley holds the record for the hottest air temperature on Earth: 134°F in 1913.'
