days.guide: Draft the remaining sections with one short quotation and its source.

questions.q: How do you include a quotation?
questions.a: Put exact words in quotation marks and name the source: According to the National Park Service, "..."

days.guide: Practice commas in series and after introductory phrases; apply to the draft.

questions.q: Add commas: 'In 1864 President Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant protecting the valley and the giant sequoias.'
questions.a: 'In 1864, President Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant, protecting the valley and the giant sequoias.' (The comma after 1864 is the key correction.)

days.guide: Write the conclusion and a source list in a consistent format.

questions.q: Show one source entry.
questions.a: 'Yosemite National Park. National Park Service. nps.gov/yose.'

weeks.assessment_key: Draft check (4-point): 4 = hook intro, 3-4 headed sections paraphrased from notes, one cited quotation, conclusion, consistent source list of 3+ sources; 3 = all parts, minor gaps; 2 = missing sections or sources; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Computer, printer, images (with source credits), a blank map of California.
misconceptions: Captions that just name the picture ('Half Dome'). A good caption explains what it shows and why it matters.
Lowercasing proper nouns (sierra nevada). Names of specific places, mountains and deserts are capitalized.

days.guide: The child rereads aloud, marks confusing sentences and revises so each section begins with its main idea.

questions.q: What should the first sentence of a section do?
questions.a: State the main idea of that section.

days.guide: Edit for proper nouns, commas and spelling with a checklist and dictionary.

questions.q: Correct: 'the mojave desert is in southern california.'
questions.a: 'The Mojave Desert is in Southern California.' (southern may be lowercase as a direction; both accepted)

days.guide: Add a labeled map and two captioned images.

questions.q: Write a caption for a photo of Half Dome.
questions.a: Example: 'Half Dome rises about 4,700 feet above Yosemite Valley; glaciers helped shape its sheer face.'

days.guide: Type and print the final report with headings, visuals and source list.

questions.q: What final checks before printing?
questions.a: Headings in place, images credited, page numbers/title, source list complete, spelling checked.

days.guide: Self-assess with the rubric; write two sentences on strongest and weakest parts.

questions.q: What is a useful self-assessment sentence?
questions.a: One that names a specific part and evidence: 'My strongest part is the Glaciers section because...'

weeks.assessment_key: Research report rubric: 4 = clear focus; intro hook; 3-4 headed sections with accurate paraphrased facts; at least one cited quote; labeled map and 2 captioned images; conclusion; correct proper nouns and commas; consistent source list of 3+ credible sources. 3 = all parts, minor errors. 2 = missing visuals or sources, several errors. 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Slides software or poster board, a timer, a recording device. Prepare the Unit 8 test with two short texts about the same event (one firsthand, one secondhand) — key below.
misconceptions: Reading slides word for word. Slides show key facts and pictures; the speaker explains.
Answering audience questions with guesses. Say 'I'm not sure, but my notes say...' or look it up.

days.guide: The child turns the report into 5 slides or a poster: one key fact and visual per section.

questions.q: How much text belongs on a slide?
questions.a: A title and a few key words or one fact — not paragraphs.

days.guide: Rehearse a 3-minute talk with a timer, practicing eye contact, volume and pace.

questions.q: What should you do if you finish early?
questions.a: Add an example or a fact from your notes; aim for about 3 minutes.

days.guide: Record a 30-second narrated intro or add a fitting nature sound clip.

questions.q: Why add audio?
questions.a: To engage listeners and help them imagine the place.

days.guide: Present to family and answer at least three questions with facts from notes.

questions.q: How do you answer a question well?
questions.a: Listen fully, repeat the question, answer with a specific fact, check if it answered them.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test.

questions.q: What does it mean to integrate information from two texts?
questions.a: Combine facts from both to explain a topic more completely than either text alone.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric: 4 = organized 3-minute talk, slides/poster with key facts and visuals, eye contact, clear volume and pace, accurate answers to 3 questions; 3 = minor issues; 2 = reads notes or very short; 1 = incomplete. Unit 8 test key: 1) Identify each text as firsthand or secondhand 2) Focus of the firsthand text: personal experience and feelings 3) Focus of the secondhand: facts, dates, overview 4) One piece of information only in text A, one only in text B 5) Write a paragraph integrating both (proficient: uses information from each with transition words). Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: A grade 4 passage of similar difficulty to week 1, graph paper for WCPM, reading log; end-of-year assessment with one literary and one informational passage (e.g., from ReadWorks or CommonLit, using their answer keys); library visit.
misconceptions: Thinking reading faster is always better. Fluency includes accuracy and expression.
Summary instead of reflection. A reflection explains why the book mattered to you, with scenes as evidence.

days.guide: The child reads 1 minute; compute WCPM, graph it against week 1, and celebrate growth.

questions.q: If you read 132 words with 4 errors in 1 minute, what is your WCPM?

days.guide: The child writes a one-page reflection citing two memorable scenes.

questions.q: What makes a reflection strong?
questions.a: Clear statement of why the book mattered, two specific scenes described, and the reader's feelings or lessons.

days.guide: The child gives a 2-minute book talk with a short read-aloud excerpt.

questions.q: What should a book talk avoid?
questions.a: Giving away the ending.

days.guide: Give the end-of-year reading assessment.

questions.q: What strategies help on a reading test?
questions.a: Read questions first, reread to find evidence, cross out wrong answers, check that answers are supported by the text.

days.guide: Build a summer reading list of 10 books across genres, with reasons.

questions.q: Name four genres to include.
questions.a: Examples: realistic fiction, fantasy, mystery, biography, informational, poetry, graphic novel, historical fiction.

weeks.assessment_key: End-of-year reading assessment: use the passage source's answer key; score literary questions (theme, character, inference, vocabulary in context, summary) and informational questions (main idea, text structure, text features, evidence). Proficient: 80%. Fluency: compare WCPM to week 1 and to grade 4 end-of-year norms (roughly 120-140 WCPM).

weeks.prep: Writing folder with all pieces from the year; a cumulative grammar test (key below); three on-demand opinion prompts (e.g., Should kids have homework? Is it better to live in a city or the country? Should every student learn an instrument?).
misconceptions: Choosing portfolio pieces only by length. Pick pieces that show your best skills and growth.
Rushing on-demand writing without planning. Spend 5 minutes planning reasons before drafting.

days.guide: The child selects the best narrative, report, opinion essay and poem and labels why each was chosen.

questions.q: What is a good reason to choose a piece?
questions.a: It shows a specific skill well (e.g., strong dialogue, well-supported reasons) or shows growth.

days.guide: The child writes a reflection letter comparing week 4's narrative with a recent piece, naming two improvements.

questions.q: Give an example of a specific improvement.
questions.a: 'In September I had no dialogue; now I punctuate dialogue correctly and use it to show feelings.'

days.guide: Give the cumulative grammar assessment.

questions.q: Choose the correct relative pronoun: 'The girl ___ bike is red lives next door.'
questions.a: whose.

questions.q: Write 'I read' in the future progressive.
questions.a: I will be reading.

days.guide: The child chooses one prompt and writes an opinion piece in 45 minutes.

questions.q: What should the first 5 minutes be used for?
questions.a: Planning: opinion, three reasons and quick evidence notes.

days.guide: Author celebration: share the portfolio and write three grade 5 goals.

questions.q: Write one specific goal.
questions.a: Example: 'I will read 25 books next year, including 5 biographies.'

weeks.assessment_key: Grammar test key (sample): 1) who/whose/which/that items — The boy who...; the dog whose...; the book that/which... 2) Progressive: was walking / is walking / will be walking 3) Modals: must (necessity), may (permission), can (ability), should (advice) 4) Commas: 'I packed apples, cheese, and bread.' 'After lunch, we hiked.' 'It rained, but we played.' 5) Quotation marks: "Where are you going?" asked Dad. Proficient: 80%. On-demand writing rubric: 4 = clear opinion, 3 reasons with supporting details, linking words, conclusion, few errors; 3 = 2 reasons or some errors; 2 = weak organization; 1 = off-topic. Portfolio: complete with 4 pieces, labels and reflection letter.

HSS.overview: Grade 4 history-social science is the story of California, taught chronologically from geography and first peoples through missions, Mexican rule, the Gold Rush, statehood and modern government. Each week pairs a short reading with maps and primary sources (many from Calisphere): have the child observe, infer and question before you explain, and always ask whose perspective a source shows and whose is missing. Topics such as mission life, the Gold Rush's violence against Native Californians and Japanese American incarceration should be previewed and discussed honestly and age-appropriately.

weeks.prep: Globe, world and California maps (with latitude/longitude lines), an orange and a marker. Coordinates for reference: Sacramento about 38.6°N, 121.5°W; San Francisco 37.8°N, 122.4°W; Los Angeles 34.1°N, 118.2°W; San Diego 32.7°N, 117.2°W; Fresno 36.7°N, 119.8°W; Eureka 40.8°N, 124.2°W.
misconceptions: Mixing up latitude and longitude. Latitude lines run east-west like ladder rungs ('lat-itude is flat') and measure north-south; longitude lines run pole to pole.
Writing coordinates without N/S or E/W. 37°N, 122°W is in California; 37°S, 122°E is in the ocean near Australia.

days.guide: Draw the equator and prime meridian on the orange and name the four hemispheres. Find California.

questions.q: Which two hemispheres is California in?
questions.a: The Northern and Western Hemispheres.

questions.q: What is the equator's latitude?

days.guide: Use the map to find latitudes of Sacramento, San Diego and the North Pole and record them.

questions.q: What are the approximate latitudes of Sacramento and San Diego?
questions.a: Sacramento about 38.5°N; San Diego about 32.7°N.

questions.q: What is the latitude of the North Pole?

days.guide: Find longitudes for five California cities. Discuss why lines meet at the poles.

questions.q: Why do longitude lines meet at the poles?
questions.a: They run from pole to pole around the round Earth, so they come together at the North and South Poles.

days.guide: Give coordinates; the child locates the place.

questions.q: What city is near 37.7°N, 122.4°W?
questions.a: San Francisco.

questions.q: What city is near 34°N, 118°W?
questions.a: Los Angeles.

days.guide: Give the plotting quiz.

questions.q: What are the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn latitudes?
questions.a: About 23.5°N and 23.5°S.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: plot 6 locations within about 1° (e.g., San Diego 32.7°N, 117.2°W; Sacramento 38.6°N, 121.5°W; Los Angeles 34.1°N, 118.2°W; Eureka 40.8°N, 124.2°W; Fresno 36.7°N, 119.8°W; San Francisco 37.8°N, 122.4°W). Label: equator 0°, Tropic of Cancer 23.5°N, Tropic of Capricorn 23.5°S, North Pole 90°N, South Pole 90°S, prime meridian 0°, Northern/Southern/Eastern/Western Hemispheres. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: California physical map, blank outline map, colored pencils, photos of Imperial Valley farms, a Sierra ski town, a Central Valley orchard and a coastal harbor.
misconceptions: Thinking the Central Valley is mountainous or a desert. It is a large, flat, fertile valley between the Coast Ranges and the Sierra Nevada.
Thinking the desert region is useless. Irrigation turned desert valleys like the Imperial Valley into farmland.

days.guide: Color the four regions and star Sacramento.

questions.q: Name California's four main regions.
questions.a: Coastal, mountain, Central Valley and desert.

questions.q: What is California's capital?
questions.a: Sacramento.

days.guide: Read about each region and make a 4-column chart (climate, landforms, vegetation).

questions.q: Describe the desert region's climate.
questions.a: Hot, very dry, little rain; includes the Mojave and Colorado Deserts and Death Valley.

days.guide: Compare the four photos and explain how land shapes jobs.

questions.q: Why is the Central Valley good for farming?
questions.a: Flat land, rich soil, long sunny growing season and irrigation water from rivers.

questions.q: What jobs fit the coastal region?
questions.a: Fishing, shipping, tourism, trade at ports.

days.guide: The child describes their own region with five details and a photo.

questions.q: What details describe a region?
questions.a: Landforms, climate, plants, animals, water and how people use the land.

days.guide: Give the quiz and the paragraph.

questions.q: Which mountain range runs along California's eastern side?
questions.a: The Sierra Nevada.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Regions: coast, mountains, Central Valley, desert 2) Capital: Sacramento 3) Sierra Nevada = eastern mountain range 4) Central Valley lies between the Coast Ranges and the Sierra Nevada 5) Mojave Desert in the southeast 6) Mild climate along the coast. Paragraph rubric: 4 = names a region, describes 2+ environmental features, explains how they affect jobs, housing or travel with examples; 3 = one feature and effect; 2 = description only; 1 = off-topic.

weeks.prep: California physical map, tracing paper; Library of Congress online 1850s California map (search loc.gov 'California 1850 map').
misconceptions: Thinking cities grew randomly. Most grew near water, harbors, river junctions, passes or fertile valleys.
Thinking the San Joaquin River flows south. It flows north to meet the Sacramento River in the Delta.

days.guide: Trace the Sacramento and San Joaquin Rivers, the Delta and San Francisco Bay.

questions.q: Where do the Sacramento and San Joaquin Rivers meet?
questions.a: In the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, which flows into San Francisco Bay.

questions.q: Which direction does the Sacramento River flow?
questions.a: South (the San Joaquin flows north); both meet in the Delta.

days.guide: Locate Donner, Tehachapi and Cajon Passes and explain why travelers needed them.

questions.q: What is a mountain pass?
questions.a: A low gap through mountains that travelers can cross more easily.

questions.q: Which pass crosses the Sierra Nevada near Lake Tahoe?
questions.a: Donner Pass.

days.guide: Mark 8 cities and explain why each grew there.

questions.q: Why did San Francisco grow?
questions.a: Its large natural harbor on San Francisco Bay made it a port for shipping and Gold Rush arrivals.

questions.q: Why did San Diego grow?
questions.a: It has a protected natural harbor.

days.guide: Compare place names on an 1850s map to today.

questions.q: Why might place names be in Spanish?
questions.a: Spanish explorers, missionaries and Mexican Californios named many places before statehood (e.g., Los Angeles, San Francisco, Sacramento).

days.guide: The child writes why Sacramento grew where two rivers meet.

questions.q: Which two rivers meet at Sacramento?
questions.a: The Sacramento and American Rivers.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = explains that Sacramento grew where the American and Sacramento Rivers meet; rivers allowed boats to carry goods and people from San Francisco Bay; nearness to the gold fields (gold found on the American River) and Sutter's Fort; fertile valley; 3 = two reasons; 2 = one reason; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Photos of Los Angeles, Fresno suburbs and a Modoc County ranch; county population density chart (U.S. Census/QuickFacts); Calisphere (calisphere.org) set 'City Scenes in California History'; poster board. Unit 1 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking rural means poor or 'less important.' Rural areas grow much of the food and resources cities depend on.
Confusing population with density. Density is people per square mile.

days.guide: Compare the photos for land use, architecture and transportation.

questions.q: How does transportation differ between Los Angeles and a Modoc County ranch?
questions.a: LA has freeways, buses and trains with heavy traffic; rural Modoc has few roads, long distances and people drive trucks.

days.guide: Read the density chart and rank 6 counties.

questions.q: Which county is California's most populous?
questions.a: Los Angeles County (about 10 million people).

questions.q: What does population density mean?
questions.a: How many people live in each square mile.

days.guide: Analyze 3 Calisphere images: what changed and what stayed the same?

questions.q: What questions help analyze a historical photo?
questions.a: Who/what is shown, when and where was it taken, what has changed since then, what has stayed the same.

days.guide: Create a community profile poster.

questions.q: What services does a community provide?
questions.a: Schools, libraries, police, fire, parks, water and trash.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test.

questions.q: Name an urban, a suburban and a rural community.
questions.a: Urban: Los Angeles or San Francisco; suburban: neighborhoods around Fresno or Sacramento; rural: a Modoc County ranch area.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test key: 1) Latitude/longitude definitions 2) California in Northern and Western Hemispheres 3) Four regions 4) Capital Sacramento 5) Sierra Nevada, Central Valley, Mojave located on map 6) Rivers meet in the Delta; Sacramento + American Rivers at Sacramento 7) Passes help travel through mountains 8) Urban/suburban/rural definitions 9) Population density = people per square mile 10) Why one city grew where it did. Community profile rubric: 4 = climate, land use, services, transportation with accurate details and visuals; 3 = 3 areas; 2 = 2; 1 = incomplete. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: Map of California Indian language groups/tribal territories (e.g., from a California Indian Library collection or textbook), Calisphere set 'Native Americans: Pre-Columbian.' Homelands: Chumash — Santa Barbara coast and Channel Islands; Tongva — Los Angeles Basin; Ohlone — San Francisco Bay to Monterey; Miwok — Sierra foothills, Central Valley and Marin coast; Pomo — north coast and Clear Lake; Yurok — Klamath River and northwest coast; Mojave — Colorado River; Kumeyaay — San Diego area.
misconceptions: Thinking California Indians were one group. Over 100 distinct nations spoke many languages.
Talking about Native peoples only in the past tense. Many nations are thriving communities today.

days.guide: Label the 8 homelands on the map.

questions.q: Where were the Chumash homelands?
questions.a: The Santa Barbara coast and the Channel Islands.

questions.q: Which nation lived along the Colorado River?
questions.a: The Mojave.

days.guide: Chart how coastal, valley, mountain and desert peoples got food and shelter.

questions.q: How did coastal peoples like the Chumash get food?
questions.a: Fishing, gathering shellfish, hunting sea mammals, and gathering acorns and seeds.

questions.q: How did the Mojave farm in the desert?
questions.a: They planted corn, beans and squash in soil left by the Colorado River's floods.

days.guide: Examine Calisphere images; describe tools and dwellings.

questions.q: Name a type of California Indian dwelling.
questions.a: Tule-reed or brush houses (Chumash domed houses of willow and tule), redwood plank houses (Yurok), bark houses (Miwok).

days.guide: Read about acorn processing and sequence the steps.

questions.q: List the steps of acorn processing.
questions.a: Gather acorns → dry and store → crack and shell → grind into flour in a mortar → leach with water to remove bitter tannins → cook as mush or bread (often with hot stones in baskets).

days.guide: The child writes a paragraph on one nation's adaptation.

questions.q: Example: How did the Yurok adapt to their environment?
questions.a: They lived along the Klamath River, fished for salmon, built redwood plank houses and dugout redwood canoes.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = names one nation and its region, explains 2-3 specific adaptations (food, shelter, tools, clothing) linked to the environment; 3 = two adaptations; 2 = general; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Calisphere set 'Native Americans: Arts and Traditions,' paper and yarn for basket-pattern drawing, a California map.
misconceptions: Thinking Native people simply 'lived off the land' without managing it. They actively managed land with burning, pruning and harvesting practices.
Thinking there was no trade. Extensive trade networks moved shells, obsidian, salt and other goods.

days.guide: Read about the Chumash tomol and draw a labeled diagram.

questions.q: How was a tomol built?
questions.a: Planks (often redwood driftwood or pine) were split, shaped, sewn together with plant-fiber cord and sealed with a tar (asphaltum) and pine-pitch mixture called yop.

questions.q: Why was the tomol important?
questions.a: It allowed travel and trade between the mainland and Channel Islands and deep-sea fishing.

days.guide: Study basket images; describe patterns and uses.

questions.q: Name three uses of baskets.
questions.a: Cooking (with hot stones), storing food, gathering seeds, carrying babies, and ceremonies.

days.guide: Read about controlled burns.

questions.q: How did controlled burns help?
questions.a: They cleared brush, encouraged new growth of food plants and basketry materials, improved hunting grounds and reduced big wildfires.

days.guide: Map trade of shell beads, obsidian and salt.

questions.q: Why was obsidian valuable?
questions.a: It is volcanic glass that can be chipped into very sharp arrowheads and knives.

questions.q: Where did shell beads come from?
questions.a: Coastal peoples like the Chumash made beads from shells; they were traded inland and used like money.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What is asphaltum used for?
questions.a: Waterproofing canoes and baskets and attaching tools.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Tomol = Chumash plank canoe sealed with tar 2) Baskets used for cooking, storage, carrying 3) Controlled burns improved plant growth and hunting and reduced wildfires 4) Shell beads used as money/trade 5) Obsidian traded for tools 6) Salt traded from areas where it was gathered 7) Trade connected coastal, valley, mountain and desert nations. Proficient: 6/7.

weeks.prep: A collection of California Indian stories (library), source cards (basket, photograph, textbook, oral story recording, diary, encyclopedia, mission record, painting, interview, map). Read the creation story ahead to answer from your version.
misconceptions: Calling Native stories 'just myths.' They are sacred oral traditions that carry history, values and knowledge.
Thinking an oral story recording is secondary. A recording of a tradition-bearer telling their people's story is a primary source.

days.guide: Read a Chumash or Miwok creation story; identify what it teaches about nature.

questions.q: What does your story teach about the natural world?
questions.a: Answers depend on the story; e.g., it explains how animals or landforms came to be and teaches respect for animals and land.

days.guide: Discuss how oral tradition preserves history and values.

questions.q: How is history passed on through oral tradition?
questions.a: Elders tell stories, songs and teachings to younger generations, who memorize and retell them.

days.guide: Sort 10 sources as primary or secondary.

questions.q: Is a basket made in 1850 primary or secondary?
questions.a: Primary — an object made at the time.

questions.q: Is a textbook primary or secondary?
questions.a: Secondary — written later by someone not there.

days.guide: Read about the World Renewal ceremony of the Karuk and Hupa.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the World Renewal ceremony?
questions.a: To renew and balance the world, ensuring plentiful food (salmon, acorns) and well-being; it includes dances such as the White Deerskin Dance and Jump Dance.

days.guide: The child writes a reflection on how legends connect people and place.

questions.q: How do legends connect people to a place?
questions.a: They name and explain local landforms, animals and events, so the land itself holds the people's history and values.

weeks.assessment_key: Source sort key: primary — basket, photograph, oral story recording by a tradition bearer, diary, mission record, interview with an eyewitness, map made at the time; secondary — textbook, encyclopedia, modern painting of the past. Reflection rubric: 4 = explains with a specific story example how legends teach values and tie people to local places; 3 = general; 2 = vague; 1 = off-topic.

weeks.prep: Calisphere set 'Native Americans: 20th Century to Today,' tribal websites (e.g., Yurok Tribe yuroktribe.org, Chumash, Tongva). Unit 2 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking California Indian cultures disappeared. Today California has more Native people than any other state and over 100 federally recognized tribes.
Assuming all tribes are the same today. Each has its own government, language programs and traditions.

days.guide: Explore images; list what continued and changed.

questions.q: Name something that has continued.
questions.a: Basket weaving, ceremonies (e.g., World Renewal), language, tomol voyages (the Chumash revived them), tribal governments.

days.guide: Read about Yurok language revitalization.

questions.q: Why are language programs important?
questions.a: Many California Indian languages were nearly lost; teaching them to children keeps culture, knowledge and identity alive. Yurok is now taught in some local schools.

days.guide: Write 5 questions for a tribal historian.

questions.q: Give one respectful, open question.
questions.a: 'What traditions are most important to your community today?'

days.guide: Create a mini-book on one nation.

questions.q: What sections belong in the mini-book?
questions.a: Land, food, shelter, beliefs and today's community.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test.

questions.q: Name two California Indian nations and their regions.
questions.a: E.g., Chumash — Santa Barbara coast; Yurok — Klamath River.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test key: 1) Locate Chumash, Tongva, Ohlone, Miwok, Pomo, Yurok, Mojave, Kumeyaay on a map 2) Acorn processing steps 3) Tomol canoe 4) Controlled burns 5) Trade goods: shell beads, obsidian, salt 6) Oral tradition preserves history 7) Primary vs. secondary 8) World Renewal ceremony purpose 9) Example of revitalization today. Mini-book rubric: 4 = accurate sections on land, food, shelter, beliefs and today with illustrations; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing sections; 1 = incomplete. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: World map, timeline strip. Facts: Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo sailed for Spain in 1542, entered San Diego Bay, died during the voyage (1543). Francis Drake (England) landed in 1579 north of San Francisco (likely Drakes Bay), claimed 'Nova Albion' for England. Sebastián Vizcaíno (Spain) sailed in 1602, named Monterey Bay for the viceroy (Count of Monterey) and praised it. Manila galleons sailed between Manila and Acapulco from 1565.
misconceptions: Thinking explorers 'discovered' an empty land. Native nations had lived there for thousands of years.
Mixing up explorers' countries. Cabrillo and Vizcaíno sailed for Spain; Drake for England.

days.guide: Read about Cabrillo; trace his route.

questions.q: When did Cabrillo reach California and which bay did he enter?
questions.a: In 1542; he entered San Diego Bay (he called it San Miguel).

questions.q: What was Cabrillo looking for?
questions.a: Riches and a sea passage connecting the Pacific and Atlantic (Strait of Anián).

days.guide: Read about Drake's 1579 landing and compare motives.

questions.q: Why was Drake on the Pacific coast?
questions.a: He was raiding Spanish ships and towns for treasure and looking for a way home; he repaired his ship, the Golden Hind, and claimed the land for England.

days.guide: Read about Vizcaíno and Monterey.

questions.q: Why did Vizcaíno's report about Monterey matter?
questions.a: He described it as an excellent harbor, which later encouraged Spain to settle there (1770).

days.guide: Explain why Spain needed a California port for the Manila galleons.

questions.q: Why did the Manila galleons need a port?
questions.a: After months crossing the Pacific from the Philippines, sailors were sick (scurvy) and needed fresh water, food and repairs before reaching Acapulco.

days.guide: Create a timeline with routes and motives.

questions.q: Put in order: Vizcaíno, Cabrillo, Drake.
questions.a: Cabrillo (1542), Drake (1579), Vizcaíno (1602).

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline rubric: 4 = Cabrillo 1542 (Spain, riches/passage, San Diego Bay), Drake 1579 (England, treasure, Nova Albion claim), Vizcaíno 1602 (Spain, mapped coast, named Monterey), Manila galleon trade explained; routes drawn; 3 = one error; 2 = missing motives; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Map, Calisphere set 'Early California Exploration and Settlement.' Facts: Juan Bautista de Anza led expeditions in 1774 and 1775-76 from Tubac (Sonora, now Arizona) — the second brought about 240 settlers who founded the San Francisco presidio and mission in 1776. Russians built Fort Ross in 1812 on the Sonoma coast to hunt sea otters and grow food for Russian Alaska; it was sold to John Sutter in 1841. Unit 3 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking only Spain was interested in California. Russia and England also had interests, which pushed Spain to settle.
Thinking Fort Ross was only Russians. Alaska Native hunters (Alutiiq and others) and local Kashaya Pomo also lived and worked there.

days.guide: Trace Anza's route.

questions.q: Why was Anza's overland route important?
questions.a: It created a land route to bring settlers and livestock to Alta California instead of risky sea voyages; his settlers founded San Francisco in 1776.

days.guide: Read about Fort Ross.

questions.q: Why did the Russians build Fort Ross?
questions.a: To hunt sea otters for valuable furs and to grow food for Russian settlements in Alaska.

questions.q: What happened to Fort Ross?
questions.a: Sea otters were overhunted, farming failed, and Russia sold it to John Sutter in 1841.

days.guide: Analyze Calisphere images.

questions.q: What can a drawing of a mission or ship tell us?
questions.a: Clothing, buildings, tools and who was present at the time; also the artist's point of view.

days.guide: Compare Spanish, English and Russian goals.

questions.q: What were Spain's goals?
questions.a: Claim land, spread Catholicism, protect trade routes, keep other empires out.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test.

questions.q: Which explorer named Monterey?
questions.a: Sebastián Vizcaíno (1602).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test key: 1) Cabrillo 1542, Spain, San Diego Bay 2) Drake 1579, England, Nova Albion 3) Vizcaíno 1602, named Monterey 4) Manila galleons needed a port for supplies 5) Anza's land route, San Francisco settled 1776 6) Fort Ross 1812, Russians, sea otters 7) Fort Ross sold to Sutter 1841 8) Compare motives (wealth, claim land, religion, furs). Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: Map, Calisphere set 'Hispanic Americans: Spanish Colonization,' an excerpt of Juan Crespí's diary (many textbook/online excerpts). Facts: in 1769 Gaspar de Portolá (military leader) and Father Junípero Serra founded San Diego (presidio and mission); Portolá marched north, missed Monterey Bay, and his scouts saw San Francisco Bay; Monterey was founded in 1770. Preview: Kumeyaay resisted the newcomers (an attack on the San Diego mission in 1769 and a larger revolt in 1775).
misconceptions: Thinking Spanish colonization was peaceful for everyone. Native people lost land and freedom and often resisted.
Confusing Portolá and Serra's roles. Portolá led soldiers and was governor; Serra led the Franciscan missionaries.

days.guide: Read about Spain's reasons for colonizing Alta California.

questions.q: Give three reasons Spain colonized Alta California.
questions.a: To keep Russia and England out, to spread Catholicism to Native people, and to expand the empire and provide ports.

days.guide: Trace the 1769 route.

questions.q: What was founded at San Diego in 1769?
questions.a: The first presidio and mission (San Diego de Alcalá).

questions.q: What did Portolá's party see that later became important?
questions.a: San Francisco Bay.

days.guide: Read Crespí's diary excerpt and list observations.

questions.q: Why is Crespí's diary a primary source?
questions.a: He was a Franciscan priest on the expedition and wrote what he saw at the time.

days.guide: Discuss the Kumeyaay perspective.

questions.q: How might the Kumeyaay have viewed the newcomers?
questions.a: With curiosity at first, then concern or anger as soldiers took land and resources and tried to change their way of life; some resisted.

days.guide: Write about the goals of soldiers, missionaries and Native people.

questions.q: What were the soldiers' goals?
questions.a: Protect Spain's claim, guard missions and control the land.

weeks.assessment_key: Writing rubric: 4 = explains soldiers (protect claim/control), missionaries (convert to Catholicism, build missions), Native people (keep land, families, beliefs and way of life) with specific examples; 3 = all three groups, general; 2 = two groups; 1 = one group.

weeks.prep: California map, list of the 21 missions with founding dates (from San Diego de Alcalá 1769 to San Francisco Solano in Sonoma 1823), Calisphere set 'California Missions.'
misconceptions: Thinking missions were placed randomly. They were placed near water, fertile soil and Native villages, about a day's travel apart along El Camino Real.
Thinking missions were only churches. They were large communities with farms, workshops and livestock.

days.guide: Map all 21 missions with dates along El Camino Real.

questions.q: Which was the first mission and which the last?
questions.a: First: San Diego de Alcalá (1769). Last: San Francisco Solano in Sonoma (1823).

questions.q: About how far apart were missions?
questions.a: About a day's journey (roughly 30 miles) along El Camino Real.

days.guide: Identify why missions were placed near water, soil and villages.

questions.q: Why build near Native villages?
questions.a: Missionaries wanted to convert Native people and needed their labor.

days.guide: Explain how missions expanded Spain's and Catholicism's influence.

questions.q: How did missions help Spain claim land?
questions.a: They created permanent settlements with people, farms and churches that showed Spanish control.

days.guide: Compare two missions' layouts in images.

questions.q: What was the quadrangle?
questions.a: The central courtyard surrounded by the church, living quarters and workshops.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What does El Camino Real mean?
questions.a: 'The Royal Road' — the route connecting the missions.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 21 missions 2) First: San Diego de Alcalá 1769 3) Last: San Francisco Solano, Sonoma, 1823 4) Connected by El Camino Real 5) Placed near fresh water, fertile soil, Native villages, and about a day apart 6) Locate 3 missions on a map (e.g., San Carlos Borromeo in Carmel, Santa Barbara, San Gabriel). Proficient: 5/6.

weeks.prep: Calisphere sets 'California Missions' and 'Native Americans and Contact.' Preview: readings describe forced labor, punishment and disease; the Native population fell sharply during the mission period.
misconceptions: Presenting mission life only through the missionaries' view. Include Native experiences and resistance.
Thinking disease was caused by bad behavior. European diseases like measles and smallpox were new to Native people, who had no immunity.

days.guide: Make an hour-by-hour schedule of a typical mission day.

questions.q: What signaled the times of day at a mission?
questions.a: Bells (for prayer, meals and work).

days.guide: Read accounts of Native life at missions.

questions.q: Why did many Native people die at missions?
questions.a: Diseases like measles and smallpox spread quickly in crowded conditions; poor food and hard labor also weakened people.

questions.q: Could neophytes (baptized Native people) leave freely?
questions.a: No — they were usually not allowed to leave without permission and were sometimes brought back by soldiers and punished.

days.guide: Explain economic change to agriculture and ranching.

questions.q: How did the missions change California's economy?
questions.a: They introduced cattle, sheep, wheat, grapes and orchards, shifting from hunting and gathering to farming and ranching.

days.guide: Analyze an image with See-Think-Wonder.

questions.q: What are the three steps of See-Think-Wonder?
questions.a: See: describe what is shown. Think: what it might mean. Wonder: questions it raises.

days.guide: Write a paragraph about how missions changed Native lives.

questions.q: Name two changes.
questions.a: Loss of land and freedom; new religion, language and work; disease and population decline; loss of traditional food sources.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = topic sentence plus at least three accurate changes (loss of land/freedom, forced labor, disease, new religion/language, farming) with a detail and a concluding sentence; 3 = two changes; 2 = one change; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Map, Calisphere images. Facts: four presidios — San Diego (1769), Monterey (1770), San Francisco (1776), Santa Barbara (1782). Pueblos — San José (1777, first civilian town) and Los Angeles (1781). Los Angeles was founded by 44 pobladores (11 families) of Spanish, Native American and African ancestry.
misconceptions: Thinking all Spanish settlers were from Spain. Many pobladores were mestizo, Native and of African ancestry from New Spain (Mexico).
Mixing up purposes. Missions = religion; presidios = military; pueblos = towns and farms.

days.guide: Read about the four presidios.

questions.q: What was a presidio's purpose?
questions.a: A fort where soldiers protected Spain's claim and the missions.

days.guide: Read about San José and Los Angeles.

questions.q: Why were pueblos founded?
questions.a: To grow food and raise livestock for the presidios and to bring civilian settlers.

days.guide: Read about Los Pobladores.

questions.q: Who founded Los Angeles in 1781?
questions.a: 44 settlers (11 families) from Sonora and Sinaloa of mixed Spanish, Native and African heritage.

days.guide: Compare mission, presidio and pueblo.

questions.q: Who lived in each?
questions.a: Mission: priests and Native neophytes; presidio: soldiers and families; pueblo: civilian settler families.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: Name the four presidios.
questions.a: San Diego, Monterey, San Francisco, Santa Barbara.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Mission purpose: convert Native people to Catholicism; farming 2) Presidio: military protection 3) Pueblo: civilian town to grow food 4) Four presidios: San Diego, Monterey, San Francisco, Santa Barbara 5) Pueblos: San José 1777, Los Angeles 1781 6) Los Angeles's 44 pobladores were of diverse backgrounds. Proficient: 5/6.

weeks.prep: Short accounts from a Franciscan, a soldier and a Native leader; a reading on Toypurina (Tongva woman who in 1785 helped plan a revolt at Mission San Gabriel). Unit 4 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking there was one 'true' view of the missions. Different groups experienced them differently; historians use multiple sources.
Treating Native people only as victims. Many resisted — revolts, running away, keeping traditions.

days.guide: Read three perspective accounts.

questions.q: How might a Franciscan priest view the missions differently from a Native leader?
questions.a: The priest saw them as saving souls and 'civilizing'; a Native leader saw loss of land, freedom and culture.

days.guide: Read about Toypurina.

questions.q: Who was Toypurina and what did she do?
questions.a: A Tongva spiritual leader who in 1785 helped organize a revolt against Mission San Gabriel; it was stopped, and she was put on trial and exiled.

days.guide: Discuss the legacy of missions today.

questions.q: Name a legacy of the missions.
questions.a: Place names (San Diego, Santa Barbara), Spanish-style architecture, mission buildings as museums, and painful history for Native descendants.

days.guide: The child writes an informative essay on how missions affected different groups.

questions.q: What groups should the essay cover?
questions.a: Native Californians, Spanish missionaries and soldiers/settlers.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test.

questions.q: Which mission is the 'first'?
questions.a: San Diego de Alcalá (1769).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test key: 1) Spain's reasons for colonizing 2) 1769 Portolá and Serra at San Diego 3) 21 missions along El Camino Real 4) Placement near water, soil, villages 5) Mission daily life ruled by bells 6) Economic change to farming and ranching 7) Disease reduced Native populations 8) Presidio and pueblo purposes 9) Toypurina's 1785 resistance. Essay rubric: 4 = introduction, paragraphs on 2-3 groups with accurate facts, conclusion; 3 = two groups; 2 = one group; 1 = incomplete. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: Maps of North America in 1819 and 1822; an excerpt from Richard Henry Dana's 'Two Years Before the Mast' (1840) describing hides — he called them 'California bank-notes.' Facts: Mexico's war for independence began in 1810 (Father Miguel Hidalgo's call, Sept 16) and ended in 1821.
misconceptions: Thinking California became American right after Spain. It was part of Mexico from 1822 to 1848.
Confusing Mexican Independence Day (September 16) with Cinco de Mayo (a later battle in 1862).

days.guide: Read about the 1810-1821 Mexican War for Independence.

questions.q: When did Mexico win independence from Spain?
Who began the independence movement in 1810?
questions.a: Father Miguel Hidalgo.

days.guide: Compare maps before and after 1821.

questions.q: Who controlled Alta California after 1821?
questions.a: Mexico.

days.guide: List effects on Alta California's government and trade.

questions.q: How did trade change under Mexico?
questions.a: Mexico allowed trade with foreign ships (American, British), unlike Spain's restrictions.

days.guide: Read about the hide and tallow trade and the Dana excerpt.

questions.q: What did Yankee ships trade for California hides?
questions.a: Manufactured goods like cloth, shoes, tools and furniture; hides went to New England to make leather.

days.guide: Complete the cause-and-effect chart.

questions.q: What was one effect of Mexican independence on the missions?
questions.a: Mexico moved to secularize the missions (done in 1834).

weeks.assessment_key: Chart key: cause — Mexico wins independence (1821); effects — Alta California becomes part of Mexico; new Mexican governors; foreign trade allowed (hide and tallow trade with American ships); missions secularized (1834); land grants create ranchos. Proficient: 4 accurate effects.

weeks.prep: Calisphere set 'Californio Society,' an image of a diseño (hand-drawn rancho map — many at the Library of Congress/Bancroft Library).
misconceptions: Thinking Native people received mission lands. The law intended that, but most land went to Californio families through land grants.
Thinking diseños were exact surveys. They were rough sketches using landmarks like rivers, trees and hills.

days.guide: Read about the 1834 secularization.

questions.q: What does secularization of the missions mean?
questions.a: Taking control of mission lands away from the Catholic Church and placing them under the Mexican government.

days.guide: Examine a diseño and explain how land was granted.

questions.q: What is a diseño?
questions.a: A hand-drawn map showing a rancho's boundaries using landmarks, submitted to request a land grant.

questions.q: Who could apply for land grants?
questions.a: Mexican citizens, including Californios and some naturalized foreigners.

days.guide: Discuss outcomes for Native peoples.

questions.q: What happened to most Native people after secularization?
questions.a: Most did not receive land; many worked as laborers on ranchos, and some returned to their homelands or moved inland.

days.guide: Analyze Californio Society images.

questions.q: Who were the Californios?
questions.a: Spanish-speaking people of Mexican and Spanish heritage born in California.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: When were the missions secularized?
questions.a: Beginning in 1834.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Secularization = mission lands taken from the Church by Mexico, 1834 2) Lands were supposed to go to Native people 3) Most went to Californios as ranchos 4) Diseño = hand-drawn rancho map with landmarks 5) Land grants were given by the Mexican governor 6) Native people often became rancho workers. Proficient: 5/6.

weeks.prep: Calisphere set 'Californio Society,' biographies of Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo and Pío Pico, map. Unit 5 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking cowboy culture started in Texas. Vaqueros in Mexico and California developed roping, riding and gear later used by American cowboys.
Thinking rancho life was the same for everyone. Rancho owners lived well; Native workers did much of the hard labor.

days.guide: Read about rancho life; list jobs of each family member.

questions.q: What were rancho products?
questions.a: Cattle hides and tallow (fat for candles and soap).

days.guide: Read about vaqueros.

questions.q: Name two vaquero contributions to American cowboy culture.
questions.a: The lariat/lasso (la reata), the rodeo, the saddle horn, chaps (chaparreras) and spurs.

days.guide: Read biographies of Vallejo and Pío Pico.

questions.q: Who was Pío Pico?
questions.a: The last governor of Mexican California, of mixed African, Native and Spanish ancestry.

questions.q: Who was Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo?
questions.a: A Californio military commander at Sonoma with large ranchos; he later supported joining the U.S. and helped write California's first constitution.

days.guide: Map Mexican settlements, Fort Ross and Sutter's Fort.

questions.q: Where was Sutter's Fort?
questions.a: In the Sacramento Valley, at present-day Sacramento (New Helvetia).

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test.

questions.q: What were hides called in the trade?
questions.a: 'California bank notes.'

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test key: 1) Mexico independent 1821 2) Foreign trade opened; hide and tallow trade 3) Secularization 1834 4) Diseño and land grants 5) Rancho products: hides and tallow 6) Vaqueros' skills shaped the cowboy 7) Vallejo — Sonoma commander, later helped write the constitution 8) Pío Pico — last Mexican governor 9) Sutter's Fort location. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: U.S. map, Calisphere set 'Transportation in California History,' Virginia Reed's 1847 letter excerpt (widely reprinted). Facts: the Bidwell-Bartleson party (1841) was the first organized emigrant group to cross overland to California (they abandoned their wagons before the Sierra); James Beckwourth found Beckwourth Pass (1850); the Donner Party (1846-47) took the untested Hastings Cutoff, was trapped by snow near what is now Donner Lake, and about half died. Preview: the Donner story involves starvation; choose an age-appropriate account.
misconceptions: Thinking the overland trail was the fastest route. It took about 4-6 months; the Panama route could take 6-8 weeks if ships connected.
Thinking push and pull factors are the same. Push = reasons to leave home; pull = reasons attracted to California.

days.guide: List and rank push and pull factors.

questions.q: Give a push factor and a pull factor.
questions.a: Push: hard times or crowded farms back East. Pull: free or cheap land, mild climate, trade, adventure.

days.guide: Read about the Bidwell-Bartleson party; trace its route.

questions.q: Why is the 1841 Bidwell-Bartleson party important?
questions.a: It was the first organized group of American emigrants to travel overland to California; John Bidwell later founded Chico.

days.guide: Read about James Beckwourth; mark Beckwourth Pass.

questions.q: Who was James Beckwourth?
questions.a: An African American mountain man and trapper who found a lower, easier pass through the northern Sierra Nevada (Beckwourth Pass) and led emigrants over it.

days.guide: Read about the Donner Party and Virginia Reed's letter; list decisions that led to disaster.

questions.q: What decisions led to the Donner Party's disaster?
questions.a: Taking the untested Hastings Cutoff, which cost weeks; starting late in the season; delays and conflicts; reaching the Sierra just as heavy snow began.

questions.q: What advice did Virginia Reed give?
questions.a: 'Never take no cutoffs and hurry along as fast as you can.'

days.guide: Compare the three routes in a chart.

questions.q: What was the main danger on the Panama route?
questions.a: Tropical diseases such as malaria, yellow fever and cholera.

weeks.assessment_key: Chart key: Cape Horn — about 5-8 months by ship, around South America (13,000+ miles), storms, seasickness, scurvy, moderate-to-high cost; Panama — 6-8 weeks if connections worked, ship + crossing the Isthmus by canoe/mule (railroad from 1855), tropical diseases, most expensive; Overland — 4-6 months, about 2,000 miles by wagon from Missouri, river crossings, deserts, mountains, snow, sickness, cheapest. Proficient: accurate time, cost and dangers for all three.

weeks.prep: Image of the original Bear Flag (search Calisphere 'Bear Flag'; the original was destroyed in the 1906 San Francisco fire, but photos exist), map of Sonoma. Facts: on June 14, 1846, American settlers seized Sonoma, arrested General Vallejo and declared the 'California Republic,' which lasted about 25 days until the U.S. Navy raised the U.S. flag at Monterey (July 7, 1846).
misconceptions: Thinking the Bear Flag Revolt was a big war. It was a small uprising that lasted about 25 days and was absorbed into the Mexican-American War.
Thinking Vallejo opposed the United States. He actually favored joining the U.S., yet was imprisoned by the rebels.

days.guide: Read about tensions in the 1840s.

questions.q: Why were Mexican officials worried about American settlers?
questions.a: Growing numbers of Americans were arriving without permission and some wanted California to join the U.S.

days.guide: Read about Frémont.

questions.q: Who was John C. Frémont?
questions.a: A U.S. Army explorer and mapmaker ('the Pathfinder') who was in California in 1846 and supported the Bear Flaggers, later leading the California Battalion.

days.guide: Read about the capture of Sonoma; sequence events.

questions.q: What happened on June 14, 1846?
questions.a: Americans seized Sonoma, took Vallejo prisoner and declared the California Republic.

days.guide: Analyze the Bear Flag photo.

questions.q: What symbols are on the Bear Flag?
questions.a: A grizzly bear (strength), a red star (inspired by Texas's Lone Star Republic), a red stripe, and the words 'California Republic.'

days.guide: Write two journal entries: settler and Vallejo.

questions.q: How might Vallejo feel about being arrested?
questions.a: Shocked and betrayed — he had been friendly to Americans and favored joining the U.S.

weeks.assessment_key: Journal rubric: 4 = two entries in first person with accurate facts (date, Sonoma, Vallejo's arrest, the flag) and clearly different viewpoints (settler: freedom/land; Vallejo: betrayal, concern for family and property); 3 = accurate but similar viewpoints; 2 = few facts; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Maps of North America in 1846 and 1848. Facts: the war began in 1846 over the Texas border dispute and U.S. expansion; Commodore John Sloat raised the U.S. flag at Monterey on July 7, 1846; at the Battle of San Pasqual (December 6, 1846) Californio lancers under Andrés Pico inflicted heavy losses on General Stephen Kearny's troops; the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (February 2, 1848) ended the war — Mexico gave up about half its territory (the Mexican Cession) and the U.S. paid $15 million; Mexicans living there could stay and become U.S. citizens, with property rights promised. Unit 6 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking the treaty's promises were all kept. Many Californios later lost land in long, costly court cases.
Thinking the Mexican Cession was only California. It also included Nevada, Utah and parts of Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Wyoming.

days.guide: Read about causes and the raising of the U.S. flag at Monterey.

questions.q: What were causes of the Mexican-American War?
questions.a: A border dispute after the U.S. annexed Texas and the U.S. desire to expand west (Manifest Destiny).

days.guide: Read about San Pasqual.

questions.q: What happened at the Battle of San Pasqual?
questions.a: Californio lancers on horseback led by Andrés Pico defeated/badly hurt General Kearny's U.S. troops near present-day Escondido (December 1846).

days.guide: Read key promises of the treaty.

questions.q: What did the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo promise Mexicans in the ceded lands?
questions.a: They could stay, become U.S. citizens and keep their property.

days.guide: Color the Mexican Cession and compare borders.

questions.q: Name three present-day states that came from the Mexican Cession.
questions.a: California, Nevada, Utah (also parts of Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado, Wyoming).

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test.

questions.q: When was the treaty signed?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test key: 1) Push/pull factors 2) Bidwell-Bartleson 1841 first overland party 3) Beckwourth Pass 4) Donner Party — Hastings Cutoff, trapped by snow 5) Route comparison 6) Bear Flag Revolt June 14, 1846 at Sonoma 7) Frémont's role 8) U.S. flag at Monterey July 1846 9) Battle of San Pasqual — Andrés Pico 10) Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo 1848 — Mexican Cession, $15 million, citizenship promise. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: Calisphere set 'The Gold Rush Era: Everyday Life and People'; a pie tin, sand, pebbles, gravel painted gold, a tub of water. Facts: James Marshall found gold on January 24, 1848 at John Sutter's sawmill at Coloma on the South Fork of the American River; Sutter wanted it kept secret; in May 1848 Sam Brannan (a merchant who also published the California Star newspaper) ran through San Francisco shouting 'Gold! Gold from the American River!'; President Polk confirmed the discovery in December 1848, setting off the 1849 rush.
misconceptions: Thinking the Gold Rush began in 1849. Gold was found in January 1848; '49ers' arrived in huge numbers in 1849.
Thinking most miners got rich. Most found little; many merchants earned more.

days.guide: Read about Marshall's discovery.

questions.q: Who found gold, when and where?
questions.a: James Marshall, January 24, 1848, at Sutter's Mill in Coloma on the American River.

questions.q: How did John Sutter react?
questions.a: He wanted to keep it secret, fearing his workers would leave and his land would be overrun — which happened.

days.guide: Read Brannan's announcement; track how news spread.

questions.q: Why did Sam Brannan spread the news?
questions.a: He owned a store and wanted to sell mining supplies (he had bought up pans and shovels).

questions.q: How did the news spread around the world?
questions.a: By newspapers, ships, letters and President Polk's December 1848 message to Congress.

days.guide: Pan in the tub; compare pans, rockers and sluices.

questions.q: Why does gold stay in the pan?
questions.a: Gold is much heavier (denser) than sand and gravel, so it sinks to the bottom while water washes lighter material out.

questions.q: Which method could process the most dirt?
questions.a: The sluice (a long box with ridges), worked by teams.

days.guide: Analyze two daguerreotypes with See-Think-Wonder.

questions.q: What is a daguerreotype?
questions.a: An early type of photograph on a silver-coated copper plate (1840s-1850s).

days.guide: Write a Forty-Niner diary entry with five facts.

questions.q: Why were miners called Forty-Niners?
questions.a: Most arrived in 1849.

weeks.assessment_key: Diary rubric: 4 = first-person entry with at least five accurate facts (e.g., Sutter's Mill 1848, route taken, high prices, panning/rockers, tents/camp life, diverse miners) and vivid detail; 3 = 3-4 facts; 2 = 1-2 facts; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Calisphere sets 'African Americans in the Gold Rush' and 'Asian Americans: Gold Rush Era to 1890s'; excerpt of Louise Clappe's 'Shirley Letters' (1851-52, written from Rich Bar on the Feather River). Facts: Biddy Mason was brought to California enslaved, won her freedom in a Los Angeles court in 1856, became a nurse/midwife and landowner, and helped found the First AME Church of Los Angeles. California's 1850 Foreign Miners' Tax charged $20 a month (later a $3/month tax targeted Chinese miners). Preview: violence against Native Californians during this era was severe.
misconceptions: Thinking all miners were white Americans. Miners came from Mexico, Chile, China, Europe, Hawaii, and included African Americans and Native Californians.
Thinking the Foreign Miners' Tax was fair because it applied to 'foreigners.' It was enforced mainly against Mexican, Chilean and Chinese miners to push them out.

days.guide: Read Dame Shirley's excerpt; list camp-life details.

questions.q: Why are the Shirley Letters a valuable primary source?
questions.a: Louise Clappe lived in a mining camp and described daily life, people and events as they happened.

days.guide: Read about Biddy Mason.

questions.q: How did Biddy Mason gain her freedom?
questions.a: She petitioned a Los Angeles court in 1856, which ruled that she and her family were free because California was a free state.

questions.q: What did she do with her freedom?
questions.a: Worked as a nurse and midwife, bought land, became wealthy, and helped found the First AME Church and helped people in need.

days.guide: Analyze images; note who came and from where.

questions.q: Name three places Gold Rush miners came from.
questions.a: China, Mexico, Chile (also Peru, Ireland, Germany, France, Australia, the eastern U.S.).

days.guide: Read about the Foreign Miners' Tax and violence; discuss fairness.

questions.q: Why was the Foreign Miners' Tax unfair?
questions.a: It was aimed at non-white and foreign miners to drive them from the gold fields, and was enforced unequally.

days.guide: Write who profited most from the Gold Rush with evidence.

questions.q: Give evidence that merchants profited.
questions.a: Prices were very high (eggs and tools cost many times normal); merchants like Levi Strauss (dry goods, later jeans) and Sam Brannan grew rich selling supplies.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear claim (usually merchants), two or more pieces of specific evidence (high prices, Levi Strauss, Sam Brannan; most miners found little), counterpoint acknowledged, conclusion; 3 = claim and one piece of evidence; 2 = opinion without evidence; 1 = off-topic.

weeks.prep: Calisphere sets 'Growth of Cities in the Gold Rush Era' and 'Environmental Impact in the Gold Rush Era'; population figures (approx.): California's non-Native population about 14,000 in 1848; about 100,000 by late 1849; about 250,000 by 1852. San Francisco grew from about 500-800 people in 1847-48 to tens of thousands by 1850. A tray of soil and spray bottle. Unit 7 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking the Gold Rush helped everyone. California's Native population fell catastrophically (roughly 150,000 in 1848 to about 30,000 by 1870) from violence, disease and loss of land.
Thinking hydraulic mining only affected the hills. Debris flooded rivers and farms far downstream; it was largely stopped by a court ruling in 1884.

days.guide: Compare San Francisco images from 1847 and 1851.

questions.q: List two changes in San Francisco.
questions.a: It grew from a small village into a crowded city with many buildings, wharves and hundreds of abandoned ships in the harbor.

days.guide: Graph population from 1848 to 1852.

questions.q: About how much did the non-Native population grow from 1848 to 1852?
questions.a: From about 14,000 to about 250,000 — more than 15 times larger.

days.guide: Spray water at a soil hillside to model hydraulic mining.

questions.q: What did the model show?
questions.a: High-pressure water washed away the hillside, sending mud and debris downhill — like real hydraulic mining clogging rivers.

days.guide: Analyze environmental impact images.

questions.q: List two environmental effects of the Gold Rush.
questions.a: Hillsides washed away by hydraulic mining; rivers clogged with sediment and mercury pollution; forests cut; salmon runs harmed.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test and cause-effect chart.

questions.q: Name one long-term effect of the Gold Rush.
questions.a: Rapid statehood (1850), growth of cities like San Francisco and Sacramento, diverse population.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test key: 1) Marshall, Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848 2) Brannan spread the news 3) Forty-Niners 4) Mining methods: pan, rocker, sluice, hydraulic 5) Diverse miners from many nations 6) Foreign Miners' Tax unfair 7) Biddy Mason won freedom 1856 8) Merchants like Levi Strauss profited 9) Population boom; San Francisco grows 10) Environmental damage and Native population decline. Cause-effect chart: proficient lists 4+ accurate effects (statehood, cities, immigration, environmental damage, harm to Native peoples, economic growth).

weeks.prep: Simplified excerpts of the 1849 California Constitution (Online Archive of California / California State Archives), timeline strip. Facts: delegates met at Colton Hall, Monterey, in September-October 1849; 48 delegates including 8 Californios such as Mariano Vallejo; the constitution was published in English and Spanish, banned slavery, set the capital at San Jose, and protected married women's separate property; voting was limited to white men. California became the 31st state on September 9, 1850, as part of the Compromise of 1850.
misconceptions: Thinking California was a territory first. It skipped the territory stage and became a state directly.
Thinking 'free state' meant everyone had equal rights. Native Californians, Chinese immigrants, African Americans and women were denied many rights.

days.guide: Discuss why Gold Rush California needed a government.

questions.q: Why did California need a government quickly?
questions.a: Crime, disputes over mining claims and land, and no courts or laws to settle them as the population exploded.

days.guide: Read about the convention at Colton Hall.

questions.q: Where and when was California's first constitution written?
questions.a: Colton Hall in Monterey, in the fall of 1849.

days.guide: Read constitution excerpts; list 4 key decisions.

questions.q: Name four decisions in the 1849 constitution.
questions.a: Banned slavery; printed laws in English and Spanish; set boundaries; married women could own separate property; (also capital in San Jose; voting limited to white men).

days.guide: Read about the Compromise of 1850.

questions.q: Why was California's admission controversial?
questions.a: Adding a free state would upset the balance between free and slave states in the Senate; the Compromise of 1850 settled this with deals for both sides.

days.guide: Build the statehood timeline.

questions.q: When did California become a state and which number?
questions.a: September 9, 1850; the 31st state.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline key: June 1846 Bear Flag Revolt; July 1846 U.S. flag raised at Monterey; Dec 1846 Battle of San Pasqual; Jan 1848 gold discovered; Feb 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo; 1849 Gold Rush and constitutional convention at Colton Hall; Sept 9, 1850 statehood (31st state, free state, Compromise of 1850). Proficient: 6 events in correct order with illustrations.

weeks.prep: Calisphere set 'Civic Buildings in California History,' an image of the Great Seal of California. Capitals: San Jose (1849-51), Vallejo (1852-53), Benicia (1853-54), Sacramento (1854-present). Unit 8 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking the new government gave everyone a voice. Only white men could vote; Native people could not testify against whites in court.
Thinking the bear on the seal is the main symbol. The central figure is Minerva, Roman goddess of wisdom.

days.guide: Compare lawmaking and rights under Spanish, Mexican and American rule.

questions.q: Who made laws under Spain?
questions.a: The king and his appointed officials (viceroy, governors); under Mexico, a national congress and appointed governors with local councils; under the U.S. state system, elected legislators.

days.guide: Discuss who was left out of rights.

questions.q: Name one way early state laws limited Native Californians.
questions.a: They could not vote, could not testify against white people in court, and a 1850 law allowed them to be forced into labor.

days.guide: Trace the capital's moves.

questions.q: List California's capitals in order.
questions.a: San Jose, Vallejo, Benicia, Sacramento.

days.guide: Analyze the Great Seal.

questions.q: What do the symbols on the Great Seal mean?
questions.a: Minerva (wisdom; California became a state without being a territory, like Minerva born grown), grizzly bear (strength), wheat and grapes (agriculture), miner (Gold Rush), ships (trade), Sierra Nevada, 'Eureka' ('I have found it'), 31 stars (31st state).

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test.

questions.q: What does 'Eureka' mean?
questions.a: 'I have found it.'

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test key: 1) Need for government during the Gold Rush 2) Colton Hall, Monterey, 1849 3) Constitution: no slavery, English/Spanish 4) Compromise of 1850; statehood Sept 9, 1850 5) 31st state 6) Comparison of Spanish, Mexican and American government 7) Groups denied rights: Native Californians, Chinese, African Americans, women 8) Capital moves ending in Sacramento 9) Seal symbols. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: U.S. map, Morse code chart, flashlight, stopwatch. Facts: Butterfield Overland Mail stagecoaches (1858-61) carried mail from Missouri to San Francisco in about 25 days; the Pony Express (April 1860-October 1861) carried mail about 1,900 miles from St. Joseph, Missouri to Sacramento in about 10 days, with riders changing horses every 10-15 miles; the transcontinental telegraph was completed October 24, 1861.
misconceptions: Thinking the Pony Express lasted for decades. It lasted only about 18 months.
Thinking one rider rode the whole way. Riders relayed the mail, each covering roughly 75-100 miles.

days.guide: Read about Butterfield Overland Mail.

questions.q: How long did the stagecoach mail take?
questions.a: About 25 days.

days.guide: Read about the Pony Express; calculate travel time.

questions.q: If the Pony Express covered about 1,900 miles in 10 days, about how far per day?
questions.a: About 190 miles per day.

questions.q: Where did the route start and end?
questions.a: St. Joseph, Missouri to Sacramento, California.

days.guide: Read about the 1861 telegraph; send a Morse message.

questions.q: How long did a telegraph message take?
questions.a: Minutes (almost instantly).

days.guide: Chart message times by ship, stagecoach, Pony Express and telegraph.

questions.q: Order the methods from slowest to fastest.
questions.a: Ship (weeks to months), stagecoach (about 25 days), Pony Express (about 10 days), telegraph (minutes).

days.guide: Write why the Pony Express ended.

questions.q: Why did the Pony Express end?
questions.a: The transcontinental telegraph (October 1861) sent messages almost instantly, and the Pony Express lost money.

weeks.assessment_key: Speed chart: ship around Cape Horn months / via Panama weeks; stagecoach ~25 days; Pony Express ~10 days; telegraph minutes. Paragraph rubric: 4 = explains the telegraph's speed made it obsolete and that it was costly, with dates (1860-61, ~18 months); 3 = main reason only; 2 = vague; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Calisphere set 'The Transcontinental Railroad,' map. Facts: the Central Pacific (from Sacramento, begun 1863) was led by the 'Big Four' — Leland Stanford, Collis Huntington, Mark Hopkins and Charles Crocker; Chinese workers (about 12,000-20,000, most of the workforce) blasted tunnels and built through the Sierra Nevada for lower pay than white workers and without board; the lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869 (Golden Spike) — Chinese workers were not shown in the famous celebration photograph.
misconceptions: Thinking the railroad was built by one company from both coasts. Central Pacific built east from Sacramento; Union Pacific built west from Omaha.
Overlooking Chinese workers' role. They did the most dangerous work in the Sierra.

days.guide: Read about the Big Four.

questions.q: Who were the Big Four?
questions.a: Leland Stanford, Collis Huntington, Mark Hopkins and Charles Crocker — Sacramento merchants who ran the Central Pacific.

days.guide: Read about Chinese workers.

questions.q: Why was the Sierra Nevada the hardest part?
questions.a: Workers had to blast tunnels through solid granite, build on steep cliffs and work through deep snow and avalanches.

questions.q: How were Chinese workers treated unfairly?
questions.a: They were paid less than white workers, had to buy their own food and lodging, and did the most dangerous jobs.

days.guide: Analyze railroad photographs and write captions.

questions.q: What should a good caption include?
questions.a: Who/what is shown, where and when, and why it matters.

days.guide: Read about the Golden Spike ceremony.

questions.q: When and where were the rails joined?
questions.a: May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit, Utah.

questions.q: Who was left out of the famous photo?
questions.a: Chinese workers.

days.guide: Write how the railroad changed California's economy.

questions.q: Name two economic effects.
questions.a: Goods and people traveled coast to coast in about a week instead of months; California farm products could be shipped east; more settlers and businesses came.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = topic sentence plus 3 accurate effects (faster travel ~1 week, shipping crops east, population growth, cheaper goods, rise of railroad monopoly), mention of Chinese labor, conclusion; 3 = two effects; 2 = one; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Calisphere sets 'Chinese Exclusion Act' and 'Diversity in the Changing State,' world map. Facts: the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) banned Chinese laborers from immigrating — the first U.S. law to bar a specific ethnic group; it was extended and not repealed until 1943. Chinese Americans fought back in court (e.g., Yick Wo v. Hopkins, 1886; Wong Kim Ark, 1898, which confirmed citizenship for people born in the U.S.).
misconceptions: Thinking the act was about all immigrants. It specifically targeted Chinese workers.
Thinking immigrants accepted unfair laws silently. Many organized, sued and won important court cases.

days.guide: Map immigrant origins 1850-1900.

questions.q: Name four countries California immigrants came from 1850-1900.
questions.a: China, Mexico, Ireland, Germany (also Chile, Japan, Italy).

days.guide: Analyze 'Diversity in the Changing State' images; list communities.

questions.q: Name a community that formed in this era.
questions.a: Chinatown in San Francisco (also Japanese, Italian, Portuguese, Mexican communities).

days.guide: Read about the Chinese Exclusion Act; analyze a document.

questions.q: What did the Chinese Exclusion Act do?
questions.a: It stopped Chinese laborers from immigrating to the U.S. (from 1882) and kept Chinese immigrants from becoming citizens.

questions.q: When was it repealed?

days.guide: Read about people who defended immigrants' rights.

questions.q: What did the Wong Kim Ark case decide?
questions.a: A person born in the U.S. (even to Chinese parents) is a U.S. citizen (1898).

days.guide: Write whether the act was fair, with two pieces of evidence.

questions.q: Give one piece of evidence that it was unfair.
questions.a: It singled out one ethnic group, even though Chinese workers had built the railroad and contributed to California's economy.

weeks.assessment_key: Response rubric: 4 = clear answer (most will argue it was unfair), two specific pieces of evidence (targeted one group; Chinese contributions to railroad/farming; families separated; repealed in 1943), conclusion; 3 = one piece of evidence; 2 = opinion only; 1 = off-topic.

weeks.prep: Calisphere set 'Everyday Life and People in Late 19th Century California,' citrus crate label images, population data: San Francisco 1850 ~35,000 (1852 state census), 1870 149,473, 1890 298,997, 1910 416,912, 1920 506,676; Los Angeles 1850 1,610, 1870 5,728, 1890 50,395, 1910 319,198, 1920 576,673. Unit 9 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking Los Angeles was always California's biggest city. San Francisco was larger until Los Angeles passed it by 1920.
Thinking crate labels are just art. They were advertising that sold California as a sunny paradise to attract settlers.

days.guide: Read about the 1880s land boom.

questions.q: What caused the 1880s Los Angeles land boom?
questions.a: Railroads (Southern Pacific, then the Santa Fe) reached LA, and a fare war made tickets very cheap, bringing thousands of newcomers.

days.guide: Read about citrus and oil; analyze crate labels.

questions.q: Who discovered oil in Los Angeles in 1892?
questions.a: Edward Doheny.

questions.q: What image did crate labels give of California?
questions.a: Sunny, healthy, abundant land — advertising to attract buyers and settlers.

days.guide: Analyze everyday life images.

questions.q: Name one change in everyday life by the 1890s.
questions.a: Electric streetcars, telephones, larger cities, new schools.

days.guide: Graph SF and LA populations 1850-1920.

questions.q: When did Los Angeles pass San Francisco in population?

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test.

questions.q: Name the Big Four.
questions.a: Stanford, Huntington, Hopkins, Crocker.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test key: 1) Overland Mail ~25 days 2) Pony Express 1860-61, ~10 days 3) Telegraph 1861 ended the Pony Express 4) Big Four and Central Pacific 5) Chinese workers' role and unequal pay 6) Golden Spike May 10, 1869 at Promontory Summit 7) Chinese Exclusion Act 1882 8) Immigrant origins 9) LA boom after railroads 10) LA passed SF by 1920. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: California water project map (California Department of Water Resources), rainfall and population maps, Calisphere set 'Building Bridges, Dams and Power Plants.' Facts: most rain and snow fall in the north and the Sierra, while most people live in the south; William Mulholland's Los Angeles Aqueduct (1913) carried Owens Valley water about 230 miles, leading to conflict ('California Water Wars') as the valley dried; Hetch Hetchy (O'Shaughnessy Dam, 1923) supplies San Francisco despite John Muir's opposition; Shasta Dam (completed 1945) anchors the federal Central Valley Project; the State Water Project (Oroville Dam, California Aqueduct) carries water south.
misconceptions: Thinking water is evenly spread. About two-thirds of precipitation falls in the northern part of the state, but most people live in the south.
Thinking water projects had no downsides. They flooded valleys, harmed fish, and took water from other communities.

days.guide: Compare rainfall and population maps.

questions.q: What problem do the maps show?
questions.a: Most water falls in the north and mountains, but most people and farms are in the south and Central Valley.

days.guide: Read about Mulholland and the LA Aqueduct.

questions.q: Why were Owens Valley residents angry?
questions.a: Los Angeles bought land and water rights and diverted the river, drying up Owens Lake and harming farms; some residents dynamited the aqueduct.

days.guide: Map Hetch Hetchy, Shasta Dam, CVP and SWP.

questions.q: Which city gets water from Hetch Hetchy?
questions.a: San Francisco.

questions.q: Why did John Muir oppose Hetch Hetchy Dam?
questions.a: It flooded a beautiful valley in Yosemite National Park.

days.guide: Analyze photos of dams and power plants.

questions.q: Besides storing water, what do dams provide?
questions.a: Hydroelectric power and flood control.

days.guide: Draw water's path from Sierra snow to your faucet.

questions.q: Describe the path.
questions.a: Snow melts in the Sierra → flows into rivers → stored behind dams in reservoirs → carried by aqueducts/canals → treated at a plant → pipes → your faucet.

weeks.assessment_key: Diagram rubric: 4 = labeled steps from snowpack, rivers, reservoir/dam, aqueduct, treatment, pipes to faucet, naming at least one real project; 3 = steps correct without real project; 2 = missing steps; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Calisphere sets 'The Great Depression: Hard Times,' 'Dust Bowl Migration,' 'Life on the Home Front During World War II' and 'Japanese American Internment'; Dorothea Lange's 'Migrant Mother' (1936, Nipomo, California). Facts: Executive Order 9066 (February 19, 1942) led to the forced removal of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most U.S. citizens, to camps such as Manzanar and Tule Lake; the U.S. formally apologized and paid reparations in 1988. Preview: discuss unfairness and fear sensitively.
misconceptions: Thinking the Japanese American incarceration was about crimes. No one was charged; it was based on ancestry and prejudice.
Thinking Dust Bowl migrants were welcomed. Many were called 'Okies,' faced prejudice and lived in poor camps.

days.guide: Read about the Depression in California; analyze images.

questions.q: What was the Great Depression?
questions.a: A severe economic crisis in the 1930s when banks failed, businesses closed and many people lost jobs.

days.guide: Analyze 'Migrant Mother' and Dust Bowl photos.

questions.q: What does 'Migrant Mother' show?
questions.a: A worried mother with her children in a pea-pickers' camp in 1936, showing the hardship of migrant farm workers.

questions.q: Why did Dust Bowl families come to California?
questions.a: Drought and dust storms ruined farms in Oklahoma, Texas and nearby states; they hoped for farm work in California.

days.guide: Read about the home front.

questions.q: How did WWII change jobs in California?
questions.a: Shipyards (like Kaiser in Richmond) and aircraft factories hired huge numbers of workers, including women ('Rosie the Riveter') and African Americans who moved west.

days.guide: Read about EO 9066; analyze photos.

questions.q: What did Executive Order 9066 lead to?
questions.a: The forced removal and incarceration of about 120,000 Japanese Americans in camps like Manzanar.

questions.q: Was it justified?
questions.a: No — no one was charged with a crime; in 1988 the U.S. apologized and paid reparations.

days.guide: Write a paragraph on how one event changed California.
