weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Start at 3, add 4: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 2) Feature: all terms are odd 3) Start at 50, subtract 6: 50, 44, 38, 32, 26 4) Table In 2, 4, 6 → Out 7, 9, 11: rule add 5 5) In 3, 5, 8 → Out 9, 15, 24: rule ×3 6) Figure n has 3n + 1 tiles pattern: figure 10 = 31 tiles. Project rubric: 4 = clear rule, at least 6 correct terms, 3 accurate observations; 3 = rule and terms correct, observations weak; 2 = errors in terms; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Print the week 1 diagnostic for comparison, a self-check review key, an end-of-year test (key below), poster paper and markers.
misconceptions: Rushing on cumulative tests. Teach: estimate first, then check each answer with the inverse operation.
Forgetting units and labels on project work. Every answer gets a unit (miles, dollars, hours).

days.guide: The child completes the mixed whole-number review, then self-checks and redoes misses.

questions.q: Round 476,512 to the nearest ten thousand.

days.guide: The child completes the fraction, decimal and measurement review and self-checks.

questions.q: Compare 3/4 and 0.7.

days.guide: Give the cumulative assessment without help, then compare scores with the week 1 diagnostic together and celebrate growth.
The child plans a California road trip poster: distances, gas cost and drive time, showing all work.

questions.q: A 360-mile trip at 60 miles per hour takes how long?
questions.a: 6 hours.

questions.q: Gas costs $5 per gallon and the car uses 12 gallons. What is the cost?

days.guide: The child presents the poster to family and writes a reflection on the most improved skill.

questions.q: What skill improved most this year, and what evidence shows it?
questions.a: Answers vary; a strong answer names a skill (e.g., fraction comparison) and cites a test score or example from work.

weeks.assessment_key: End-of-year assessment key (sample items): 1) 504,309 in word form: five hundred four thousand, three hundred nine 2) Round 476,512 to nearest ten thousand: 480,000 3) 63,207 - 28,519 = 34,688 4) 4 × 2,345 = 9,380 5) 38 × 26 = 988 6) 6,432 ÷ 8 = 804 7) 3/4 = 9/12 8) 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 = 4 2/5 9) 5 × 2/3 = 3 1/3 10) 0.75 > 0.7 11) 3 hr 20 min = 200 min 12) Perimeter of 9 ft by 4 ft: 26 ft; area 36 sq ft 13) Angle of 120° is obtuse 14) Factor pairs of 20: 1×20, 2×10, 4×5. Proficient: 80%. Project presentation rubric: 4 = all computations correct and labeled, clear explanation, answers questions; 3 = minor errors; 2 = several errors or unclear; 1 = incomplete.

SCI.overview: Science is taught through hands-on investigations recorded in a science notebook: question, prediction, data, conclusion. Let the child do the building and measuring while you ask 'What do you notice? Why do you think that happened?' and insist on evidence from their data in every explanation (claim-evidence-reasoning). Supervise anything with hot water, glass, eggs or food, and do engineering challenges over several days so there is time to test, fail and improve.

weeks.prep: Composition notebook for science, a ball, wind-up or pull-back toy car, rubber bands. Preview a Mystery Science (free lessons available) energy intro or any short video on 'what makes things go.'
misconceptions: Thinking energy is a substance or only 'electricity.' Energy is the ability to cause change or motion; it shows up as motion, sound, light, heat and electricity.
Thinking a still object has no energy. A stretched rubber band or a lifted ball has stored energy that can become motion.

days.guide: Walk through the house together; the child lists 15 energy examples in a table with columns for type (motion, sound, light, heat, electrical).

questions.q: Is a lamp an example of light, heat or electrical energy?
questions.a: All three: electricity goes in, and it gives off light and some heat.

days.guide: Help the child set up a table of contents and an investigation template: question, prediction, materials, data, conclusion.

questions.q: Why do scientists write a prediction before testing?
questions.a: So they can compare what they expected to what happened and learn from the difference.

days.guide: Stretch a rubber band, wind the toy and lift the ball. Ask where the energy is stored and when it becomes motion.

questions.q: Where is energy stored in a stretched rubber band, and what happens when you let go?
questions.a: It is stored in the stretched band; when released, it changes to motion energy (and some sound).

questions.q: Where did the lifted ball's stored energy come from?
questions.a: From your arm — you used energy to lift it; when dropped, it changes to motion.

days.guide: Watch the intro video and discuss 'What makes things go?' The child writes 3 ideas in the notebook.

questions.q: What makes a moving car go?
questions.a: Energy stored in fuel (gas) or a battery is converted into motion.

days.guide: The child draws and labels 4 energy examples and writes a sentence for each.

questions.q: Give an example of sound energy at home.
questions.a: A doorbell, a vacuum, music from a speaker (anything vibrating to make sound).

weeks.assessment_key: Diagram rubric: 4 = four different, correctly labeled examples (e.g., moving fan = motion, ringing phone = sound, lamp = light, stove = heat) each with an accurate sentence about the energy; 3 = four examples, one mislabeled; 2 = two correct; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Cardboard ramp (1 m if possible), stack of books, marble or toy car, meter stick, stopwatch (phone), paper cup with a doorway cut in the rim. Copy a data table: height, trial 1-3 time, average, cup distance.
misconceptions: Thinking a heavier object always goes faster down a ramp. The main factor here is height; only change one variable at a time.
Recording only one trial. Do 3 trials and average to reduce errors.

days.guide: Build the ramp with 2 books, mark a 1-meter run at the bottom, and practice timing the marble over that distance until times are consistent.

questions.q: Why practice timing before collecting data?
questions.a: To make measurements more accurate and consistent (reduce reaction-time errors).

days.guide: Release the marble from 3 heights (2, 4, 6 books), 3 trials each; record times and averages.

questions.q: Which height gave the fastest (shortest) time?
questions.a: The highest ramp — the marble moves faster when released from higher.

questions.q: What variable did you change? What stayed the same?
questions.a: Changed: ramp height. Same: marble, release method, distance timed, surface.

days.guide: Put the cup at the bottom with its opening facing the ramp; measure how far the marble pushes it at each height.

questions.q: What does the cup distance tell us?
questions.a: How much energy the marble had: the faster marble pushed the cup farther, showing it had more energy.

days.guide: Graph ramp height vs. cup distance; the child writes a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph.

questions.q: Write a claim for this investigation.
questions.a: The faster an object moves, the more energy it has.

days.guide: Give the quiz with 4 scenarios.

questions.q: Which has more energy: a bike rolling slowly or the same bike speeding downhill?
questions.a: The speeding bike — faster motion means more energy.

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric: 4 = Claim: faster objects have more energy; Evidence: specific data (e.g., from 6 books the marble pushed the cup 30 cm vs. 10 cm from 2 books); Reasoning: higher release → greater speed → more energy transferred to the cup; 3 = claim and evidence, weak reasoning; 2 = claim only; 1 = incorrect. Quiz key: faster object has more energy in each scenario (same object compared) — e.g., speeding car > parked car; ball thrown hard > ball tossed gently; marble from higher ramp > lower ramp; fast runner > walker.

weeks.prep: Marbles of two sizes, a ruler with a groove (or two rulers taped side by side), dominoes, two wooden blocks. Find a short car crash test video (e.g., IIHS crash test).
misconceptions: Thinking energy disappears in a collision. It transfers to the other object and changes to sound and heat.
Testing two variables at once. Change only one (e.g., speed) and keep the rest the same.

days.guide: Roll one marble into a still marble in the groove. Observe: the moving marble slows or stops and the other moves.

questions.q: What happens to the energy when the moving marble hits the still one?
questions.a: Energy transfers to the still marble, so it starts moving while the first slows or stops.

days.guide: The child writes 5 testable questions (what will change, what will be measured).

questions.q: Make this testable: 'Do marbles like to crash?'
questions.a: Example: 'Does a heavier rolling marble make the target marble roll farther?'

days.guide: The child picks one question, runs 3 trials and records results.

questions.q: Why run 3 trials?
questions.a: To check that results are consistent and not a fluke.

days.guide: Clap hard and bang blocks together; feel palms warm and hear sound.

questions.q: What other forms of energy appear when objects collide?
questions.a: Sound and heat (the hands get warm).

days.guide: Watch the crash test video; the child explains in writing where the car's energy went.

questions.q: Where does a crashing car's motion energy go?
questions.a: Into crushing (bending) metal, sound, heat, and moving other objects (the dummies, the barrier).

weeks.assessment_key: Write-up rubric: 4 = testable question, prediction, controlled variables named, data from 3 trials, conclusion that explains energy transfer (e.g., more speed → target moved farther); 3 = one part weak; 2 = data incomplete; 1 = no investigation. Crash explanation: energy transferred to deforming the car, sound and heat.

weeks.prep: String, 5-6 metal washers, a ruler or stick for a frame, foam pipe insulation split in half (hardware store), marbles, tape, cups. Bookmark PhET 'Energy Skate Park: Basics' (free, phet.colorado.edu). Unit 1 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking a marble can climb a hill higher than where it started. Without a push, it can't go higher than its starting height because some energy changes to heat and sound.
Believing the pendulum chain moves the same balls back and forth. Energy passes through the middle balls to the last one.

days.guide: Hang 5 washers side by side by strings so they just touch. Pull back one and release; observe the far washer swing out.

questions.q: Why does the washer at the far end move?
questions.a: The energy of the first washer transfers through the middle ones to the last one.

days.guide: Build a foam-tube coaster taped to a wall or chair; measure the marble's speed at the bottom (time over a fixed distance).

questions.q: Where on the coaster is the marble moving fastest?
questions.a: At the bottom of the biggest drop.

days.guide: Add hills of different heights after the first drop and test which the marble clears.

questions.q: Can the marble go over a hill taller than its starting point? Why?
questions.a: No — it only has the energy from its starting height, and some changes to heat/sound from friction, so it can't climb higher than it started.

days.guide: Use the Energy Skate Park simulation: change the starting height and watch speed.

questions.q: In the simulation, where is the skater fastest?
questions.a: At the lowest point of the track.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test.

questions.q: Name two forms energy can change into during a collision.
questions.a: Sound and heat (also motion of the other object).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test key: 1) Energy is the ability to cause motion or change 2) Faster objects have more energy 3) Higher ramp → faster marble → more energy → pushes cup farther 4) In a collision energy transfers to the other object 5) Collisions also produce sound and heat 6) Stored energy examples: stretched rubber band, lifted ball, wound spring 7) A coaster's marble is fastest at the bottom 8) It can't go higher than its start height. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: Plastic wrap, a bowl, rice grains, a metal pot and spoon to bang, a shoebox, rubber bands of different thicknesses, 2 paper cups and 3-5 m of string, a tuning fork if available.
misconceptions: Thinking sound travels best (or only) through air. Sound travels through solids and liquids too — often faster.
Confusing loudness and pitch. Pitch is high/low (vibration speed); loudness depends on how big the vibrations are.

days.guide: Stretch plastic wrap tightly over the bowl, sprinkle rice, and bang a pot nearby. The rice jumps.

questions.q: Why does the rice move when you bang the pot nearby?
questions.a: The pot vibrates, making the air vibrate; those vibrations travel to the plastic wrap and make it (and the rice) vibrate.

days.guide: Build the guitar and test how tightness and thickness change pitch.

questions.q: How does tightening a rubber band change the sound?
questions.a: It makes the pitch higher because the band vibrates faster.

questions.q: Which makes a lower pitch: a thick or thin band?
questions.a: A thick band (vibrates more slowly).

days.guide: Tap a table with your ear on it and then lifted; tap two stones underwater in a tub while listening with an ear to the side.

questions.q: Did the tap sound louder through the table or through air?
questions.a: Through the table — sound travels well through solids.

days.guide: Build a cup telephone; test with string tight vs. loose.

questions.q: Why must the string be tight?
questions.a: A tight string carries the vibrations from one cup to the other; a loose string absorbs them.

days.guide: The child writes how sound energy moved from source to ear in each investigation.

questions.q: Describe the path of sound in the cup telephone.
questions.a: Voice vibrates the cup bottom → string vibrates → other cup bottom vibrates → air → ear.

weeks.assessment_key: Explanation rubric: 4 = for each investigation names the vibrating source, the material it traveled through (air, string, wood, water) and the ear, using the word 'vibration'; correctly states tighter/thinner = higher pitch; 3 = most investigations explained; 2 = vague; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Kitchen thermometer, ice cubes, metal/plastic/wooden spoons, mugs, foil, cloth, paper, timer. Safety: the adult pours hot (not boiling) tap water; test spoon handles with fingertips carefully.
misconceptions: Saying a coat 'makes heat.' Insulators slow heat transfer; they keep your body's heat in.
Thinking cold flows into warm things. Heat moves from warmer to cooler objects.

days.guide: Place three spoons in a mug of hot water; after 1-2 minutes, carefully touch each handle.

questions.q: Which handle warmed first? Why?
questions.a: The metal spoon — metal is a good conductor of heat; plastic and wood are insulators.

days.guide: Wrap equal ice cubes in foil, cloth and paper and one unwrapped; time melting.

questions.q: Which wrapping kept the ice from melting longest?
questions.a: Usually the cloth (it traps air and insulates); report your actual data.

days.guide: Measure warm water temperature every 2 minutes for 20 minutes; graph it.

questions.q: What pattern does the graph show?
questions.a: Temperature drops quickly at first, then more slowly as it nears room temperature.

questions.q: Where does the heat go?
questions.a: Into the cooler air and the cup around it.

days.guide: The child designs a cup cozy from household materials and tests it against a bare cup (same starting temperature, 20 minutes).

questions.q: How do you make the test fair?
questions.a: Same amount and starting temperature of water, same cups, same time, same place.

days.guide: Give the quiz on conductors, insulators and heat transfer.

questions.q: Is foil a conductor or insulator?
questions.a: Conductor (it is metal), although shiny foil can reflect heat.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Heat moves from warmer to cooler 2) Conductor examples: metal spoon, pot, foil 3) Insulator examples: wood, plastic, cloth, foam 4) The metal spoon handle heats first 5) A cozy works by slowing heat transfer 6) Why pot handles are plastic: insulator protects hands. Design rubric: 4 = cozy tested fairly against a control with recorded temperatures and a conclusion; 3 = data but test not fully fair; 2 = no data; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: D-cell batteries, small flashlight bulbs (or LEDs), insulated wires with stripped ends (or foil strips), paper clips, brass fasteners, a buzzer. Bookmark PhET 'Circuit Construction Kit: DC.' Safety: never use wall outlets; batteries only; don't leave a wire connected straight across a battery (it gets hot).
misconceptions: Thinking one wire to a bulb is enough. A circuit must be a complete loop from one end of the battery, through the bulb, back to the other end.
Thinking electricity is 'used up' by the bulb. Energy is transferred to light and heat; the charge flows around the loop.

days.guide: Challenge: light a bulb with one battery and one wire. The child finds and draws 4 arrangements that work.

questions.q: What must touch the bulb to light it?
questions.a: The bulb's tip and its metal side (casing) must each connect to opposite ends of the battery, forming a complete loop.

days.guide: Build a circuit tester with a gap; test 12 objects.

questions.q: Which objects let the bulb light?
questions.a: Metal objects (paper clip, foil, coin, key) — conductors.

questions.q: Which did not?
questions.a: Plastic, rubber, wood, paper, glass — insulators.

days.guide: Make a switch from a paper clip and two brass fasteners on cardboard and add it.

questions.q: How does a switch work?
questions.a: Closing it completes the circuit so current flows; opening it breaks the loop.

days.guide: Build series and parallel circuits in the simulation.

questions.q: If one bulb is removed in a series circuit, what happens?
questions.a: All bulbs go out — there is only one path.

questions.q: In a parallel circuit?
questions.a: The other bulbs stay lit — each has its own path.

days.guide: The child draws a circuit diagram and explains how energy travels.

questions.q: Explain how energy gets from the battery to the light.
questions.a: Stored energy in the battery is carried by electric current through wires to the bulb, where it changes to light and heat.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = correct closed-circuit diagram with battery, wires, switch and bulb; explanation of energy transfer; conductor data table of 12 objects correctly sorted (metals conduct); 3 = minor error; 2 = open circuit drawn or many sorting errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Batteries, LEDs or a buzzer, foil, a clothespin or cardboard flaps, tape, wire. Unit 2 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking devices 'make' energy. They convert energy from one form to another.
Mixing criteria and constraints. Criteria = what success looks like; constraints = limits (materials, time, cost).

days.guide: List 8 home devices and identify input and output energy.

questions.q: What energy goes into a toaster and comes out?
questions.a: Electrical in; heat (and some light) out.

questions.q: What about a fan?
questions.a: Electrical in; motion (and some sound/heat) out.

days.guide: Define the door alarm problem with criteria (lights/buzzes when the door opens, loud enough to hear) and constraints (only household materials, safe battery power).

questions.q: Give a criterion and a constraint.
questions.a: Criterion: the buzzer sounds every time the door opens. Constraint: must use only batteries and household materials.

days.guide: Build the alarm: a foil switch that closes when the door opens (or a clothespin with foil on its jaws, held apart by a cardboard tab tied to the door).

questions.q: What energy conversion happens in your alarm?
questions.a: Stored chemical energy in the battery → electrical → sound (buzzer) or light (LED).

days.guide: Test 5 times; record results and fix a failure point.

questions.q: Why test more than once?
questions.a: To find whether the alarm works reliably and to identify failure points.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test.

questions.q: Name a material that conducts electricity.
questions.a: Copper (any metal, foil).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test key: 1) Conductors: metals; insulators: plastic, rubber, wood 2) A complete circuit is needed for current 3) Switch opens/closes the circuit 4) Series vs. parallel 5) Heat flows from warm to cool 6) Toaster: electrical → heat 7) Sound: produced by vibrations 8) Energy can be transferred by sound, light, heat and electric currents. Prototype rubric: 4 = works in 5/5 trials, data recorded, one improvement documented; 3 = works 3-4/5; 2 = partially works; 1 = not built.

weeks.prep: Jump rope or slinky, a tub of water, a cork or small floating toy, ruler. Bookmark PhET 'Wave on a String.' Vocabulary: crest (top), trough (bottom), amplitude (height from rest to crest), wavelength (distance crest to crest).
misconceptions: Thinking water in a wave travels along with the wave. The water mostly moves up and down; the wave (energy) moves forward.
Measuring amplitude from trough to crest. Amplitude is from the resting line to the crest.

days.guide: Tie one end of the rope; shake it gently, then harder, then faster.

questions.q: What changed when you shook harder?
questions.a: The waves got taller — greater amplitude.

questions.q: What changed when you shook faster?
questions.a: The waves got closer together — shorter wavelength.

days.guide: Float a cork in the tub and make waves at one end; watch the cork.

questions.q: Does the cork move along with the wave?
questions.a: No — it bobs up and down in mostly the same place as the wave passes.

days.guide: The child draws waves with large/small amplitude and long/short wavelength and labels crest, trough, amplitude, wavelength.

questions.q: How do you measure wavelength?
questions.a: From one crest to the next crest (or trough to trough).

days.guide: In the simulation, change amplitude and frequency and record observations.

questions.q: What happens to wavelength when frequency increases?
questions.a: Wavelength gets shorter.

days.guide: Give the labeling quiz.

questions.q: What is the bottom of a wave called?
questions.a: The trough.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: label crest (high point), trough (low point), amplitude (rest line to crest), wavelength (crest to crest); bigger shake → bigger amplitude; faster shake → shorter wavelength; water moves up and down while energy moves forward. Diagram rubric: all four parts correctly labeled = proficient.

weeks.prep: Tub of water, sand, pebbles, a small toy boat or plastic block, ruler. Video on California surf/tsunamis (e.g., NOAA or USGS educational clips).
misconceptions: Thinking waves carry water across the ocean. Waves carry energy; near shore that energy moves sand and objects.
Thinking only big waves move things. All waves transfer energy; bigger amplitude transfers more.

days.guide: Make small and large waves toward a floating toy; measure how far it moves.

questions.q: Which waves moved the boat farther?
questions.a: Larger-amplitude waves — they carry more energy.

days.guide: Build a sloped sand beach in the tub and make waves for 2 minutes.

questions.q: What happened to the sand?
questions.a: Waves moved sand down the slope and along the beach — the shape of the beach changed.

days.guide: Watch the video and list how waves carry energy.

questions.q: Why can a tsunami cause damage far inland?
questions.a: It carries a huge amount of energy and a large volume of water, so it rushes far inland when it reaches shore.

days.guide: Stretch the slinky and push one end to send a pulse (compression wave). Connect to sound.

questions.q: How is a slinky pulse like sound?
questions.a: Sound is also a wave — vibrations pass along through air (or other matter) without the air itself traveling to your ear.

days.guide: The child writes a CER on how waves cause objects to move.

questions.q: Write the claim.
questions.a: Waves transfer energy that can move objects; bigger waves move them more.

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric: 4 = claim that waves carry energy which moves objects; evidence from the boat measurements and sand beach; reasoning connecting amplitude to energy; 3 = claim and evidence, weak reasoning; 2 = observation only; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Flashlight, Morse code chart (A .-, B -..., C -.-., E ., H ...., I .., L .-.., O ---, S ..., T -), grid paper for pixel pictures, a drum or pot.
misconceptions: Thinking codes only work if long. A code works if sender and receiver agree on the pattern.
Speed over accuracy. A fast code with errors doesn't transfer information well.

days.guide: Teach a few Morse letters; send short words with the flashlight (short flash = dot, long = dash).

questions.q: What is SOS in Morse code?
questions.a: ... --- ... (three short, three long, three short).

days.guide: The child colors a simple picture on an 8×8 grid and writes each row as 1s (filled) and 0s (empty); you decode it.

questions.q: Decode the row 00111100.
questions.a: Two empty squares, four filled, two empty.

days.guide: Invent a drum code for 10 words; send 3 messages to someone in another room.

questions.q: What must both people have to use the code?
questions.a: The same code key (agreed patterns).

days.guide: Compare which code was fastest and most accurate and why.

questions.q: Why might binary be accurate?
questions.a: It has only two symbols (1 and 0), so there are fewer ways to misread it.

days.guide: The child writes a paragraph about how patterns transfer information.

questions.q: How do computers and phones send information?
questions.a: They turn information into patterns of digital signals (1s and 0s) sent by electricity, light or radio waves.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = explains that information can be turned into patterns (flashes, beats, 1s and 0s), compares speed and accuracy of at least two codes with evidence, connects to modern technology; 3 = compares codes with little evidence; 2 = describes one code; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Flashlight, string and cups, paper, poster board for signs. Unit 3 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Picking a solution without testing. Engineers test each option against the criteria.
Changing many things at once in an improvement. Change one thing so you know what helped.

days.guide: State the challenge: send a 5-word message across the yard without speaking. Define criteria (accuracy, speed) and constraints.

questions.q: What are the criteria?
questions.a: The message arrives correctly (accurate) and quickly.

days.guide: Brainstorm 3 solutions (flashlight Morse, picture signs, hand signals) with pros and cons.

questions.q: What is a con of flashlight Morse in daytime?
questions.a: The light may be hard to see in bright sunlight.

days.guide: Test each solution; record time and number of errors.

questions.q: How do you measure accuracy?
questions.a: Count correctly received words out of 5.

days.guide: Improve the most accurate solution to be faster and retest twice.

questions.q: What is one way to speed up a code?
questions.a: Use shorter signals for common words, or abbreviations.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test.

questions.q: Label a wave's amplitude.
questions.a: Distance from the resting line to the crest.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test key: 1) crest/trough/amplitude/wavelength labeled 2) bigger amplitude = more energy 3) water moves up and down, not along 4) waves can move sand and objects 5) sound travels as waves 6) a code is a pattern for sending information 7) SOS = ... --- ... 8) compare two codes for speed and accuracy. Design comparison rubric: 4 = three solutions tested with data on time and accuracy, best chosen and improved with retest data; 3 = data incomplete; 2 = no testing data; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Flashlight, 3 index cards with a hole punched in the same spot, clay to stand them, 2 small mirrors, a milk/juice carton, tape, foil, white and black paper. Safety: never shine light or point mirrors at eyes.
misconceptions: Thinking light travels around corners on its own. It travels in straight lines until it hits something and reflects.
Thinking only mirrors reflect light. All objects we see reflect some light; mirrors and shiny surfaces reflect it in one direction.

days.guide: Stand cards in clay in a line so holes align; shine light through. Then move the middle card.

questions.q: Why does the light stop reaching the wall when one card is moved?
questions.a: Light travels in straight lines; when the holes don't line up, the card blocks it.

days.guide: Use a mirror to bounce the flashlight beam to a target on the wall.

questions.q: What happens to light when it hits a mirror?
questions.a: It reflects (bounces off) at the same angle it hit.

days.guide: Build a periscope: mirrors at 45° at top and bottom of the carton, openings facing opposite ways.

questions.q: How does a periscope let you see over a wall?
questions.a: Light from the object reflects off the top mirror down to the bottom mirror and then into your eye.

days.guide: Shine light on foil, white paper and black paper; see how much bounces onto a nearby card.

questions.q: Which reflected the most light? The least?
questions.a: Foil (and white paper) reflected the most; black paper absorbed most of the light.

days.guide: The child draws ray diagrams with arrows for each setup.

questions.q: In a ray diagram, what do arrows show?
questions.a: The direction the light is traveling.

weeks.assessment_key: Ray diagram rubric: 4 = straight-line arrows from the source through aligned holes; arrows reflecting off the mirror; periscope path source → top mirror → bottom mirror → eye; 3 = one error; 2 = arrows missing or curved; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A shoebox with a lid, a small object, a flashlight, a diagram of the eye (cornea, pupil, iris, lens, retina, optic nerve), a hand mirror.
misconceptions: Thinking eyes send out rays to see. Light from a source reflects off objects and enters the eye.
Thinking we can see in total darkness after our eyes adjust. Without any light, nothing can reflect into the eye.

days.guide: Place an object in a closed shoebox; peek through a small eye hole — nothing is visible. Then open a light hole.

questions.q: Why could you see the object only after opening the light hole?
questions.a: Light entered, reflected off the object and traveled into your eye.

days.guide: Draw and label the eye: light passes through the cornea and pupil, the lens focuses it on the retina, the optic nerve carries signals to the brain.

questions.q: What does the retina do?
questions.a: Senses the light and sends signals through the optic nerve to the brain.

days.guide: In dim light, the child looks in a mirror; then turn on a bright light and watch the pupils.

questions.q: What happens to the pupil in bright light? Why?
questions.a: It gets smaller to let in less light and protect the eye; in dim light it gets larger.

days.guide: Draw the model: lamp → light ray to book → reflected ray to eye → brain.

questions.q: Is the book a light source?
questions.a: No — it reflects light from the lamp.

days.guide: The child explains in writing how light allows us to see.

questions.q: Explain how we see a red apple.
questions.a: Light from a source hits the apple, which reflects red light into our eyes; the eye sends signals to the brain, which makes sense of the image.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = model shows light from a source reflecting off an object into the eye with arrows in the correct direction, and the explanation mentions the brain; 3 = arrows correct, brain missing; 2 = arrows from eye to object; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Glass of water or prism, sunny window, 2 thermometers, black and white paper, a pizza box, foil, plastic wrap, black paper, chocolate or s'mores ingredients. Unit 4 test for Day 5. Safety: never look at the sun.
misconceptions: Thinking white light is one color. It contains all the colors of the rainbow.
Thinking black things are 'cold.' Black absorbs more light, which turns into heat.

days.guide: Place a glass of water on a sunny windowsill and find the rainbow on the floor or paper.

questions.q: Where do the rainbow colors come from?
questions.a: White sunlight is made of all colors; the water bends (refracts) each color a different amount, separating them.

questions.q: Name the colors in order.
questions.a: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

days.guide: Place thermometers under black and white paper in the sun; read every 5 minutes for 20 minutes.

questions.q: Which thermometer got warmer? Why?
questions.a: Under the black paper — black absorbs more light energy, which turns into heat; white reflects more.

days.guide: Build the solar oven: foil flap to reflect sunlight, black paper inside to absorb, plastic wrap window to trap heat.

questions.q: What does each part of the oven do?
questions.a: Foil reflects sunlight in; black paper absorbs it and heats up; plastic wrap traps warm air.

days.guide: Put chocolate in the oven in full sun; record temperature and melt time.

questions.q: What energy change happens in the solar oven?
questions.a: Light energy changes into heat energy.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test.

questions.q: How does light allow us to see?
questions.a: Light reflects off objects into our eyes.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test key: 1) Light travels in straight lines 2) Mirrors reflect light 3) We see when light reflects off objects into our eyes 4) Pupil shrinks in bright light 5) Black absorbs more light → warmer 6) White light contains all colors 7) Solar oven: foil reflects, black absorbs, plastic traps heat 8) Draw a seeing model with arrows source → object → eye. Proficient: 80%. Solar oven data: proficient includes temperature readings over time and a conclusion.

weeks.prep: Celery stalk with leaves, food coloring, clear cup, a few flowers (lilies or tulips have large parts), magnifying glass, plastic knife, a carrot with top and a clump of grass with roots.
misconceptions: Thinking plants get food from the soil. Roots take in water and minerals; leaves make food using sunlight.
Thinking all roots look the same. Taproots (carrot) store food and reach deep; fibrous roots (grass) spread out and hold soil.

days.guide: Put celery in colored water; after 24 hours cut across the stalk and look at colored dots.

questions.q: What do the colored dots in the celery show?
questions.a: The tubes (xylem) that carry water up from the roots to the leaves.

days.guide: Dissect a flower: count petals, find stamens (pollen) and the pistil.

questions.q: What is the job of the stamen and pistil?
questions.a: The stamen makes pollen; the pistil receives pollen and contains the ovary, where seeds form.

questions.q: Why are petals often brightly colored?
questions.a: To attract pollinators like bees and hummingbirds.

days.guide: Compare the carrot taproot and the grass's fibrous roots.

questions.q: How are the two root systems' functions different?
questions.a: The carrot's taproot reaches deep and stores food; grass's fibrous roots spread wide to absorb water near the surface and hold soil in place.

days.guide: Research a cactus and a coast redwood.

questions.q: How does a cactus survive in the desert?
questions.a: Thick stem stores water; spines (modified leaves) reduce water loss and protect; waxy skin; shallow, wide roots catch rain quickly.

questions.q: How do redwoods get water in summer?
questions.a: Their needles absorb moisture from coastal fog (and fog drip waters roots); thick bark protects them from fire.

days.guide: The child writes an argument (claim, evidence, reasoning) on how one plant structure supports survival.

questions.q: Give an example claim.
questions.a: A cactus's thick stem helps it survive drought because it stores water for dry months.

weeks.assessment_key: Argument rubric: 4 = clear claim about one structure's function, evidence from the week's labs or research, reasoning linking structure to survival/growth/reproduction; 3 = claim and evidence; 2 = description only; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Tweezers, spoons, clothespins, cups; seeds, rice, gummy worms; colored paper 'insects' (some matching lawn colors, some bright); egg carton and raw eggs (do the drop outside); pictures of a desert tortoise and a sea otter.
misconceptions: Thinking animals choose or grow structures because they need them. Structures are inherited traits that helped ancestors survive.
Thinking camouflage means being invisible. It means blending in so predators/prey notice it less.

days.guide: Each 'beak' tool gets 30 seconds to pick up each food; record counts.

questions.q: Which beak worked best for gummy worms? Seeds?
questions.a: Usually tweezers (like a long thin beak) for worms; clothespin or tweezers for seeds; use your data.

questions.q: How does a beak's shape relate to food?
questions.a: Different beak shapes are suited to different foods (e.g., a hummingbird's long beak reaches nectar).

days.guide: Scatter paper insects in the yard for 1 minute; count which you find first.

questions.q: Which colors were found first? Why?
questions.a: Bright colors that don't match the background; green/brown ones blended in (camouflage).

days.guide: Drop an egg in an egg-carton 'shell' and one without from the same height.

questions.q: What does this model about shells?
questions.a: A hard or cushioned outer structure protects soft body parts, like a turtle or tortoise shell.

days.guide: Research the desert tortoise and sea otter.

questions.q: How do a sea otter's external structures help it survive?
questions.a: Very dense fur traps air to keep it warm in cold ocean water (it has no blubber); webbed hind feet for swimming.

questions.q: How does a desert tortoise's structure help?
questions.a: A hard shell protects it, and strong front legs dig burrows to escape heat.

days.guide: The child writes a CER about one external structure.

questions.q: Give an example claim.
questions.a: A sea otter's dense fur helps it survive in cold water by keeping it warm.

weeks.assessment_key: Beak lab: data table with counts for each tool and food. CER rubric: 4 = claim about one external structure, evidence (lab data or research facts), reasoning on how it aids survival; 3 = weak reasoning; 2 = claim only; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Cleaned, boiled chicken bones (thigh, wing), a plastic bottle with bottom cut off, 2 small balloons, 1 large balloon, a straw, clay; a zip bag, crackers, water; a timer for pulse. Safety: wash hands after handling bones.
misconceptions: Thinking lungs pull air in by themselves. The diaphragm muscle moves down to make room, and air rushes in.
Thinking digestion only happens in the stomach. It starts in the mouth and continues in the intestines.

days.guide: Compare chicken bones with a human skeleton diagram: hollow bird bones vs. our bones.

questions.q: What are three jobs of the skeleton?
questions.a: Support the body, protect organs (skull protects brain, ribs protect heart/lungs), and help movement with muscles.

questions.q: Why are bird bones light/hollow?
questions.a: Lighter bones help birds fly.

days.guide: Build the lung model; pull the bottom balloon (diaphragm) down and watch inner balloons inflate.

questions.q: What happens when the diaphragm moves down?
questions.a: Space in the chest gets bigger and air rushes into the lungs.

days.guide: Measure pulse for 15 seconds × 4 at rest and after 1 minute of jumping jacks.

questions.q: Why does your heart beat faster after exercise?
questions.a: Muscles need more oxygen and energy, so the heart pumps blood faster to deliver it.

questions.q: What is the heart's job?
questions.a: Pumping blood carrying oxygen and nutrients through the body.

days.guide: Mash crackers with water in a zip bag to model chewing and stomach churning.

questions.q: What order does food travel through the digestive system?
questions.a: Mouth → esophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine.

days.guide: The child labels a diagram of brain, heart, lungs, stomach, intestines, skeleton and states each function.

questions.q: What is the brain's job?
questions.a: To control the body, process information from the senses and send signals for responses.

weeks.assessment_key: Diagram key: brain — controls body and processes senses; heart — pumps blood; lungs — take in oxygen, release carbon dioxide; stomach — breaks down food; small intestine — absorbs nutrients; large intestine — absorbs water; skeleton — support and protection; muscles — movement. Proficient: 7/8 correct labels and functions.

weeks.prep: A 30-cm ruler, blindfold, apple and raw potato cubes (peeled), spices, fabrics and textures (sandpaper, silk, felt, foil...). Unit 5 test for Day 5. Check food allergies before tasting.
misconceptions: Thinking the senses alone do the sensing and responding. Sense organs send signals to the brain, which processes them and sends signals to muscles to respond.
Thinking taste works alone. Much of 'flavor' comes from smell.

days.guide: Hold the ruler at 0 cm between the child's open fingers; drop without warning; record cm caught, 5 times.

questions.q: Describe the path of information in the ruler drop.
questions.a: Eyes see the ruler fall → signal to brain → brain sends signal to hand muscles → fingers close.

questions.q: A 15 cm catch is about how long a reaction?
questions.a: About 0.17 seconds (rough chart: 10 cm ≈ 0.14 s, 20 cm ≈ 0.20 s).

days.guide: Blindfolded and nose plugged, the child tastes apple and potato cubes and guesses; repeat unplugged.

questions.q: Why is it hard to tell apple from potato with your nose plugged?
questions.a: Flavor depends on smell; without it the tongue only senses basic tastes and texture, which are similar.

days.guide: Identify 8 textures blindfolded; record which were hardest.

questions.q: What senses touch?
questions.a: Receptors (nerve endings) in the skin, which send signals to the brain.

days.guide: Research owls, bats and sharks.

questions.q: How do bats find food in the dark?
questions.a: Echolocation — they make high sounds and listen to the echoes.

questions.q: What special sense do sharks have?
questions.a: They can sense tiny electric fields from prey (and have a strong sense of smell).

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test and have the child draw a sense → brain → response model.

questions.q: Draw the model for touching a hot pan.
questions.a: Skin senses heat → nerves carry signal to brain/spinal cord → signal to arm muscles → hand pulls away.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test key: 1) Plant structures: roots absorb water, stem supports and transports, leaves make food, flowers reproduce 2) Celery shows water transport 3) Camouflage helps animals hide 4) Beak shape matches food 5) Lungs/diaphragm breathing 6) Heart pumps blood; pulse rises with exercise 7) Senses send information to the brain 8) Brain processes and sends signals to muscles 9) Echolocation in bats 10) Model: stimulus → sense organ → brain → response. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: Sugar cubes, a jar with lid, sidewalk chalk, white vinegar, cups, plastic straws and clay, freezer, a variety of rocks. List 10 weathering examples for the quiz (key below).
misconceptions: Confusing weathering and erosion. Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion moves the pieces away.
Thinking weathering is always fast. Most weathering takes years to thousands of years; our models speed it up.

days.guide: Shake sugar cubes for 1, 2 and 3 minutes, comparing shapes after each.

questions.q: What happened to the cubes' corners? What does this model?
questions.a: They wore down and became rounded — physical weathering, like rocks tumbling in a stream.

days.guide: Put chalk in vinegar and in water overnight; compare.

questions.q: What happened to the chalk in vinegar? Why?
questions.a: It fizzed and dissolved/broke down — the acid reacted with the chalk (chemical weathering, like acid rain on limestone).

questions.q: Why use water as a comparison?
questions.a: It is the control, showing the vinegar caused the change.

days.guide: Fill a straw with water, seal both ends with clay and freeze overnight.

questions.q: What happened to the clay plugs? Why?
questions.a: They were pushed out because water expands when it freezes — frost wedging cracks rocks the same way.

days.guide: Walk the neighborhood looking for roots cracking sidewalks and lichen on rocks.

questions.q: How do roots weather rock?
questions.a: Roots grow into cracks and widen them as they grow (physical weathering).

days.guide: Give the sorting quiz.

questions.q: Is rust on a rock physical or chemical weathering?
questions.a: Chemical — iron reacts with oxygen and water.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key — Physical: 1) ice wedging 2) roots cracking rock 3) rocks tumbling in a river 4) wind-blown sand scraping rock 5) waves pounding cliffs 6) animals burrowing. Chemical: 7) acid rain dissolving limestone 8) rust forming on iron-rich rock 9) vinegar fizzing on chalk 10) cave formation by acidic water dissolving limestone. Proficient: 8/10.

weeks.prep: Baking pan or plastic bin, sand and soil, a water bottle with holes in the cap, books to prop the pan, straws, ice cubes with sand frozen into the bottom, clay. Do this outside or on a towel.
misconceptions: Thinking erosion only happens from rivers. Wind, ice (glaciers), gravity and waves also erode.
Forgetting deposition. Eroded material is dropped somewhere else (deltas, beaches, dunes).

days.guide: Make a sand slope in the pan; pour water slowly from the top.

questions.q: Where did the sand go?
questions.a: It was carried downhill (erosion) and dropped at the bottom where the water slowed (deposition), forming a fan or delta.

days.guide: Test 3 slopes (1, 2, 3 books); collect and compare sediment moved.

questions.q: How did slope affect erosion?
questions.a: Steeper slopes moved more sediment because the water flowed faster.

days.guide: Blow through a straw at a sand pile from a fixed distance; measure distance moved.

questions.q: How is this like desert sand dunes?
questions.a: Wind picks up and moves sand, piling it into dunes.

days.guide: Drag a sandy ice cube across flat clay.

questions.q: What did the ice cube leave behind?
questions.a: Scratches and grooves — glaciers carry rocks that scrape bedrock, as seen in Yosemite.

days.guide: The child writes a CER comparing water, wind and ice erosion in the models using measurements.

questions.q: Which agent eroded most in your model?
questions.a: Usually water on the steepest slope; answer must cite the child's own measurements.

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric: 4 = claim ranking water, wind and ice erosion in the models; evidence with specific measurements (sediment amount, distance); reasoning about speed of water/wind and weight of ice; notes that real glaciers work slowly but carve deeply; 3 = claim with partial data; 2 = no measurements; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Clear jar with lid, sand, soil, gravel, water; shells and leaves; clay; white glue or plaster of Paris. Photo of Grand Canyon rock layers. (Painted Cave in Santa Barbara has Chumash rock paintings, not fossils; a California fossil site such as the La Brea Tar Pits works well as a second photo.)
misconceptions: Thinking the top layer is oldest. In undisturbed layers the bottom is oldest (law of superposition).
Thinking fossils are the actual animals. Most fossils are imprints, casts or minerals that replaced the original material.

days.guide: Shake sediments with water in a jar; let settle overnight.

questions.q: Which material settled first and why?
questions.a: Gravel settled first at the bottom (heaviest/largest), then sand, then fine soil on top.

days.guide: Order 6 layer drawings from oldest to youngest.

questions.q: In a stack of rock layers, which is oldest?
questions.a: The bottom layer, because it was deposited first (superposition).

days.guide: Press shells/leaves into clay for imprints; fill one with glue or plaster for a cast.

questions.q: What is the difference between a mold and a cast?
questions.a: A mold is the hollow imprint; a cast forms when the mold is filled and hardens into the shape of the organism.

days.guide: Analyze the Grand Canyon photo; infer past environments.

questions.q: What does a fish or shell fossil in a desert canyon tell us?
questions.a: The area was once covered by water (an ocean or lake).

questions.q: What do you infer from a layer with fern fossils?
questions.a: The area was once a warm, wet environment where ferns grew.

days.guide: The child explains changes in a landscape over time using layers.

questions.q: Explain how a canyon with layers formed.
questions.a: Layers of sediment were deposited over long periods (oldest at bottom); later a river eroded down through them, exposing the layers.

weeks.assessment_key: Explanation rubric: 4 = uses superposition (bottom oldest), fossils as evidence of past environments (e.g., marine fossils = once under water), and erosion exposing layers; 3 = two of these; 2 = one; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Photos of Yosemite Valley (U-shaped valley, Half Dome, El Capitan), coastal cliffs at Pacifica and Big Sur, a sea arch (e.g., Natural Bridges State Beach in Santa Cruz). Sugar cubes, a tray, water. Unit 6 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking a river alone carved Yosemite Valley. The Merced River started it, but glaciers widened and deepened it into a U shape.
Thinking coastal erosion happens evenly. Weaker rock erodes faster, forming caves, arches and stacks.

days.guide: Read about Yosemite's glaciers.

questions.q: What shape does a glacier carve a valley into?
questions.a: A U shape (rivers usually carve V shapes).

questions.q: What evidence of glaciers can be seen in Yosemite?
questions.a: U-shaped valley, polished granite, hanging valleys with waterfalls (like Bridalveil Fall), and large boulders moved by ice (erratics).

days.guide: Look at Pacifica and Big Sur photos; list agents of erosion.

questions.q: What causes coastal cliffs at Pacifica to erode?
questions.a: Waves pounding the base, storms, rain and runoff, and landslides/gravity; houses near the edge are at risk.

days.guide: Line sugar cubes as a headland; squirt water at a weak spot to make a cave, then an arch.

questions.q: How does a sea arch form?
questions.a: Waves erode a cave into a weak part of a headland; when the cave cuts all the way through, it becomes an arch. When the top collapses, a sea stack remains.

days.guide: The child sketches a before/after landscape with an explanation.

questions.q: What should the explanation include?
questions.a: Which agent (water, wind, ice, gravity) changed the land and about how long it took.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test.

questions.q: Weathering or erosion: a river carrying sand to the ocean.
questions.a: Erosion (and deposition at the ocean).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test key: 1) Weathering breaks down; erosion moves 2) Physical example: ice wedging; chemical: acid dissolving limestone 3) Steeper slope → more erosion 4) Wind forms dunes 5) Glaciers carve U-shaped valleys (Yosemite) 6) Bottom rock layer is oldest 7) Marine fossils on land show it was once under water 8) Sea arches form from wave erosion of caves 9) Deposition forms deltas/beaches 10) Before/after sketch explained. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: Modeling clay, dental floss or string to slice, a ruler, a marker, paper. Printed topographic map of Half Dome (USGS or nps.gov), an ocean floor map, a world map.
misconceptions: Thinking contour lines show roads or paths. Each line connects points of equal elevation.
Thinking widely spaced lines mean steep. Close lines = steep; far apart = gentle.

days.guide: Build a clay mountain; mark heights every 1 cm with a ruler; slice horizontally and trace each slice on paper.

questions.q: What does each traced line represent?
questions.a: All points at the same elevation (a contour line).

days.guide: Find the steepest side of Half Dome on the topo map.

questions.q: How can you tell which side is steepest?
questions.a: Where contour lines are closest together — Half Dome's sheer northwest face.

days.guide: Read the ocean floor map; find trenches and ridges.

questions.q: What is an ocean trench?
questions.a: A long, very deep, narrow valley in the ocean floor (e.g., the Mariana Trench, the deepest).

questions.q: What is a mid-ocean ridge?
questions.a: An underwater mountain chain, such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

days.guide: Mark the Sierra Nevada, Andes, Rockies and Himalayas on the world map.

questions.q: What pattern do you notice?
questions.a: The Sierra Nevada, Andes and Rockies run along western edges of the Americas near the Pacific; the Himalayas are inland, where India meets Asia.

days.guide: Give the map quiz.

questions.q: Contour interval is 100 ft. A hill has 5 lines above the 0 ft line. About how tall is it?
questions.a: About 500 ft (at least 500 ft).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Contour lines connect equal elevations 2) Close lines = steep 3) Far apart = gentle 4) Circles inside circles = hill/peak 5) Find elevation by counting lines × interval 6) Trench = deep underwater valley 7) Ridge = underwater mountain range 8) Many mountain ranges lie near coasts/plate edges. Proficient: 7/8.

weeks.prep: World map, red and orange dot stickers, USGS 'Latest Earthquakes' map (earthquake.usgs.gov), a list of active volcanoes (USGS/Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program).
misconceptions: Thinking earthquakes happen randomly everywhere. Most occur in belts along plate boundaries.
Thinking California has only earthquakes, not volcanoes. Mount Shasta and Lassen Peak are active Cascade volcanoes (Lassen last erupted 1914-1917).

days.guide: Filter the USGS map to M4.5+ for the past week; plot 20 quakes.

questions.q: Where did most quakes cluster?
questions.a: Around the edges of the Pacific Ocean (and other plate boundaries), not randomly.

days.guide: Plot 15 active volcanoes including Mount Shasta and Lassen Peak.

questions.q: When did Lassen Peak last erupt?

days.guide: Describe the Ring of Fire pattern.

questions.q: What is the Ring of Fire?
questions.a: A horseshoe-shaped belt of earthquakes and volcanoes around the edges of the Pacific Ocean.

days.guide: Locate the San Andreas Fault (about 750-800 miles long) and explain why California has earthquakes.

questions.q: Why does California have many earthquakes?
questions.a: The Pacific Plate and North American Plate slide past each other along the San Andreas Fault; when stuck rock suddenly slips, an earthquake occurs.

days.guide: The child writes a paragraph explaining the patterns on the map.

questions.q: What is the main pattern?
questions.a: Earthquakes, volcanoes and many mountain ranges occur together in belts, especially around the Pacific (Ring of Fire), along plate boundaries.

weeks.assessment_key: Map analysis rubric: 4 = map with 20 quakes and 15 volcanoes plotted accurately; paragraph identifies the Ring of Fire, notes that quakes, volcanoes and mountains occur together along boundaries, and explains California's San Andreas Fault; 3 = pattern described without explanation; 2 = map only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Toothpicks, mini marshmallows, a 9×13 pan of firm gelatin (make the day before), rubber bands or marbles and cardboard for base isolation, timer. Family earthquake kit list (Ready.gov / earthquakecountry.org). Great ShakeOut is held each October.
misconceptions: Thinking taller is always weaker. Design (bracing, base isolation) matters more than height alone.
Thinking you should run outside during an earthquake. Drop, Cover and Hold On where you are.

days.guide: Build a 2-story toothpick building; shake the gelatin pan the same way each time.

questions.q: Why use the same shake each time?
questions.a: So the test is fair; only the building design changes.

days.guide: Add diagonal cross-braces; retest and count seconds until collapse.

questions.q: Why do triangles (cross-bracing) help?
questions.a: Triangles are rigid shapes that keep the frame from swaying and collapsing.

days.guide: Build a base-isolation version (building on a cardboard base sitting on marbles); compare shaking.

questions.q: How does base isolation protect a building?
questions.a: The base moves with the ground while the building on top shakes less, because the rollers/pads separate it from ground motion.

days.guide: Plan a family earthquake kit and practice Drop, Cover and Hold On.

questions.q: What are the three steps?
questions.a: Drop to hands and knees, Cover your head and neck (under a sturdy table), Hold On until shaking stops.

questions.q: Name four items for an earthquake kit.
questions.a: Water (1 gallon per person per day), food, flashlight, batteries, first aid kit, whistle, medicines, copies of documents.

days.guide: The child writes a comparison of bracing and base isolation using data, cost and materials.

questions.q: Which solution is cheaper for a small house?
questions.a: Cross-bracing is usually cheaper and simpler; base isolation costs more and is used for large important buildings (hospitals, city halls).

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison rubric: 4 = data from both tests (seconds standing, amount of sway), comparison of cost/materials, recommendation with reasons; 3 = data for both, weak recommendation; 2 = one design tested; 1 = incomplete. Kit plan: includes water, food, flashlight, first aid, and meeting place.

weeks.prep: Tub, sand, water, craft sticks, clay, small plants or toothpicks, a NOAA tsunami page (tsunami.gov) and a photo of a California 'Tsunami Hazard Zone' sign. Unit 7 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking engineering can eliminate hazards. Solutions reduce impacts; they can't stop natural events.
Thinking a tsunami is one big wave. It is a series of waves; the first may not be the largest.

days.guide: Build a sand shore with toy houses; make a big wave with a board; then test a craft-stick sea wall.

questions.q: Did the sea wall reduce damage? What are its trade-offs?
questions.a: Usually yes for small waves; trade-offs: cost, blocked beach access, and very large waves can still overtop it.

days.guide: Model a hillside; pour water to cause a slide; then add plant roots/stakes and retest.

questions.q: Why do plants reduce landslides?
questions.a: Roots hold soil together and absorb water.

days.guide: Build a sand river and a clay/sand levee; pour a flood.

questions.q: Which held better, clay or sand?
questions.a: Usually clay — it absorbs less water and resists erosion; use your data.

days.guide: Read about the NOAA tsunami warning system and evacuation signs.

questions.q: If you feel a strong earthquake at the beach, what should you do?
questions.a: Move quickly inland or to high ground right away; don't wait for an official warning.

questions.q: How do tsunami warnings work?
questions.a: Sensors (seismometers and deep-ocean buoys) detect earthquakes and wave changes; warning centers send alerts to coastal areas.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test.

questions.q: On a topo map, what do close lines mean?
questions.a: Steep slope.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test key: 1) Contour lines and steepness 2) Trench and ridge definitions 3) Ring of Fire pattern 4) San Andreas Fault — plates slide past each other 5) Cross-bracing vs. base isolation compared 6) Drop, Cover, Hold On 7) Sea walls reduce wave damage but have trade-offs 8) Plants reduce landslides 9) Levees hold back floods 10) Warning systems save lives. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: 12 resource picture cards (sun, wind, water, trees, soil, coal, oil, natural gas, uranium, copper, geothermal heat, plants for biofuel), a family energy bill, a pie chart of California's electricity sources (California Energy Commission 'Total System Electric Generation').
misconceptions: Thinking all renewable resources are unlimited. Renewable means replaced naturally in a human lifetime; trees and water can still be overused.
Thinking fossil fuels come from dinosaurs. Most come from ancient plants (coal) and tiny ocean organisms (oil and gas).

days.guide: Sort the 12 cards.

questions.q: Is natural gas renewable?
questions.a: No — it takes millions of years to form.

questions.q: Is wind renewable?
questions.a: Yes — it is constantly replenished.

days.guide: Read how fossil fuels formed and draw 3 steps.

questions.q: What are the 3 steps of fossil fuel formation?
questions.a: 1) Ancient plants and tiny sea organisms died; 2) they were buried under layers of sediment; 3) over millions of years heat and pressure turned them into coal, oil and natural gas.

days.guide: Read the energy bill; find kilowatt-hours used and sources if listed.

questions.q: What unit measures electricity use on a bill?
questions.a: Kilowatt-hours (kWh).

days.guide: Read California's electricity pie chart and list the top three sources.

questions.q: What are the largest sources?
questions.a: Answer from your chart; in recent California Energy Commission data, natural gas has been the largest single source, followed by solar, with wind, large hydro and nuclear next.

days.guide: Give the resource quiz.

questions.q: Name a use of oil.
questions.a: Gasoline for cars (also plastics, heating).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Renewable — sunlight (solar power), wind (turbines), moving water (hydroelectric), geothermal heat, trees (wood/paper, if replanted), biofuel plants. Nonrenewable — coal (electricity), oil (gasoline, plastics), natural gas (electricity, heating, cooking), uranium (nuclear power), copper (wires). Proficient: 10/12 classified and used correctly.

weeks.prep: Paper/cardstock for a pinwheel, a pencil, straw, thread, paper clip, a fan; a plastic plate, small cups, tape, a skewer for a water wheel; two identical containers (one painted black or wrapped in black paper), thermometer.
misconceptions: Thinking one energy source is best everywhere. Each depends on local conditions (sun, wind, rivers).
Forgetting reliability. Solar doesn't work at night; wind varies; storage or backup is needed.

days.guide: Build a pinwheel on a straw axle with thread wound around it; use the fan to lift a paper clip.

questions.q: What energy conversion happens?
questions.a: Wind (motion energy of air) → turning motion of the pinwheel → lifting the paper clip.

days.guide: Build a water wheel; pour water to turn it.

questions.q: How does a hydroelectric dam use this idea?
questions.a: Falling water turns turbines connected to generators that make electricity.

days.guide: Place water in the black container in sun and shade; record temperature every 10 minutes for 40 minutes.

questions.q: What did the data show?
questions.a: The container in the sun warmed more — sunlight energy is absorbed and turned to heat.

days.guide: Make a chart comparing wind, water and solar models by output, reliability and needs.

questions.q: Which needs the most specific location?
questions.a: Hydroelectric — it needs a river or falling water.

days.guide: The child writes which source fits California best and why.

questions.q: Give a good reason for solar in California.
questions.a: California has many sunny days, especially in the Central Valley and deserts, so solar panels produce a lot of electricity.

weeks.assessment_key: Chart: proficient compares all three on output, reliability (e.g., solar only in daytime) and needs. Explanation rubric: 4 = clear choice, 2+ reasons using California conditions (sunshine, windy passes like Altamont, rivers and dams) and at least one drawback; 3 = choice with one reason; 2 = vague; 1 = no choice.

weeks.prep: Pan of water, vegetable oil, feathers, cotton balls, sponges, spoons, dish soap; chocolate chip cookies and toothpicks; index cards, petroleum jelly, magnifying glass.
misconceptions: Thinking renewable sources have no environmental effects. Wind farms affect birds, dams change rivers and fish habitat, solar farms use land.
Thinking oil spills are easy to clean. Even with tools, much oil remains.

days.guide: Make an 'ocean' with a small oil spill; test cotton, sponge, spoon and soap.

questions.q: What happened to the feather dipped in oil?
questions.a: It became matted and heavy — birds with oily feathers can't fly or stay warm.

questions.q: Which cleanup worked best?
questions.a: Answer from data; usually absorbents (cotton/sponge) collect surface oil, but none removed all of it.

days.guide: Extract chips from a cookie with toothpicks; observe damage.

questions.q: What does the broken cookie model?
questions.a: Mining disturbs and damages land and habitats even when you carefully remove resources.

days.guide: Place jelly-coated cards near a road and in the yard for 3 days; compare particles.

questions.q: Which card collected more particles? Why?
questions.a: Usually the one near the road — car exhaust and dust add particles to the air.

days.guide: Rank 4 sources by cost, pollution, reliability and land use.

questions.q: What is a trade-off of natural gas?
questions.a: It is reliable and available day or night, but burning it releases carbon dioxide and air pollution.

days.guide: The child writes how one energy source affects the environment.

questions.q: Give an example of an environmental effect of a dam.
questions.a: It blocks salmon migration and floods valleys to make reservoirs.

weeks.assessment_key: Writing rubric: 4 = names one source, explains at least two environmental effects accurately (e.g., oil: spills, air pollution), connects to evidence from a model, mentions a way to reduce impacts; 3 = one effect explained; 2 = vague; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Library books and websites (California Energy Commission, U.S. Energy Information Administration kids' site 'EIA Energy Kids'), poster board. Facts: Diablo Canyon is California's last operating nuclear plant (near San Luis Obispo); Altamont Pass has one of the earliest large U.S. wind farms; Hoover Dam on the Colorado River supplies hydroelectric power to Southern California; Kern County is California's main oil-producing county. Unit 8 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Listing only pros or only cons. Every source has trade-offs.
Copying text onto the poster. Use diagrams and short phrases.

days.guide: The child chooses one California energy source and writes 3 research questions.

questions.q: Give a good research question.
questions.a: Example: 'How does Altamont Pass wind farm turn wind into electricity, and what are its effects on birds?'

days.guide: The child takes notes from two sources on how energy is made, resource origin and effects.

questions.q: How does a nuclear plant make electricity?
questions.a: Splitting uranium atoms releases heat that boils water into steam, which spins turbines connected to generators.

days.guide: Create the poster: labeled diagram from resource to electricity and a pros/cons chart.

questions.q: What steps are common to most power plants?
questions.a: An energy source turns a turbine; the turbine spins a generator that makes electricity sent over power lines.

days.guide: The child presents in 3 minutes and answers trade-off questions.

questions.q: What is a con of solar farms?
questions.a: They need a lot of land and produce power only when the sun shines.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test.

questions.q: Is uranium renewable?
questions.a: No — it is a mined, nonrenewable resource.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test key: 1) Renewable vs. nonrenewable definitions 2) Classify: solar R, wind R, coal N, oil N, natural gas N, uranium N, hydro R 3) Fossil fuels formed from ancient organisms over millions of years 4) Turbines + generators make electricity 5) One environmental effect each of oil, dams, wind 6) Top California sources from the chart 7) Trade-off explained. Poster rubric: 4 = accurate diagram of resource → electricity, balanced pros/cons, clear 3-minute presentation, accurate answers; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = inaccurate or one-sided; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Box fan, science notebook, photos/diagrams of historic windmills and modern turbines (EIA Energy Kids). Read the challenge yourself first: lift 10 pennies 30 cm using only wind from the fan.
misconceptions: Writing criteria that can't be measured ('works well'). Use numbers: lifts 10 pennies 30 cm in under 60 seconds.
Treating constraints as optional. They are limits the design must follow.

days.guide: Read the challenge and have the child restate it in their own words.

questions.q: Restate the challenge.
questions.a: Build a device that uses wind from a fan to turn something and wind up a string to lift 10 pennies 30 cm.

days.guide: List measurable criteria in a table.

questions.q: Give three measurable criteria.
questions.a: Lifts at least 10 pennies; lifts them 30 cm; does so within a set time (e.g., 60 seconds).

days.guide: List constraints.

questions.q: What are the constraints?
questions.a: Only household materials listed, 3 days of building, no batteries (wind only).

days.guide: Study windmill and turbine photos; note how blades and axles convert wind to rotation.

questions.q: Why are turbine blades angled?
questions.a: Angled blades catch the wind so it pushes them sideways, making them rotate.

days.guide: The child writes a one-page design brief with a first sketch.

questions.q: What goes in a design brief?
questions.a: The problem, criteria, constraints and an initial idea/sketch.

weeks.assessment_key: Design brief rubric: 4 = problem clearly stated, 3+ measurable criteria, all constraints, labeled first sketch showing blades, axle, string and cup; 3 = criteria partly measurable; 2 = missing criteria or constraints; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Paper, ruler, colored pencils; straws, skewers, cardstock for blade tests; box fan; timer.
misconceptions: Judging ideas during brainstorming. First generate many ideas, then evaluate.
Choosing the 'coolest' design instead of the one that best meets criteria. Use the decision matrix.

days.guide: Brainstorm at least 5 blade and axle ideas, sketching quickly without judging.

questions.q: Why brainstorm without judging?
questions.a: So more ideas come out; a strange idea might lead to a good one.

days.guide: Test flat, angled and cupped blades on a straw axle; count rotations in 10 seconds.

questions.q: Which blade shape spun fastest?
questions.a: Answer from data; angled or cupped blades usually turn faster than flat blades facing straight into the wind.

days.guide: Draw three full designs with labels and energy flow.

questions.q: Describe the energy changes in your design.
questions.a: Wind (moving air) → blades rotate → axle turns and winds string → pennies are lifted (stored energy from height).

days.guide: Score each design 1-3 on each criterion and constraint in a matrix.

questions.q: How does a decision matrix help?
questions.a: It compares designs fairly on the same criteria using scores.

days.guide: The child chooses one design and justifies it in a paragraph.

questions.q: What should the justification include?
questions.a: Matrix scores, test data (e.g., rotation counts), and how the design meets the criteria and constraints.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = matrix with 3 designs scored on all criteria/constraints, chosen design has the highest or well-justified score, paragraph cites blade-test data; 3 = matrix complete, weak justification; 2 = incomplete matrix; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: Cups, straws, skewers, cardstock, string, tape, 10 pennies, box fan, meter stick, stopwatch, phone camera.
misconceptions: Changing the fan distance or speed between trials. Keep conditions identical for a fair test.
Hiding failures. Failures show what to improve; record them.

days.guide: Build the base and axle from the chosen sketch.

questions.q: Why must the axle turn freely?
questions.a: Friction wastes energy; a smooth axle lets more wind energy go into lifting.

days.guide: Attach blades, string and penny cup; first trial run.

questions.q: What happened on the first run?
questions.a: Record actual results; common issues: string slips off axle, blades hit the base.

days.guide: Write the test plan: fan distance, fan speed and load constant.

questions.q: Name the variables kept the same.
questions.a: Fan distance, fan speed setting, number of pennies, string length.

days.guide: Run 5 trials; record lift height and time.

questions.q: How do you find the average time?
questions.a: Add the 5 times and divide by 5.

days.guide: Identify and sketch/photograph failure points.

questions.q: Give an example of a failure point and fix.
questions.a: Axle wobbles → add a second support or tape a straw bearing; blades slip → glue blades to a cork hub.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = test plan lists controlled variables; data table with 5 trials (height, time, average); at least two failure points identified with evidence and possible fixes; 3 = data complete, analysis weak; 2 = fewer than 5 trials; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Prototype and spare materials, graph paper, poster board or slides.
misconceptions: Changing several things at once in the redesign. Change one variable to know what caused the improvement.
Comparing single trials instead of averages.

days.guide: Change one variable to fix the biggest failure point.

questions.q: Why change only one variable?
questions.a: So you know that change caused any difference in results.

days.guide: Run 5 new trials under the same conditions.

questions.q: Why must conditions match the first tests?
questions.a: To compare fairly; otherwise you can't tell if the design change made the difference.

days.guide: Graph before-and-after averages; decide whether the change helped.

questions.q: If average lift time went from 40 s to 28 s, did it improve?
questions.a: Yes — it lifted 12 seconds faster on average.

days.guide: Present the device and data, explaining each energy conversion.

questions.q: Explain the energy conversions.
questions.a: Electrical energy runs the fan → moving air (wind) → rotating blades and axle → string winds → pennies gain height (stored energy).

days.guide: The child writes a reflection on what they'd change with more time.

questions.q: What makes a strong reflection?
questions.a: Specific next steps tied to data or failures observed.

weeks.assessment_key: Engineering rubric: 4 = one variable changed with reason; before/after data and graph of averages; correct conclusion; clear presentation of energy conversions; thoughtful reflection; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = no comparison data; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Science notebook, index cards, a ruler, a photo of California coastal cliffs; end-of-year assessment (key below).
misconceptions: Mixing units (e.g., calling erosion 'weathering'). Review vocabulary cards.
Memorizing without explaining. Practice explaining each idea in your own words with an example.

days.guide: The child makes concept-map flashcards for energy, collisions, circuits, waves and light and self-quizzes.

questions.q: What is the relationship between speed and energy?
questions.a: The faster an object moves, the more energy it has.

days.guide: Redo the ruler drop and explain the senses-brain-response model.

questions.q: Explain the model from memory.
questions.a: Sense organ detects a stimulus → nerves send a signal to the brain → brain processes and sends a signal to muscles → response.

days.guide: Explain the cliff photo using weathering, erosion and rock layer vocabulary.

questions.q: Which agent most likely shaped the cliffs?
questions.a: Waves eroding the base, with weathering (water, wind, plant roots) breaking the rock.

days.guide: Give the end-of-year assessment.

questions.q: How do we see objects?
questions.a: Light reflects off them into our eyes.

days.guide: The child presents three favorite investigations to family.

questions.q: What should each explanation include?
questions.a: The question, what was done, the results, and what it showed.

weeks.assessment_key: End-of-year key (sample): 1) faster = more energy 2) energy transfers in collisions and becomes sound/heat 3) complete circuit needed; metals conduct 4) heat moves warm → cool 5) label wave crest, trough, amplitude, wavelength 6) codes transfer information 7) light reflects into eyes 8) plant/animal structures support survival (example) 9) senses → brain → response 10) weathering vs. erosion 11) bottom rock layer oldest 12) Ring of Fire pattern 13) one hazard solution with trade-off 14) renewable vs. nonrenewable examples. Proficient: 80%.
